items.title: New Cortex XDR Integration with Claude Cowork Secures Desktop AI Agents
items.summary: AI agents working directly on the desktop offer new ways to automate complex tasks, yet they operate outside traditional endpoint controls and pose unacceptable risks to many security leaders. Today, we're announcing a new Cortex XDR integration with Claude Cowork to deliver visibility and threat detection for this new agentic workspace. Claude Cowork brings agentic capabilities directly to desktop applications as part of Claude Enterprise. Instead of responding to a single prompt, it plans and completes multi-step tasks by reading files, navigating applications and executing workflows. This work takes place inside a small, local virtual machine that is designed to act as a security boundary. However, this isolation also prevents the EDR agent from monitoring the agent’s activity. With this integration, XDR bridges that gap to deliver deep visibility and threat detection across local agentic workflows without compromising host security. Delivering Runtime Visibility and Threat Detection Inside the Virtual Machine With this new integration with Claude Cowork, we’re bringing XDR directly into the virtual machine using a lightweight sensor. XDR will extend runtime visibility into the agent’s actions, tracking accessed systems, file changes and executed commands while detecting and preventing malicious behavior in real time. Behind this protection, XDR brings together Unit 42 Threat intelligence and machine learning models trained on global telemetry to block zero day threats by default. To prevent alert fatigue, the sensor feeds virtual machine telemetry directly into XDR analytics, automatically correlating related events into unified incident stories. The Cortex platform will consolidate the agent’s activity from inside the virtual machine and tie it back to the desktop in a single view. This gives security teams complete context into agent’s actions alongside the rest of their endpoint data. Securing Every Agent on the Endpoint EDR coverage across all execution environments is a baseline requirement for enterprise security teams, but it’s no longer sufficient if it doesn’t secure AI agents. Just as we brought together XDR and Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security to protect both traditional system processes and AI agents with XDR One , through this integration with Claude Cowork we are once again expanding XDR to seamlessly monitor every agent on the endpoint. The integration will be available in private preview in the coming months. This integration builds on our broader work securing AI across the enterprise. Palo Alto Networks is a launch participant in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing , an initiative that gives a small group of organizations that build or maintain critical software early access to frontier AI capabilities for defensive cybersecurity. Earlier this year, we introduced Prisma AIRS Unified Data Protection for Claude to monitor prompts across Claude Code, Claude.ai, and Claude Cowork for data leaks and prompt injections. Now, with Cortex XDR extending into Claude Cowork, security teams can protect data in transit to Claude and monitor agent activity directly on the endpoint. items.title: That One Artifact: The video that mapped a murder
items.summary: By Chad Gish In this series, Chad Gish draws on more than two decades of digital investigative experience to examine cases that were solved, or dramatically advanced, by a single piece of digital evidence. Note: This series is based on real-world criminal investigations, and some content may be graphic or disturbing. In my That One Artifact series , I’m often asked what kind of digital evidence can change the direction of an investigation. Sometimes it’s a text message, a location point, or a search history. In this case, it was a video recorded on a suspect’s phone only a short time before a planned carjacking turned into a murder. Over the years, I’ve seen suspects create some of the strongest evidence against themselves without ever realizing it. This video did more than connect two people. It identified a second suspect, captured them discussing the plan, showed the weapon, and laid out how they intended to take the victim’s vehicle and get away. When you’re working through changing stories, deleted messages, and multiple devices, finding one artifact that maps out the plan in the suspects’ own words can change everything. A story that kept changing When officers arrived, they found the victim in the driver’s seat of his vehicle. The engine was still running, and the vehicle was in reverse. A woman at the scene said she knew the victim and had planned to meet him that night, but as investigators began asking questions, her story changed. In one version, she said she had been sitting in the passenger seat before going inside and hearing gunshots. In another, she said the victim had just arrived when the shots were fired. Investigators repeatedly asked whether anyone else had been there, but she kept insisting she was alone. We knew there was more to the story, but inconsistencies alone were not enough. We needed evidence that could tell us what happened before the victim arrived and whether another person had been involved. There were no other witnesses and no surveillance video. The phone held what the story left out The woman allowed investigators very limited access to her phone, but some messages from that evening appeared to have been deleted. After investigators obtained a search warrant, I conducted a full forensic examination of the phone. During that examination, I recovered a video recorded only a short time before the homicide. I still don’t know why the woman chose to record it. Whatever her reason, the video became the smoking gun in the case, capturing the suspects together as they discussed the plan that would soon cost a man his life. In the recording, the woman was with a second person she had never mentioned to investigators. The two talked about waiting for the victim, taking his vehicle, and how they would get away afterward. A handgun was visible and was handled as they talked. In just a few minutes of video, we could see the preparation, hear the intent, and begin to understand the role each suspect would play. Finding that video required a more traditional forensic review at the time. In a similar investigation today, Magnet Axiom’s Mobile View could help an examiner locate and review relevant media more efficiently. Mobile View presents the extracted device in a familiar phone-style layout, allowing an examiner, detective, or prosecutor to select the Photos app and review the recovered images and videos in a thumbnail view. From there, the media can be filtered, sorted, and previewed alongside details such as timestamps and available location information. Instead of working through the phone data only as rows of artifacts, the investigator can navigate the evidence much as they would use the device itself and quickly focus on the video that matters. That one video provided the breakthrough we needed. It also provided a map of the crime before it happened. Magnet Axiom Mobile View presents extracted mobile evidence in a familiar device layout, making it easy to open the Photos app, review media as thumbnails, and quickly locate and preview a case-relevant video. Identifying the second suspect The video immediately showed us that the woman had not been alone. The second suspect could clearly be heard discussing the victim and the planned carjacking shortly before the victim arrived. That gave investigators a way to identify the other person involved and a clear direction for the next phase of the case. Other digital evidence helped build out the timeline. Communications showed contact with the victim leading up to the homicide, and another conversation referenced the idea of “jacking” him. A later search also recovered firearms and additional evidence connected to the investigation. I also recovered iOS cached locations from the suspect’s phone, which helped corroborate the video evidence. The cached location data placed the device inside the residence at the time the video was created. Around the time of the murder, the data placed the device outside near the dumpster where the victim was shot. Shortly afterward, it showed the device moving back into the apartment. This created another digital trail that followed the suspect through the critical moments of the crime and supported the emerging timeline. In a similar case today, Magnet Axiom’s Route View could help investigators interpret this type of location evidence by plotting geolocation artifacts, including iOS cached locations, on a map in chronological order. Instead of reviewing individual latitude and longitude points in isolation, investigators can play back a device’s movement to see where it traveled, when it stopped, and how that movement fits within the case timeline. Investigators can view the route at different playback speeds, examine key locations along the way, and record the playback as a video to share with investigators and prosecutors or to help explain the evidence in court. Magnet Axiom Route View turns individual geolocation artifacts into an animated timeline, allowing investigators to play back and record the route a device traveled. Each piece was important, but the video from the phone gave the other evidence context. It showed us that the encounter was not random, while the cached locations helped confirm where the device was during the planning, the shooting, and the return to the apartment. Together, the evidence helped explain how the victim was brought to the location, what the suspects intended to take, and how they planned to get away. From evidence to leverage The video became important for another reason. It gave investigators leverage during later interviews. Both suspects could change their stories, minimize their involvement, or deny that there had ever been a plan. But they could not easily explain away a recording made in their own voices shortly before the victim was killed. Investigators were no longer asking questions based only on suspicion or one person’s changing account; the evidence showed the planning in real time. Investigators could use the video to challenge parts of each story that did not make sense and to show both suspects that they already knew far more about the crime. The evidence ultimately helped obtain confessions from both of them. The artifact that preserved the plan In digital forensics, we often find one artifact that changes the direction of an investigation. It might be a message that establishes contact, location data that places someone near a scene, or a search that helps show intent. In this case, one video provided the breakthrough. It identified both suspects, documented the original carjacking plan, showed the weapon, explained the setup and getaway, and preserved the moments leading up to a murder. The cached location evidence then helped place the device at key locations and complete the timeline. The suspects created that evidence themselves, likely never imagining how important it would become. The case began with a murder victim, a running vehicle, and a story that kept changing. The video provided a starting point. From there, the rest of the digital evidence helped build the timeline, identify the second suspect, and reveal how the plan unfolded. As the investigation came together, the motive behind the carjacking was revealed. The suspects simply wanted a vehicle so they could joyride through the city. That was it. A decision made for a few hours of joyriding cost one man his life and left two other young people facing the better part of their lives in prison. That one artifact did more than help solve the case. It preserved the suspects’ plan in their own words, while the cached locations helped confirm their movements through the critical moments that followed. Together, these artifacts gave investigators the leverage needed to uncover the truth and ultimately helped bring justice to the victim. About the author Chad Gish, Senior Principal Forensic Specialist at Magnet Forensics, is a retired police detective with more than 25 years of experience investigating homicides, mass casualty events, and crimes against children. He is a recognized expert in digital forensics, playing a key role in high-profile cases and the development of forensic labs and crime centers.

items.title: Beyond DKIM key rotation: understanding email replay attacks
items.summary: As the email administrator for your organization’s domain, you receive a Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) aggregate report showing email passing DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) verification as though it came from your domain, sent from IP addresses you don’t recognize to recipients you didn’t contact. To clear the issue, you rotate your DKIM key, confirm the new selector is live, and verify that your DMARC policy is already set to p=reject. Days later, you see that the same unfamiliar traffic is still authenticating as you. In this post, you learn why rotation alone can’t stop a DKIM replay attack, how to confirm that you’re looking at a replay rather than a legitimate relay or ordinary spoofing, and the DNS cleanup step that most rotation guidance leaves out. You also learn how you can use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to detect and respond to this activity faster. How DKIM replay works DKIM verifies one thing: that specific parts of a message didn’t change between the signer and the receiver. The signer signs the message with a private key, and receivers fetch the matching public key from your domain’s DNS to check the signature. A valid signature continues to validate wherever the message travels afterward. Mailing lists, .forward rules, and third-party relays all preserve it, which is the protocol working as designed. A replay attack takes advantage of that durability. The attack works as follows: Your ecommerce platform sends a customer a legitimate response email, signed with your DKIM key. An attacker obtains one copy of that message. They might subscribe to your mailing list, compromise a mailbox, retrieve it from a list archive, or capture it through a forwarding rule. The attacker resends that message, unchanged, from their own servers to thousands of new recipients. Each receiving server fetches your public key from DNS and checks the signature. The signature passes, because the body wasn’t modified. Sender Policy Framework (SPF) fails, because the sending IP isn’t yours, but DMARC requires only one of SPF or DKIM to pass with alignment. Because DKIM passes, DMARC passes, and the message is delivered as authenticated email from your domain. Understanding what an attacker can and can’t do matters, because the limits define the problem. An attacker can’t modify your message, add new content, or read your email. The signature is only valid while the message remains byte-for-byte identical. What an attacker gains is your domain’s reputation, which they use to deliver your genuine message to an audience you didn’t intend. A receipt or invoice becomes a lure, and email that would normally be filtered is delivered because receivers trust your domain. This is abuse of reputation and reach, not content forgery, and the distinction matters when you explain the incident to your security team. This also explains why an enforcing DMARC policy doesn’t stop an attack. DMARC passes when SPF or DKIM passes with alignment. During a replay, DKIM passes, so DMARC passes, and p=reject does not apply. A p=reject policy is designed to stop spoofing, where a forger has no valid signature and DKIM fails. It does nothing against a message that you signed. Determining which of the two was used is what tells you how to respond. Is it replay, spoofing, or a legitimate relay? Email from an unfamiliar IP address that passes DKIM has three common explanations, and each requires a different response. Confirm which you’re dealing with before you make any changes. DMARC aggregate (rua) reports provide the source IP address, message volume, and SPF and DKIM results. This is enough to identify an anomaly, but not to prove a replay. A report row might read as follows: source IP: 203.0.113.45 | count: 4,200 | SPF: fail | DKIM: pass (d=yourdomain.com) You need to evaluate that row against the three possibilities: The first possibility is a legitimate relay that you haven’t inventoried, such as a mailing list, a forwarder, or an email security gateway such as an inline cloud access security broker (CASB) that you route through. The signature validly survives the relay, and this is normal email flow. In the report, the source IP address usually resolves to a known provider, and the volume tracks your actual sending. The second possibility is replay abuse, in which an attacker redistributes a message that you legitimately signed. In this case, the DKIM-passing volume comes from an IP address that has no business relationship with you, often well above the usual number of recipients that you send to, and frequently to recipient domains that you haven’t worked with. The third possibility is ordinary spoofing, which is a forgery with no valid signature. That row shows DKIM: fail. DKIM that passes from an unknown IP address is therefore usually not ordinary spoofing. Aggregate counts can’t prove a replay on their own. To confirm a replay, you need message-level evidence: a specific message that you sent matched to one that reached recipients you didn’t address. If you can’t make that match, treat the activity as an unconfirmed anomaly, and begin with the enforcement and monitoring steps that follow rather than removing keys. Set up an enforcing DMARC policy first Before you take any other action, confirm that you’re enforcing DMARC. Many domains that encounter this problem are still at p=none, which is monitoring only. This situation is common. Every DMARC deployment begins at p=none, and many organizations do not advance beyond it because nothing appears to be broken. At p=none, receivers take no action on failures, so no change you make affects delivery, and you can’t determine what enforcement would have caught. The first step is therefore not key removal; it’s completing your sender inventory and reaching enforcement: Inventory every legitimate sender and relay for your domain, including your email service providers, mailing lists, and any security gateways that send on your behalf. Bring each sender into SPF and DKIM alignment so that legitimate email authenticates. Advance the policy one stage at a time, from p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject. Review your rua reports at each stage before you advance, typically for a week or two per stage, and longer if you have many senders to work through. The pct tag lets you ramp up gradually, for example by quarantining 25% of failing email before you increase the percentage. After you’re enforcing DMARC, receivers that honor DMARC drop unauthenticated spoofing on your behalf. Only after this baseline is in place, and only after you have confirmed a replay of genuinely signed email, does the next step apply. Remove the old key from DNS: routine hygiene after rotation Most rotation guidance omits this step. Rotating a key and removing the old key are two separate actions. Rotation means that your provider begins signing new email with a new key and selector. Removal means deleting the old public key from DNS, so that previously signed messages, including the copies that an attacker captured, can no longer be verified. If you rotate but leave the old public key published, every message ever signed with that key remains replayable for as long as the record exists. Removing the old key is what closes that window and is the step that’s commonly overlooked. Removal affects only messages that are still in transit and were signed with the old key. After email is delivered, the receiver no longer needs your key, so we recommend that you leave the old key published long enough for in-flight email to arrive and then remove it. How much of this process you manage yourself depends on your DKIM method, which the following section describes. During a confirmed active replay, closing this window is essential. How you manage keys depends on the DKIM method that you use with Amazon SES. With Bring Your Own DKIM (BYODKIM), you generate the key pair and publish the public key as a TXT record that you control. You can rotate and remove keys whenever you want, including removing an old key on demand during an incident. As the BYODKIM documentation states, “you can rotate the DKIM keys for your domains as often as you want.” With Easy DKIM, a feature where Amazon SES generates and manages the keys for you, you publish CNAME records that point to AWS-hosted keys. Because your DNS points to AWS-hosted keys through those CNAME records, Amazon SES manages the underlying key material for you, so you don’t publish or remove individual keys yourself. Unlike BYODKIM, Easy DKIM doesn’t provide an on-demand option to delete a specific key immediately. If you’re an Easy DKIM sender during a confirmed replay, your defenses are early detection (described in the following section), the duplicate-message throttling that receivers already apply, and, over the longer term, the emerging DKIM2 effort, an IETF initiative to update the DKIM specification with built-in replay resistance, which is being designed to give receivers better signals to identify and act on replayed messages at the protocol level. How Amazon SES helps you detect and respond Your first response is detection, not DNS changes. The goal is to identify anomalous DKIM-passing volume early, while you build the message-level evidence that distinguishes a replay from a legitimate relay. Begin by enabling logging. Create an Amazon SES configuration set with an event destination (see Monitor email sending using Amazon SES event publishing ) that streams per-message events (Send, Delivery, Bounce, and Complaint) to Amazon Data Firehose or Amazon EventBridge (see Add an event destination ), tagged with the From domain. Separately, confirm that you’re receiving rua reports for your domain. You enable these reports by adding a rua= address to your domain’s DMARC TXT record, for example rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com. For the record syntax and a phased p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject rollout, see Complying with DMARC authentication protocol in Amazon SES . Reports arrive as daily XML digests, and most teams process them with a DMARC analyzer rather than reading the raw XML. With both sources in place, you can correlate them. Compare the email that your account emitted—based on your Amazon SES delivery events—against what DMARC reports show that receivers accepted as your domain. When DMARC shows DKIM-passing volume from IP addresses outside your SPF record that exceeds the delivery events that Amazon SES recorded for that From domain in the same window, that gap is your signal. It’s also how you build the message-level case that distinguishes a replay from a legitimate relay. We recommend three additional controls. Amazon SES sending authorization restricts which AWS principals can send using your verified identity. items.summary_html:
As the email administrator for your organization’s domain, you receive a Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) aggregate report showing email passing DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) verification as though it came from your domain, sent from IP addresses you don’t recognize to recipients you didn’t contact. To clear the issue, you rotate your DKIM key, confirm the new selector is live, and verify that your DMARC policy is already set to p=reject. Days later, you see that the same unfamiliar traffic is still authenticating as you.

In this post, you learn why rotation alone can’t stop a DKIM replay attack, how to confirm that you’re looking at a replay rather than a legitimate relay or ordinary spoofing, and the DNS cleanup step that most rotation guidance leaves out. You also learn how you can use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to detect and respond to this activity faster.

How DKIM replay works

DKIM verifies one thing: that specific parts of a message didn’t change between the signer and the receiver. The signer signs the message with a private key, and receivers fetch the matching public key from your domain’s DNS to check the signature. A valid signature continues to validate wherever the message travels afterward. Mailing lists, .forward rules, and third-party relays all preserve it, which is the protocol working as designed.

A replay attack takes advantage of that durability. The attack works as follows:

  1. Your ecommerce platform sends a customer a legitimate response email, signed with your DKIM key.
  2. An attacker obtains one copy of that message. They might subscribe to your mailing list, compromise a mailbox, retrieve it from a list archive, or capture it through a forwarding rule.
  3. The attacker resends that message, unchanged, from their own servers to thousands of new recipients.
  4. Each receiving server fetches your public key from DNS and checks the signature. The signature passes, because the body wasn’t modified. Sender Policy Framework (SPF) fails, because the sending IP isn’t yours, but DMARC requires only one of SPF or DKIM to pass with alignment. Because DKIM passes, DMARC passes, and the message is delivered as authenticated email from your domain.

Understanding what an attacker can and can’t do matters, because the limits define the problem. An attacker can’t modify your message, add new content, or read your email. The signature is only valid while the message remains byte-for-byte identical.

What an attacker gains is your domain’s reputation, which they use to deliver your genuine message to an audience you didn’t intend. A receipt or invoice becomes a lure, and email that would normally be filtered is delivered because receivers trust your domain. This is abuse of reputation and reach, not content forgery, and the distinction matters when you explain the incident to your security team.

This also explains why an enforcing DMARC policy doesn’t stop an attack. DMARC passes when SPF or DKIM passes with alignment. During a replay, DKIM passes, so DMARC passes, and p=reject does not apply. A p=reject policy is designed to stop spoofing, where a forger has no valid signature and DKIM fails. It does nothing against a message that you signed. Determining which of the two was used is what tells you how to respond.

Is it replay, spoofing, or a legitimate relay?

Email from an unfamiliar IP address that passes DKIM has three common explanations, and each requires a different response. Confirm which you’re dealing with before you make any changes.

DMARC aggregate (rua) reports provide the source IP address, message volume, and SPF and DKIM results. This is enough to identify an anomaly, but not to prove a replay. A report row might read as follows:

source IP: 203.0.113.45 | count: 4,200 | SPF: fail | DKIM: pass (d=yourdomain.com)

You need to evaluate that row against the three possibilities:

  • The first possibility is a legitimate relay that you haven’t inventoried, such as a mailing list, a forwarder, or an email security gateway such as an inline cloud access security broker (CASB) that you route through. The signature validly survives the relay, and this is normal email flow. In the report, the source IP address usually resolves to a known provider, and the volume tracks your actual sending.
  • The second possibility is replay abuse, in which an attacker redistributes a message that you legitimately signed. In this case, the DKIM-passing volume comes from an IP address that has no business relationship with you, often well above the usual number of recipients that you send to, and frequently to recipient domains that you haven’t worked with.
  • The third possibility is ordinary spoofing, which is a forgery with no valid signature. That row shows DKIM: fail. DKIM that passes from an unknown IP address is therefore usually not ordinary spoofing.

Aggregate counts can’t prove a replay on their own. To confirm a replay, you need message-level evidence: a specific message that you sent matched to one that reached recipients you didn’t address. If you can’t make that match, treat the activity as an unconfirmed anomaly, and begin with the enforcement and monitoring steps that follow rather than removing keys.

Set up an enforcing DMARC policy first

Before you take any other action, confirm that you’re enforcing DMARC. Many domains that encounter this problem are still at p=none, which is monitoring only. This situation is common. Every DMARC deployment begins at p=none, and many organizations do not advance beyond it because nothing appears to be broken. At p=none, receivers take no action on failures, so no change you make affects delivery, and you can’t determine what enforcement would have caught.

The first step is therefore not key removal; it’s completing your sender inventory and reaching enforcement:

  1. Inventory every legitimate sender and relay for your domain, including your email service providers, mailing lists, and any security gateways that send on your behalf.
  2. Bring each sender into SPF and DKIM alignment so that legitimate email authenticates.
  3. Advance the policy one stage at a time, from p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject. Review your rua reports at each stage before you advance, typically for a week or two per stage, and longer if you have many senders to work through. The pct tag lets you ramp up gradually, for example by quarantining 25% of failing email before you increase the percentage.

After you’re enforcing DMARC, receivers that honor DMARC drop unauthenticated spoofing on your behalf. Only after this baseline is in place, and only after you have confirmed a replay of genuinely signed email, does the next step apply.

Remove the old key from DNS: routine hygiene after rotation

Most rotation guidance omits this step. Rotating a key and removing the old key are two separate actions.

Rotation means that your provider begins signing new email with a new key and selector. Removal means deleting the old public key from DNS, so that previously signed messages, including the copies that an attacker captured, can no longer be verified. If you rotate but leave the old public key published, every message ever signed with that key remains replayable for as long as the record exists. Removing the old key is what closes that window and is the step that’s commonly overlooked.

Removal affects only messages that are still in transit and were signed with the old key. After email is delivered, the receiver no longer needs your key, so we recommend that you leave the old key published long enough for in-flight email to arrive and then remove it. How much of this process you manage yourself depends on your DKIM method, which the following section describes. During a confirmed active replay, closing this window is essential.

How you manage keys depends on the DKIM method that you use with Amazon SES. With Bring Your Own DKIM (BYODKIM), you generate the key pair and publish the public key as a TXT record that you control. You can rotate and remove keys whenever you want, including removing an old key on demand during an incident. As the BYODKIM documentation states, “you can rotate the DKIM keys for your domains as often as you want.”

With Easy DKIM, a feature where Amazon SES generates and manages the keys for you, you publish CNAME records that point to AWS-hosted keys. Because your DNS points to AWS-hosted keys through those CNAME records, Amazon SES manages the underlying key material for you, so you don’t publish or remove individual keys yourself. Unlike BYODKIM, Easy DKIM doesn’t provide an on-demand option to delete a specific key immediately.

If you’re an Easy DKIM sender during a confirmed replay, your defenses are early detection (described in the following section), the duplicate-message throttling that receivers already apply, and, over the longer term, the emerging DKIM2 effort, an IETF initiative to update the DKIM specification with built-in replay resistance, which is being designed to give receivers better signals to identify and act on replayed messages at the protocol level.

How Amazon SES helps you detect and respond

Your first response is detection, not DNS changes. The goal is to identify anomalous DKIM-passing volume early, while you build the message-level evidence that distinguishes a replay from a legitimate relay.

Begin by enabling logging. Create an Amazon SES configuration set with an event destination (see Monitor email sending using Amazon SES event publishing) that streams per-message events (Send, Delivery, Bounce, and Complaint) to Amazon Data Firehose or Amazon EventBridge (see Add an event destination), tagged with the From domain.

Separately, confirm that you’re receiving rua reports for your domain. You enable these reports by adding a rua= address to your domain’s DMARC TXT record, for example rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com. For the record syntax and a phased p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject rollout, see Complying with DMARC authentication protocol in Amazon SES. Reports arrive as daily XML digests, and most teams process them with a DMARC analyzer rather than reading the raw XML.

With both sources in place, you can correlate them. Compare the email that your account emitted—based on your Amazon SES delivery events—against what DMARC reports show that receivers accepted as your domain. When DMARC shows DKIM-passing volume from IP addresses outside your SPF record that exceeds the delivery events that Amazon SES recorded for that From domain in the same window, that gap is your signal. It’s also how you build the message-level case that distinguishes a replay from a legitimate relay.

We recommend three additional controls. Amazon SES sending authorization restricts which AWS principals can send using your verified identity. It doesn’t stop an external replay, but it addresses the insider and third-party vector that SPF, DKIM, and DMARC don’t cover on their own, so use identity-level policies to limit sending to specific AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principals.

Use Amazon Route 53 to set short DNS time-to-live values (TTLs) (for example, 300 seconds) on your DKIM records so that changes propagate quickly; and enable DNS query logging with an Amazon CloudWatch Logs metric filter that watches for queries to a selector that you’ve rotated away from.

A spike in lookups for an old selector is a useful early indicator of a replay attempt using a retired selector. For a BYODKIM domain during a confirmed replay, Route 53 is also where you remove the old selector’s TXT record. You can automate that removal by using an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that starts an AWS Lambda function to call the Route 53 API and retire an old selector’s record.

Scope the function’s IAM role to only the specific Route 53 hosted zone and record that it needs to change, so that it follows least privilege. Because an incorrect DNS change can have a wide effect, gate any automation behind confirmed-replay criteria and test it against a non-production domain first. For most teams, alarm-to-human is safer than alarm-to-automatic-removal.

When your domain is the one being abused

Most guidance assumes that you’re either the provider preventing abuse or the receiver detecting it. In a replay, your domain is the one whose reputation is being consumed, and you aren’t on the recipient list. As a result, you don’t have the message that everyone asks for when you report the issue.

When you file an abuse report with the provider that hosts the source IP address, they ask for full message headers. The email went to people you didn’t contact, so you don’t have the message headers. You then provide DMARC aggregate reports that show the source IP address and volume, and the provider asks for headers again. At this point, you’re unable to proceed.

To break this cycle, go to the recipients. Review your rua reports for the top recipient domains—which are often .gov and .edu domains—contact those recipients directly and request a sample message with full headers. In addition to providing the headers, that sample lets you confirm a replay rather than a legitimate relay. Build your abuse report around the IP address and the DMARC evidence rather than the message content. If the source IP address belongs to Amazon Web Services (AWS), report it through the AWS abuse process and include your DMARC reports and SPF record as evidence.

Incident response: ordered actions

If your reports show suspicious DKIM-passing email from unfamiliar IP addresses, complete the following procedure.

To respond to a suspected DKIM replay

  1. Confirm that it’s a replay. Match a message that you sent to one that reached recipients you didn’t address and rule out legitimate relays and gateways. Aggregate data alone isn’t proof.
  2. Reach an enforcing DMARC policy. Inventory your legitimate senders, align them, and advance from p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject. This stops spoofing.
  3. Harden SPF to -all rather than ~all, but only after your sender inventory is complete, since -all hard-fails any legitimate source you haven’t listed.
  4. Check the DKIM-Signature header of a fresh message to confirm that your provider signs only with the current selector.
  5. Report the source IP address to the hosting provider and include your DMARC evidence.
  6. Investigate the capture point, such as a compromised mailbox, a mailing list, a forwarding rule, or a newsletter subscription.
  7. Remove the old DKIM public key after in-flight email has cleared. For BYODKIM, delete the old selector’s TXT record. For Easy DKIM, rely on the managed Amazon SES rotation together with the monitoring and receiver-side defenses described earlier.

The following table summarizes what each action does and doesn’t do.

Action What it does What it doesn’t do Confirm replay (message-level) Separates a replay from a legitimate relay or spoofing Can’t be done from aggregate DMARC data alone DMARC enforcement (p=none to p=reject) Drops unauthenticated spoofing Does nothing against a replay because DKIM still passes Key rotation Signs new email with a new key Doesn’t invalidate already signed messages Remove old key (routine, post-rotation) Invalidates old-key signatures, including captured ones Doesn’t protect in-flight old-key email; on-demand removal available only with BYODKIM Amazon SES sending authorization Restricts which principals send as your identity Doesn’t stop external replay of captured messages
Conclusion

DKIM replay succeeds because a valid signature keeps validating, and an enforcing DMARC policy doesn’t change that. To respond effectively, confirm that the activity is a replay with message-level evidence, reach an enforcing DMARC policy, and then remove the old key from DNS as routine post-rotation hygiene. Keep your primary defense on monitoring and DMARC enforcement rather than on emergency DNS changes. The durable fix for replay is receiver-side: duplicate-message counting today, and stronger protocol-level signals through DKIM2 in the future.

To get started, review your current DMARC policy and confirm that you’re receiving rua reports, enable Amazon SES event publishing, and document how you rotate and remove DKIM keys for each of your domains.

Mercado Bitcoin Suffers Cyberattack as Researchers Flag $40 Million in Suspicious Crypto Transfers
items.summary: Brazilian cryptocurrency exchange Mercado Bitcoin suspended deposits and withdrawals on November 2, 2026, after detecting a security incident in one of its systems. Blockchain security firm Hypernative flagged more than $40 million in suspicious transfers across at least 10 blockchains, raising questions about the scope of the breach. The exchange has not confirmed that amount as its actual loss. In its official statement , Mercado Bitcoin said it quickly contained the incident early Monday morning. The company said customers suffered no harm and no data leaked. It described the service suspension as a protective measure while its teams investigate, trace assets, and work with authorities. According to reports, Opsek founder Pablo Sabbatella shared findings describing transfers from wallets linked to Mercado Bitcoin into fresh addresses. The affected networks included Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Tron, Polygon, Arbitrum, Avalanche, BNB Chain and Stellar. Researchers said the activity covered at least 10 chains in total. Mercado Bitcoin Suffers Cyberattack Most of the reported outflows occurred between 06:19 and 06:53 UTC, a 34-minute window. Earlier Bitcoin activity reportedly began around 02:15 UTC, when funds from deposit addresses started moving to addresses linked to the suspected attacker. The preliminary count included approximately 2,852 ETH, 106 BTC, 10,700 SOL and 6.7 million XLM, alongside more than 200 other tokens. These figures remain researcher estimates rather than amounts verified publicly by Mercado Bitcoin. Researchers described the movements as ordinary transfers rather than a smart contract exploit. That distinction puts attention on how the transactions received valid signatures. However, the available findings do not establish how the attacker obtained signing access or which internal system was compromised. The incident follows other exchange wallet breaches covered by Cybersecurity News, including the Bitget hot wallet hack . That case involved unauthorized transfers affecting hot and warm wallet infrastructure. It offers industry context, but does not establish a shared attack method or attacker in the Mercado Bitcoin incident. Mercado Bitcoin later published destination addresses covering Ethereum-compatible networks, Bitcoin, Solana, Stellar and Tron. The exchange said it released them to help identify and track funds on public blockchains. Such tracking also featured in the Bitfinex hack investigation , which documented how investigators followed stolen cryptocurrency through laundering activity. As Bitcoin Magazine reported, Mercado Bitcoin had not announced a reopening time or disclosed the affected system. The unresolved issue remains the gap between suspicious wallet movements and confirmed losses. Its statement that customers were unharmed should not be read as confirmation that no exchange assets were taken. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: How Fidelis EDR Telemetry and Event Logging Enable Faster Incident Investigation
items.summary: Key Takeaways Fidelis EDR captures detailed endpoint telemetry across processes, files, registry activity, and network events Endpoint Collector enables retrospective investigations and enterprise-wide threat hunting from stored behavioral data Process trees and timeline playback accelerate root cause analysis for multi-stage attacks Behavioral rules and MITRE ATT&CK mapping improve detection fidelity against fileless threats Automated response, forensic collection, and XDR correlation reduce SOC workload and incident response time Alert-only endpoint security tools create an investigation problem. When a detection fires, analysts need more than a single event record. They need the process that spawned the threat, the commands that ran, the files that changed, and the network connections that followed. Without that context, root cause analysis turns into guesswork and dwell time grows while teams try to reconstruct activity that was never logged in the first place. Fidelis Endpoint ® takes a telemetry-first approach: collecting granular behavioral data from every monitored endpoint, retaining it in a centralized repository, and making it queryable in real time and retrospectively. For SOC teams, incident responders, and threat hunters, that endpoint telemetry depth directly supports faster MTTR, stronger detection fidelity, and more decisive incident response. How Fidelis EDR Collects Endpoint Telemetry A single lightweight agent runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux systems. It captures metadata continuously for every process and child process, covering behaviors, registry changes, file events, and network activity. That data feeds into the Endpoint Collector , a centralized behavioral metadata store with configurable retention of 30, 60, or 90 days. The result is a persistent record of endpoint activity that SOC teams can query long after an alert fires. The event categories logged per endpoint include: Process starts and child process creation with full command-line arguments Registry writes, modifications, and deletions File creation, write, close, and deletion events Network connections including DNS, HTTP/HTTPS, and SMB Windows Event Log entries covering logon and account activity Loaded DLL and executable files Remote thread activity The event timeline presents everything chronologically: parent and child processes, loaded DLLs, files written, network connections, and the full process tree. Stored timelines let analysts reconstruct pre- and post-detection activity without initiating a separate forensic collection, cutting overhead on every alert in high-volume environments. Command-line capture extends to the maximum length Windows supports, past the previous 512-character limit. Encoded PowerShell abuse is documented under MITRE ATT&CK T1059.001 and truncated captures leave gaps in the execution record. Full-length capture removes that blind spot. When endpoints go offline, threat intelligence and detection logic stay local on the agent so detection continues regardless of connectivity. Events cache and sync on reconnect, keeping the behavioral record intact for remote workers, air-gapped systems, and off-grid deployments. How Endpoint Event Logging Speeds Up SOC Investigations The Endpoint Collector is where stored endpoint telemetry becomes actionable during an investigation. Rather than pivoting across multiple tools after an alert fires, analysts query behavioral metadata directly from the console. The query interface supports faceted search for standard triage and a Boolean logic query builder for complex, multi-attribute correlation. Saved queries run continuously, supporting ongoing managed threat hunting campaigns and recurring monitoring requirements without rebuilding searches from scratch. NIST SP 800-61 identifies rapid data collection and evidence preservation as foundational to effective incident response. Retaining endpoint behavioral metadata over extended windows supports both. When a new indicator of compromise surfaces from an external advisory, analysts run it immediately against weeks or months of stored endpoint data to determine prior exposure, a retrospective capability alert-only tools cannot provide. Every first-time-seen executable and script is captured at execution time. Attackers routinely delete tools after use, but because capture happens before deletion is possible, a clean sample is preserved regardless. Security teams review it in the built-in hex or text editor, submit it through Threat Lookup, or download it for external analysis. Retrospective threat hunting works the same way. New suspicious behavior patterns search the full retention window immediately, and confirmed patterns convert directly into custom Behavior Rules with minimal workflow steps. Faster Threat Investigations Start with Deeper Endpoint Visibility Establish Deep Telemetry Enable Timeline-Based Investigation Continuously Validate Endpoint Visibility Read the Guide Process Trees and Event Timelines: Accelerating Root Cause Analysis Process lineage is critical for root cause analysis. The Fidelis graphical timeline reconstructs the full execution chain, showing which parent spawned which child, with arguments, file writes, registry modifications, and network connections at each step. Security teams follow a compromise from entry to exfiltration in one interface without manually joining log sources. Living-off-the-land attacks are documented in MITRE ATT&CK under T1059 and T1055. The malicious activity is in execution context, not the binary itself. Without process lineage, flat log review misses the causal chain between steps: which process spawned PowerShell, with what arguments, after which download, while malicious processes keep running while the investigation stalls. A built-in playback capability steps through key events chronologically, cutting the time needed to produce an accurate incident summary for complex multi-stage attacks. Remote thread activity and loaded DLLs are recorded per process. When attackers inject code into a legitimate process, those events appear in the process tree alongside all other activity, giving analysts full visibility into suspicious behaviors before, during, and after the injection. Behavioral Detection, Threat Intelligence, and Reducing False Positives How Behavior Rules Improve Detection Fidelity Behavioral detection runs through a continuously updated Behavior Rules library maintained by the Fidelis Threat Research Team from ongoing research, sandbox results, and machine learning outputs. Where applicable, rules map to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, giving analysts technique-level context the moment a detection fires, before manual investigation begins. CISA recommends behavior-based detection because signatures struggle against fileless attacks and living-off-the-land techniques. Detections fire on what a process does, not what it is. A threat that evades signature scanning still triggers an alert if its execution pattern matches a known attacker TTP, strengthening detection fidelity against evolving cyber threats. Custom Behavior Rules build directly from Endpoint Collector queries. A hunting query that surfaces a suspicious pattern converts into a production detection rule without additional tooling. Rules update without agent redeployment, letting teams adapt to emerging threats immediately. Vendor-maintained and analyst-developed rules work together, giving security teams broad coverage alongside environment-specific tuning that reduces false positives over time. Threat Intelligence Feeds, IOC Correlation, and the Global Threat Cache Fidelis Endpoint ® ingests threat intelligence from multiple simultaneous sources. The Scanning Indicator Library ships with hundreds of community indicators and supports additional OpenIOC and YARA rule uploads. Fidelis Insight feeds, third-party commercial feeds, and internally developed indicators are all supported across STIX, XML, JSON, and delimited formats, strengthening coverage against known and unknown threats without a separate intelligence platform. Alert-only endpoint security tools create an investigation problem. When a detection fires, analysts need more than a single event record. They need the process that spawned the threat, the commands that ran, the files that changed, and the network connections that followed. Without that context, root cause analysis turns into guesswork and dwell time grows while teams try to reconstruct activity that was never logged in the first place.

Fidelis Endpoint® takes a telemetry-first approach: collecting granular behavioral data from every monitored endpoint, retaining it in a centralized repository, and making it queryable in real time and retrospectively. For SOC teams, incident responders, and threat hunters, that endpoint telemetry depth directly supports faster MTTR, stronger detection fidelity, and more decisive incident response.

How Fidelis EDR Collects Endpoint Telemetry

A single lightweight agent runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux systems. It captures metadata continuously for every process and child process, covering behaviors, registry changes, file events, and network activity. That data feeds into the Endpoint Collector, a centralized behavioral metadata store with configurable retention of 30, 60, or 90 days. The result is a persistent record of endpoint activity that SOC teams can query long after an alert fires.

The event categories logged per endpoint include:

  • Process starts and child process creation with full command-line arguments
  • Registry writes, modifications, and deletions
  • File creation, write, close, and deletion events
  • Network connections including DNS, HTTP/HTTPS, and SMB
  • Windows Event Log entries covering logon and account activity
  • Loaded DLL and executable files
  • Remote thread activity

The event timeline presents everything chronologically: parent and child processes, loaded DLLs, files written, network connections, and the full process tree. Stored timelines let analysts reconstruct pre- and post-detection activity without initiating a separate forensic collection, cutting overhead on every alert in high-volume environments.

Command-line capture extends to the maximum length Windows supports, past the previous 512-character limit. Encoded PowerShell abuse is documented under MITRE ATT&CK T1059.001 and truncated captures leave gaps in the execution record. Full-length capture removes that blind spot.

When endpoints go offline, threat intelligence and detection logic stay local on the agent so detection continues regardless of connectivity. Events cache and sync on reconnect, keeping the behavioral record intact for remote workers, air-gapped systems, and off-grid deployments.

How Endpoint Event Logging Speeds Up SOC Investigations

The Endpoint Collector is where stored endpoint telemetry becomes actionable during an investigation. Rather than pivoting across multiple tools after an alert fires, analysts query behavioral metadata directly from the console. The query interface supports faceted search for standard triage and a Boolean logic query builder for complex, multi-attribute correlation. Saved queries run continuously, supporting ongoing managed threat hunting campaigns and recurring monitoring requirements without rebuilding searches from scratch.

NIST SP 800-61 identifies rapid data collection and evidence preservation as foundational to effective incident response. Retaining endpoint behavioral metadata over extended windows supports both. When a new indicator of compromise surfaces from an external advisory, analysts run it immediately against weeks or months of stored endpoint data to determine prior exposure, a retrospective capability alert-only tools cannot provide.

Every first-time-seen executable and script is captured at execution time. Attackers routinely delete tools after use, but because capture happens before deletion is possible, a clean sample is preserved regardless. Security teams review it in the built-in hex or text editor, submit it through Threat Lookup, or download it for external analysis.

Retrospective threat hunting works the same way. New suspicious behavior patterns search the full retention window immediately, and confirmed patterns convert directly into custom Behavior Rules with minimal workflow steps.

Living-off-the-land attacks are documented in MITRE ATT&CK under T1059 and T1055. The malicious activity is in execution context, not the binary itself. Without process lineage, flat log review misses the causal chain between steps: which process spawned PowerShell, with what arguments, after which download, while malicious processes keep running while the investigation stalls.

A built-in playback capability steps through key events chronologically, cutting the time needed to produce an accurate incident summary for complex multi-stage attacks.

Remote thread activity and loaded DLLs are recorded per process. When attackers inject code into a legitimate process, those events appear in the process tree alongside all other activity, giving analysts full visibility into suspicious behaviors before, during, and after the injection.

Guiding Customers Through Critical PHP Vulnerabilities
items.summary: Over the past week, our industry has faced a wave of critical vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). As Palo Alto Networks Chief Technology and Product Officer Lee Klarich highlighted , these high-severity vulnerability disclosures are just the beginning of a massive acceleration of cyberthreats that will define the foreseeable future. Because PHP powers more than half of the web, relying on traditional patch cycles is no longer viable: while enterprise patching averages 55 days , threat actors can move from breach to data exfiltration in as little as 39 seconds. With AI delivering a step-change in attack speed and depth, organizations simply cannot wait for patch development and deployment. They need proactive discovery and pre-emptive protection provided by Frontier Virtual Patching before the vulnerabilities are disclosed. When vulnerabilities of this magnitude emerge, enterprise customers turn immediately to their trusted advisors for clarity and direction. Palo Alto Networks partners play a pivotal role in guiding customers through this shift, moving them from reactive patching scrambles toward long-term protection. This resilience lands on one foundational imperative: Frontier Virtual Patching (FVP) must be enforced across all outbound traffic, not just at endpoints, in the cloud, or across Web Application Firewalls (WAFs). The next few months will be a critical moment for partners to step in front of customers to educate them on the modern exposure gap, help them understand their true reachability, and rapidly protect their environments before weaponized exploits land. The AI-Accelerated Threat Window With AI agents and frontier models available at the fingertips of any adversary, exploitation windows are collapsing. Nearly 30% of vulnerabilities are now weaponized by threat actors within 24 hours of disclosure. In the case of #PHP2Shell and #Brotli, telemetry revealed autonomous agents actively probing and compromising exposed entities within just 2 to 4 hours. Customers must understand the unique severity of these threats : Zero credentials required: The PHP vulnerabilities can be triggered by an unauthenticated request before any application code even runs. No safe workarounds: Temporary configuration changes are not enough to secure a server. Mitigation requires comprehensive updates or a robust preemptive defense layer. Exploits are active: We are already seeing proof-of-concept exploits in the wild, forcing governments and organizations to take websites offline as a precaution. Understanding Your Customers’ Exposure The hardest part of defending against vulnerabilities is tracking them down. Organizations must gain immediate, complete visibility into their true attack surface. Through our Frontier AI Alliance, we’ve engaged leading global systems integrators and service providers to deliver this protection at enterprise scale, already helping partners assess and secure hundreds of customer environments to date. Over the past week, Palo Alto Networks has mobilized proactive services and intelligence tools to help partners guide customers through exposure discovery. Through Cortex Xpanse, defenders have mapped internet-facing assets to pinpoint exposed PHP footprints globally, while Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense provides reachability analysis to distinguish between theoretical software flaws and weaponizable attack paths. Shielding Environments Before Day One While discovering exposure is critical, customers cannot wait until their inventory is perfect to defend themselves. Customers running Frontier Virtual Patching on Palo Alto Networks Advanced Threat Prevention (ATP) Plus were protected before the PHP vulnerabilities were even made public. Fueled by our Network and Open-Source Vulnerability Analyzer (NOVA) , our frontier AI vulnerability analyzer, our customers have been shielded from these PHP exploits since October 20, without any downtime, software restarts, or manual policy changes. Because this protection runs at the network layer, it shields every workload whose traffic passes through the firewall, including the ones that aren't in their inventory yet. Let's urge our customers to stop treating virtual patching as an emergency measure and start treating it as a foundational layer of their architecture. Our team is here to help you - learn more .

items.title: Inside the Secretive, Contradictory World of Campaign Ads Funded by AI Super PACs
items.summary: Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published . Become a member and support our work here . An online ad for Ben McAdams, the Democratic candidate for Congress in Utah, emphasised that he could be trusted because he “fought back against MAGA”. Source: Think Big / Google Ad Transparency Center In Texas, another ad promoted Republican candidate Chris Gober, calling him a “MAGA warrior”. Source: American Mission / Google Ad Transparency Center What’s interesting is that both ads were ultimately paid for with money from the same organisation – Leading the Future (LTF), a Super PAC which opposes regulations that “constrain” innovation in AI. The network has received US$125 million in funding in total from OpenAI president Greg Brockman, his wife Anna Brockman, tech-focused venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and a16z’s founders, Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings show. Directly opposing LTF is Public First Action (PFA), which calls for AI safety regulations and guardrails. PFA has received $40 million in funding from AI company Anthropic. Like the ads run by organisations funded by LTF, the Super PACs funded by PFA also ran ads that appeared supportive or critical of Trump depending on the voters they were targeting. Ads in support of Republican Carlos De La Cruz (above) and Democrat Colin Allred (below) in Texas, paid for by Defending Our Values PAC, and Jobs and Democracy PAC, respectively. Source: Defending Our Values PAC / Jobs and Democracy PAC / Google Ad Transparency Center None of these ads mentions AI. As the US 2026 midterm elections approach on Nov. 3, Super PAC spending on political advertising has reportedly soared to record highs , surpassing US$11 billion last week and exceeding the amount spent on any other election cycle to date. Super PACs are a particular type of political action committee (PAC) that may receive unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, labour unions and other PACs for the purpose of financing independent expenditures and other independent political activity. In this year’s elections, LTF’s and PFA’s Super PACs, funded by the AI industry heavyweights, have played an outsized role in supporting or opposing candidates through advertising. But as polls show distrust of AI crosses party lines , the advertisements that Silicon Valley’s leaders are paying millions of dollars to try to sway the results in their chosen candidates’ favour often do not mention AI at all. Photo: Reuters/Shannon Stapleton While LTF is a registered Super PAC itself, FEC filings show it mainly disburses money to other Super PACs in its network which run political ads. Of about $52 million that LTF has disbursed to date , $20 million went to Think Big, which targets the Democratic voter base, and another $20 million went to American Mission, which focuses on Republicans. PFA, meanwhile, is registered as a “social welfare”, or 501(c)(4) , organisation. This type of non-profit is not required to disclose its donors or disbursements. However, PFA contributes funds to three Super PACs : the bipartisan Public First PAC, Jobs and Democracy for Democratic candidates and Defending Our Values for Republicans. FEC filings for these Super PACs show Public First PAC received $1 million, Jobs and Democracy received $15.4 million and Defending Our Values received $7.9 million from PFA. Public First PAC’s FEC filings also show that $4 million of its $4.4 million in disbursements disclosed so far went to Jobs and Democracy, while another $300,000 went to Defending Our Values. Disbursements to Think Big, American Mission, Jobs and Democracy and Defending Our Values from Leading the Future, Public First PAC and Public First Action. Graphic: Bellingcat Super PACs are allowed to accept unlimited contributions from other political committees, and other similar networks of Super PACs have been observed in the current election cycle, such as cryptocurrency-linked Fairshake and its affiliated Super PACs . Bellingcat analysed data on more than 300 online video ad campaigns paid for by Think Big , American Mission , Jobs and Democracy and Defending Our Values from Google’s Ad Transparency Center. These ad campaigns, many of which used the same videos in slightly different formats or across different platforms, supported or opposed 40 candidates. items.title: How to Export Logs from Any SIEM for Free Analysis
items.summary: Every SIEM can hand its data back in one of two shapes: the original raw events, or its own parsed JSON. For analysis outside the SIEM, raw events are almost always the better choice.   2. Narrow first. Host, source, event type, time window. Count before you pull; most platforms show the number in the UI.
  3. Use the API or CLI for anything over a few thousand events. Browser exports time out, rerun searches, or silently cap the row count.
  4. Mind the permission boundary. API tokens often see less than your UI session: QRadar security profiles, Splunk roles, Graph scopes. When numbers don’t match, check the token first.
  5. Pin the time zone. Use absolute windows in UTC or with an explicit offset. Relative windows (“last 24 hours”) drift if a search reruns.

Which Log Formats Can You Analyze in LogTotal?
items.summary: LogTotal accepts three kinds of files: Windows event logs in EVTX, JSON (one event per line works best), and syslog-style text. Text and JSON uploads go through the sanitize step before analysis; EVTX files don’t yet. If your logs are in some other shape, there’s almost always a one-line command that converts them. The common ones are listed below. LogTotal is SOC Prime’s free service for running detection logic against a log file without setting anything up: upload, sanitize, review. Getting the format right is the only part that can trip you up, so this page is the short version. Get Started For Free What LogTotal reads today Format Typical sources Sanitized before analysis? How to get it EVTX Windows Security, System, Sysmon, PowerShell, Defender, DNS Server Not yet [EVTX export guide], [Sysmon], [PowerShell] JSON / JSON lines CloudTrail, Entra ID, Microsoft 365, Google Cloud, Okta, Workspace, Kubernetes audit, journalctl -o json, SIEM API exports Yes [CloudTrail], [Entra ID], [journalctl], [Sentinel] Syslog-style text auth.log and secure, Splunk raw exports, QRadar payloads, firewall syslog Yes [sshd logs], [Splunk], [QRadar] CSV Entra ID sign-in/audit downloads, Microsoft 365 audit log exports, Google Workspace audit exports, Splunk / Sentinel / Kibana search results, Event Viewer “Save as CSV” Yes [Entra ID CSV], [M365 audit export], [Splunk CSV], [Event Viewer CSV] Getting JSON right One event per line is the safest shape. Many tools wrap events in arrays or envelopes. Flatten them before uploading: You have Flatten with A JSON array (gcloud, az, many APIs) jq -c ‘.[]’ in.json > out.jsonl CloudTrail log files jq -c ‘.Records[]’ *.json > out.jsonl aws cloudtrail lookup-events output jq -c ‘.Events[].CloudTrailEvent | fromjson’ in.json > out.jsonl CloudWatch Logs events jq -c ‘.events[].message | fromjson’ in.json > out.jsonl Splunk REST JSON export jq -c ‘select(.result) | .result’ in.json > out.jsonl Watch the encoding on Windows. Windows PowerShell 5.1 writes UTF-16 when you use > or Out-File without options. Add -Encoding utf8, as every PowerShell example in our guides does. Keep the time zone. ISO 8601 timestamps with Z or an offset make findings line up with other sources. Classic syslog timestamps have no year and no zone; note the source’s time zone when you upload them. No. Uploads are analyzed and not retained. Will more formats be supported? Yes. We add formats regularly, and this page always lists what works today.

items.title: Guardz Brings Palo Alto Networks Prisma Browser Protection to Small Businesses
items.summary: Miami, United States, November 2nd, 2026, CyberNewswire Prisma Browser for Business joins Guardz to connect browser protection with email, identity and endpoint security, helping security teams investigate and respond to threats across the workspace Guardz , the Agentic Workspace Security platform built for managed service providers (MSPs), today announced the integration of Prisma Browser for Business from Palo Alto Networks. The integration connects browser protection with email, identity, endpoint, data and user risk, helping small businesses prevent threats and giving security experts the platform to streamline autonomous unified detection, investigation, and response to incidents across the workspace. Employees rely on browsers to access business applications, handle company information and use AI tools. But attacks often cross these environments: a phishing email can direct an employee to a fake login page, exposing credentials and putting connected accounts at risk. With Prisma Browser for Business built into Guardz, MSPs and the Guardz 24/7 managed detection and response (MDR) team can investigate related activity as a unified incident. If an employee clicks a phishing link, Prisma Browser for Business can block the malicious page, while Guardz correlates the browser event with the original email, related Microsoft 365 activity, and endpoint telemetry to support investigation and response for a single identity. “Identity is the new center of gravity in cybersecurity, and the browser has become the primary gateway to the modern workspace. Traditional security tools operate in silos, leaving critical gaps in visibility and response,” said Dor Eisner, CEO and Co-Founder of Guardz. “Together with Palo Alto Networks, we’re advancing a new era of identity-centric security operations, connecting signals across identity, browser, email, endpoint, and data into a unified security fabric that is powered by agents. Guardz enables MSPs to autonomously investigate, correlate, and respond to threats across the entire workspace, while giving small businesses the freedom to embrace AI securely and thrive. This is the future of cybersecurity: identity-centric, unified data fabric, and built for autonomous defense at scale,” Eisner added. Browser Protection Across the Workspace Powered by Prisma Browser for Business, the integration brings Palo Alto Networks’ browser security technology into the wider security service MSPs manage through Guardz. Capabilities include: Phishing and session-theft protection: Inline machine-learning phishing detection and Advanced URL Filtering help block malicious pages, including fake login pages and attacks designed to steal live session tokens. Malware and extension security: WildFire file analysis helps detect malicious files, while browser security scans uploads and downloads and identifies risky extensions. Connected investigation and response: Browser events are linked with email, identity and endpoint signals to support incident investigations through Guardz’s 24/7 MDR service. Simplified deployment: Guardz streamlines provisioning, setup and default configuration so MSPs can deploy browser protection within minutes. The streamlined deployment has also impressed early-access MSPs. “The rollout through our RMM was super smooth. Within minutes, the Prisma Browser for Business extension was on every Chrome and Edge profile, and it was quick and easy to configure and deploy,” said Kevin Kehoe of Datawise Networks. “For most small businesses, the browser is now the office. Working with Guardz brings Prisma Browser for Business into the security these organizations receive from the providers they already trust. It connects our browser protection with the wider coverage and support their MSP delivers, helping safeguard the applications and information employees use every day,” said Shivam Srivastava, VP Product at Palo Alto Networks. AI Usage and Control As employees increasingly use browser-based generative AI tools, small businesses need practical ways to manage which services are permitted and how company information is shared. Guardz AI Usage and Control capabilities let technicians apply client-specific policies, including restrictions on copying, pasting, uploading and downloading files by website or category. Complementing these controls, Guardz has introduced an AI usage report that gives MSPs a per-client view of AI tool usage based on all signals. The controls help enforce usage policies, while the report provides visibility into adoption. About Guardz Guardz delivers Agentic Workspace Security, helping MSPs protect the small businesses they serve. The platform unifies protection across identities, email, endpoints and browsers, alongside adaptive security awareness and user risk, connecting signals around each identity to give security teams the context to act. The Guardz 24/7 agentic MDR provides triage and response at machine speed, supported by an elite research and threat hunting team. Learn more at guardz.com . About Palo Alto Networks Palo Alto Networks is the world’s cybersecurity leader. We innovate to outpace cyberthreats, so organizations can embrace technology with confidence. We provide next-gen cybersecurity to thousands of customers globally, across all sectors. Our best-in-class cybersecurity platforms and services are backed by industry-leading threat intelligence and strengthened by state-of-the-art automation. Whether delivering Next-Generation Firewalls, pioneering Agentic AI security, or driving continuous frontier defense via Unit 42, we are committed to helping safely navigate the evolving digital landscape. Contact Omri Hurwitz omri@omrihurwitz.com

items.title: Windows Event Log Permissions: Who Can Export EVTX
items.summary: Administrators can read and export every event log, but only from an elevated prompt. For everyone else, the built-in Event Log Readers group grants read access to most logs, locally and remotely, without admin rights. Add the account with net localgroup “Event Log Readers” /add, then sign out and back in. A handful of channels set their own permissions; wevtutil gl shows exactly who can read a given log. Analysts, log collectors and IR partners all need event logs, and none of them should need to be local admins for it. This guide covers the least-privilege setup and the reasons “Access is denied” shows up even when you think you have rights. Get Started For Free Who can do what Action Who, by default Read and export most logs Administrators (elevated) and Event Log Readers Read the Security log Administrators (elevated); Event Log Readers Clear the Security log or change auditing Accounts with “Manage auditing and security log” (Administrators) Change a log’s size or retention Administrators Read logs from another machine Same rights as locally, plus the firewall open for remote event log access Why admins still get “Access is denied” User Account Control. A non-elevated session runs with a filtered token, without the Administrators group. Event Viewer and wevtutil then behave as if you were a normal user. Right-click, Run as administrator , and try again. It’s the most common cause by far. Add an account to Event Log Readers On one machine: net localgroup "Event Log Readers" analyst /add or in PowerShell: Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Event Log Readers" -Member "CORP\analyst" Sign out and back in; group membership is read at logon. Across a domain, use Group Policy (Restricted Groups, or Group Policy Preferences → Local Users and Groups) to put a domain group into Event Log Readers on every machine. On domain controllers, Event Log Readers is a domain-wide built-in group, so one change covers all DCs. Check a specific log’s permissions wevtutil gl Security Look at channelAccess. It’s an SDDL string, and the part that matters looks like (A;;0x1;;;S-1-5-32-573): A means allow, 0x1 means read, and S-1-5-32-573 is Event Log Readers. If a channel’s SDDL doesn’t include that SID, Event Log Readers can’t read it. You can change a channel’s access with wevtutil sl /ca: , but it’s easy to get wrong. Prefer group membership where you can. Remote access Firewall. Event Viewer’s “Connect to Another Computer”, wevtutil /r: and Get-WinEvent -ComputerName use RPC. Enable the rule group on the target: Enable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup “Remote Event Log Management”. PowerShell remoting (Invoke-Command) uses WinRM instead. That’s often already open where RPC isn’t. Windows Event Forwarding. To forward the Security log, add NETWORK SERVICE to Event Log Readers on the source machines. Without it, a subscription can look healthy and deliver no Security events. A note on uploading EVTX Having rights to export a log doesn’t make every destination fine. LogTotal doesn’t sanitize EVTX files yet. Treat an EVTX upload as handing over the raw file, or convert it to JSON first. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Access is denied as an admin Session isn’t elevated Run as administrator Access is denied in Event Log Readers Membership not active yet, or the channel has custom permissions Sign out and in; check wevtutil gl The RPC server is unavailable Remote event log firewall rules are off Enable “Remote Event Log Management” on the target WEF delivers everything except Security NETWORK SERVICE isn’t in Event Log Readers Add it on the sources Can read the log, but the export fails No write access to the target folder Export somewhere you can write, e.g. C:\Users\ \

items.title: How to Read Linux Logs Without Root (Permissions Guide)
items.summary: On most distributions, two group memberships cover nearly everything an analyst needs: adm for the text logs in /var/log on Debian and Ubuntu, and systemd-journal for the full system journal. Add the account with sudo usermod -aG adm,systemd-journal and start a new login session. A few logs stay root-only by design, notably /var/log/secure and /var/log/messages on Red Hat-family systems and everything under /var/log/audit.
