items.title: CVE-2026-112816: Critical LXD and MicroCloud Authentication Bypass Enables Cluster Takeover
items.summary: Canonical has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-112816, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability affecting LXD and MicroCloud. The flaw carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0 and can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to impersonate a trusted TLS client without possessing that client’s private key. Successful exploitation can provide access to the LXD or MicroCloud API with the privileges assigned to the impersonated identity. When the trusted identity has sufficient permissions, an attacker may gain full access to the cluster, managed virtual machines, and potentially root-level access to the underlying host. The vulnerability stems from improper validation of client certificate chains used for mutual TLS authentication. Instead of authenticating only the leaf certificate for which the client proves possession of the corresponding private key, vulnerable implementations compare every certificate supplied in the client-controlled chain against trusted certificates. An attacker who can reach the HTTPS API and obtain the public certificate of an already trusted client can therefore append that certificate behind an attacker-controlled leaf certificate and be accepted as the trusted identity. Canonical disclosed the issue in late October 2026 after the vulnerability was referred by the Incus project. Fixed LXD and MicroCloud releases are now available, and administrators are strongly advised to update immediately. The flaw is especially significant in infrastructure environments because LXD manages system containers and virtual machines, while MicroCloud coordinates clustered infrastructure. Compromise of an administrative identity can therefore extend beyond a single service and provide control over workloads or the host itself. For CVE-2026-112816 detection, security teams should prioritize identifying internet- or network-accessible LXD and MicroCloud HTTPS APIs, reviewing trusted client certificates, and correlating successful certificate-based authentication with unexpected source systems or unusual administrative operations. SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform enables security teams to strengthen coverage for exploitation and post-compromise behavior across network, Linux, cloud, container, and identity telemetry. Contact Sales Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-112816, defenders should combine vulnerable-version inventory with API access monitoring, certificate authentication telemetry, and suspicious administrative activity affecting containers, virtual machines, or cluster configuration. CVE-2026-112816 analysis CVE-2026-112816 is an improper certificate validation vulnerability in the HTTPS listener used by Canonical LXD and MicroCloud. Both products can use mutual TLS to authenticate remote clients. Under normal mTLS behavior, the connecting client presents a certificate and proves ownership of the private key associated with the certificate used as the leaf of the TLS chain. The problem arises because vulnerable LXD and MicroCloud implementations inspect more than that authenticated leaf certificate. According to Canonical, remote API authentication logic compared all certificates presented by a client against entries in the trusted certificate store. However, TLS proves private-key possession only for the leaf certificate. Additional certificates in the presented chain are supplied by the client and do not independently prove ownership of their corresponding private keys. This creates an authentication gap. An attacker can generate a certificate and private key they control, use that certificate as the leaf, and append the public certificate of a trusted client elsewhere in the presented chain. The vulnerable server may find the trusted certificate and associate the connection with that trusted identity even though the attacker does not possess its private key. The details for CVE-2026-112816 therefore show that exploitation depends primarily on two prerequisites: The attacker can reach the LXD or MicroCloud HTTPS API. The attacker possesses the public certificate of an identity already trusted by the target. The trusted client’s private key is not required. This distinction explains the vulnerability’s critical severity. Certificate-based authentication is expected to demonstrate possession of a secret private key, but the affected logic effectively allows possession of the public certificate alone to satisfy part of the trust decision. A standalone LXD installation does not expose its remote HTTPS API by default. The Hacker News notes that LXD normally listens only on its local Unix socket unless an administrator enables network access, for example through the core.https_address configuration. This means not every vulnerable LXD installation is remotely exploitable from another host. Exposure becomes significantly higher when administrators enable the API across a management network or expose it to the internet. MicroCloud presents another relevant attack scenario. Canonical states that an attacker who can intercept the public TLS certificate of a machine joining a MicroCloud cluster may subsequently authenticate as that joined member. CVE-2026-112816 affects vulnerable Canonical LXD releases including 4.0.14, 5.0.10, 5.21.8, and 6.9 before their corresponding fixed releases. Canonical lists these patched LXD versions: LXD 6.10.1 for the 6/stable channel LXD 5.21.9 for 5.21/stable LXD 5.0.11 for 5.0/stable LXD 4.0.15 for 4.0/stable For MicroCloud, fixed versions are: MicroCloud 3.4.1 for 3/stable MicroCloud 2.1.5 for 2/stable Ubuntu’s CVE record describes successful exploitation as allowing an unauthenticated attacker to authenticate as a trusted client and gain full access to the cluster and managed virtual machines through a crafted certificate chain. The maximum CVSS score of 10.0 reflects network accessibility, low attack complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction, combined with potentially high impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Impact ultimately depends on the privileges of the identity being impersonated. A restricted identity may provide limited API capabilities. A highly privileged client or cluster identity can provide substantially greater access. Canonical explicitly warns that impersonation of a privileged trusted user can result in root access to the host machine. That can potentially allow an attacker to: Manage or modify containers and virtual machines. Access workloads managed through the compromised LXD environment. Modify infrastructure configuration. Create new workloads or alter existing ones. Interfere with availability. Access data available to the impersonated identity. Potentially reach the host with root-level privileges when sufficient permissions are available. The flaw was originally identified in the related Incus project and then referred to Canonical, which confirmed that the same certificate-chain authentication problem affected LXD. Incus describes the underlying issue similarly: the server requested client certificates without verifying the entire submitted chain, while trust checks iterated across every supplied peer certificate rather than restricting authentication to the actual leaf certificate. Incus addressed the issue in version 7.6.0. The vulnerability appears to have existed for an extended period. Incus states that the equivalent authentication logic had been present since its initial release. Canonical’s public advisory does not provide an exact date for when the vulnerable LXD behavior was first introduced. As of November 2, 2026, an independent CVE-2026-112816 PoC and lab reproduction have been published publicly. This represents a change from The Hacker News report published on November 1, which stated that no working exploit had yet been released. The public reproduction appeared after disclosure and is not the original vulnerability research. Canonical and the referenced reporting have not indicated that the vulnerability has been exploited in real-world attacks. The Hacker News reports that the issue was not known to be exploited as of the U.S. CISA assessment dated October 30 and was not included in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog at that time. There are therefore no campaign-specific CVE-2026-112816 IOCs such as confirmed malicious IP addresses, domains, malware hashes, or known attacker infrastructure associated with exploitation. Defenders should instead focus on vulnerability exposure and behavior. Potential hunting opportunities include: Remote connections to LXD or MicroCloud HTTPS APIs from unexpected systems. Successful API authentication originating from networks not normally used by trusted administrators. A trusted certificate identity appearing from multiple unrelated source systems. Administrative API activity that does not match the expected owner of a certificate. Unexpected creation, deletion, or modification of containers and virtual machines. Changes to trusted certificate entries. New or altered cluster members. Unexpected changes to storage, networking, profiles, projects, or instance configuration. Privileged operations occurring shortly after unusual certificate-based authentication. API connections to management interfaces that were not intended to be remotely accessible. Organizations should also inventory trusted certificates associated with former administrators, retired hosts, automation systems, and cluster members. Because exploitation requires the public certificate rather than the private key, defenders should not treat the confidentiality of private keys alone as sufficient protection against this specific vulnerability. Monitoring should also account for shared management networks. An API that is not exposed directly to the public internet can still be exploitable by an attacker who has already gained a foothold on another system capable of reaching the management interface. This makes lateral movement particularly relevant. A compromised workstation, server, CI/CD runner, management host, or cloud workload with network access to the LXD API could provide the position needed to exploit an otherwise internally exposed system. CVE-2026-112816 Mitigation Canonical recommends upgrading affected LXD and MicroCloud deployments to the latest fixed versions immediately. For Snap-based deployments, administrators can update using: sudo snap refresh lxd and: sudo snap refresh microcloud After refreshing, verify the version actually installed rather than assuming that the update was applied successfully. Canonical noted during disclosure that some LXD point releases were progressing from candidate to stable channels. Administrators should therefore explicitly confirm that their system is running one of the fixed versions. The primary CVE-2026-112816 mitigation is upgrading to: Product Fixed version LXD 6.x 6.10.1 LXD 5.21 5.21.9 LXD 5.0 5.0.11 LXD 4.0 4.0.15 MicroCloud 3.x 3.4.1 MicroCloud 2.x 2.1.5 Canonical has not published a configuration-based workaround that fully eliminates the underlying authentication defect. If immediate upgrading is impossible, restrict network access to the HTTPS API as aggressively as operational requirements allow. Only authorized management hosts and trusted infrastructure should be able to establish connections to the listener. For LXD installations that do not require remote management, administrators should evaluate whether the network API needs to remain enabled at all. For environments that require remote access: Restrict the API using host or network firewalls. Permit connections only from dedicated management networks. Avoid exposing the API directly to the public internet. Use VPN or bastion-based administrative access where appropriate. Segment container and virtualization management infrastructure from user networks. Monitor all successful administrative API requests. Review trusted certificates and remove entries that are no longer necessary. These controls reduce exposure but do not correct the vulnerable certificate-validation logic. Organizations running MicroCloud should prioritize updating all relevant cluster members and review recent joining activity for unexpected systems or certificate identities. Administrators should also review their trusted certificate stores. Remove certificates belonging to decommissioned hosts, former administrators, unused automation systems, or identities that no longer require access. Where suspicious activity is discovered, investigate the affected host and cluster before rotating credentials or modifying evidence. Relevant sources of telemetry may include: LXD and MicroCloud service logs Linux system logs Firewall and network flow records Reverse proxy telemetry, if applicable Host EDR data Cloud network logs Cluster configuration and membership history Administrative change records Look for unexpected instance creation, modification, deletion, snapshot activity, storage operations, networking changes, and configuration updates. If exploitation is suspected and a privileged certificate identity was impersonated, defenders should treat potential host-level compromise seriously because Canonical confirms that root access may be possible depending on the victim identity’s permissions. Incident responders should preserve relevant evidence and inspect the system for persistence, unauthorized accounts or certificates, modified services, new workloads, suspicious processes, and abnormal outbound network communication. Organizations using Incus rather than Canonical LXD should separately update to Incus 7.6.0 or the relevant supported fixed release because the related project was affected by the same underlying certificate-chain trust issue. Ubuntu also notes that its archive-packaged LXD versions for currently listed Ubuntu releases are either not shipped through the affected package path or not affected, while Canonical’s security guidance focuses on the Snap releases. Administrators should still verify the actual LXD distribution and version running in their environment rather than assuming exposure based solely on the Ubuntu release. Disclaimer: Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. FAQ What is CVE-2026-112816 and how does it work? CVE-2026-112816 is a critical improper certificate validation vulnerability affecting Canonical LXD and MicroCloud. Vulnerable servers compare multiple certificates supplied in a client-controlled TLS chain against trusted certificates instead of limiting the authentication decision to the leaf certificate for which private-key possession was actually demonstrated. An attacker who can reach the HTTPS API and obtains the public certificate of a trusted identity can potentially authenticate as that identity without possessing its private key. When was CVE-2026-112816 first discovered? The issue was referred to Canonical by the Incus project and publicly disclosed by Canonical in late October 2026. Canonical’s security advisory was published on October 28, fixed releases followed across the relevant channels, and the CVE record was published on October 30. The available Canonical sources do not provide the exact date on which researchers first identified the underlying flaw. What is the impact of CVE-2026-112816 on systems? Successful exploitation can allow an unauthenticated attacker to impersonate a trusted LXD or MicroCloud client. The attacker receives the access associated with the impersonated identity, potentially including control over the cluster and managed virtual machines. If the trusted identity is sufficiently privileged, Canonical warns that exploitation can result in root access to the host. The flaw carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0. Can CVE-2026-112816 still affect me in 2026? Yes. LXD or MicroCloud systems that remain on vulnerable versions can still be exposed, particularly when their HTTPS API is reachable from an attacker-controlled system. The risk is higher when remote API access is broadly exposed and trusted client certificates can be obtained. There is currently no confirmed evidence in the referenced sources of exploitation in the wild, but public technical reproduction is now available, increasing the importance of prompt patching. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-112816? Upgrade LXD to 6.10.1, 5.21.9, 5.0.11, or 4.0.15 as appropriate, and update MicroCloud to 3.4.1 or 2.1.5. Verify the installed version after updating. Until patching is complete, restrict access to the HTTPS API to trusted management hosts and networks. Canonical does not provide a configuration workaround that fully fixes the certificate-validation flaw, so upgrading remains the primary remediation.

CVE-2026-112816 is an improper certificate validation vulnerability in the HTTPS listener used by Canonical LXD and MicroCloud.

Both products can use mutual TLS to authenticate remote clients. Under normal mTLS behavior, the connecting client presents a certificate and proves ownership of the private key associated with the certificate used as the leaf of the TLS chain.

The problem arises because vulnerable LXD and MicroCloud implementations inspect more than that authenticated leaf certificate.

According to Canonical, remote API authentication logic compared all certificates presented by a client against entries in the trusted certificate store. However, TLS proves private-key possession only for the leaf certificate. Additional certificates in the presented chain are supplied by the client and do not independently prove ownership of their corresponding private keys.

This creates an authentication gap.

An attacker can generate a certificate and private key they control, use that certificate as the leaf, and append the public certificate of a trusted client elsewhere in the presented chain. The vulnerable server may find the trusted certificate and associate the connection with that trusted identity even though the attacker does not possess its private key.

The details for CVE-2026-112816 therefore show that exploitation depends primarily on two prerequisites:

  • The attacker can reach the LXD or MicroCloud HTTPS API.
  • The attacker possesses the public certificate of an identity already trusted by the target.

The trusted client’s private key is not required.

This distinction explains the vulnerability’s critical severity. Certificate-based authentication is expected to demonstrate possession of a secret private key, but the affected logic effectively allows possession of the public certificate alone to satisfy part of the trust decision.

MicroCloud presents another relevant attack scenario. Canonical states that an attacker who can intercept the public TLS certificate of a machine joining a MicroCloud cluster may subsequently authenticate as that joined member.

CVE-2026-112816 affects vulnerable Canonical LXD releases including 4.0.14, 5.0.10, 5.21.8, and 6.9 before their corresponding fixed releases.

  • LXD 6.10.1 for the 6/stable channel
  • LXD 5.21.9 for 5.21/stable
  • LXD 5.0.11 for 5.0/stable
  • LXD 4.0.15 for 4.0/stable

For MicroCloud, fixed versions are:

  • MicroCloud 3.4.1 for 3/stable
  • MicroCloud 2.1.5 for 2/stable

Ubuntu’s CVE record describes successful exploitation as allowing an unauthenticated attacker to authenticate as a trusted client and gain full access to the cluster and managed virtual machines through a crafted certificate chain.

The maximum CVSS score of 10.0 reflects network accessibility, low attack complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction, combined with potentially high impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Impact ultimately depends on the privileges of the identity being impersonated.

A restricted identity may provide limited API capabilities. A highly privileged client or cluster identity can provide substantially greater access.

Canonical explicitly warns that impersonation of a privileged trusted user can result in root access to the host machine.

That can potentially allow an attacker to:

  • Manage or modify containers and virtual machines.
  • Access workloads managed through the compromised LXD environment.
  • Modify infrastructure configuration.
  • Create new workloads or alter existing ones.
  • Interfere with availability.
  • Access data available to the impersonated identity.

This represents a change from The Hacker News report published on November 1, which stated that no working exploit had yet been released. The public reproduction appeared after disclosure and is not the original vulnerability research.

Canonical and the referenced reporting have not indicated that the vulnerability has been exploited in real-world attacks.

The Hacker News reports that the issue was not known to be exploited as of the U.S. CISA assessment dated October 30 and was not included in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog at that time.

There are therefore no campaign-specific CVE-2026-112816 IOCs such as confirmed malicious IP addresses, domains, malware hashes, or known attacker infrastructure associated with exploitation.

Defenders should instead focus on vulnerability exposure and behavior.

Potential hunting opportunities include:

  • Remote connections to LXD or MicroCloud HTTPS APIs from unexpected systems.
  • Successful API authentication originating from networks not normally used by trusted administrators.
  • A trusted certificate identity appearing from multiple unrelated source systems.
  • Administrative API activity that does not match the expected owner of a certificate.
  • Unexpected creation, deletion, or modification of containers and virtual machines.
  • Changes to trusted certificate entries.
  • New or altered cluster members.
  • Unexpected changes to storage, networking, profiles, projects, or instance configuration.
  • Privileged operations occurring shortly after unusual certificate-based authentication.
  • API connections to management interfaces that were not intended to be remotely accessible.

Because exploitation requires the public certificate rather than the private key, defenders should not treat the confidentiality of private keys alone as sufficient protection against this specific vulnerability.

Monitoring should also account for shared management networks.

An API that is not exposed directly to the public internet can still be exploitable by an attacker who has already gained a foothold on another system capable of reaching the management interface.

sudo snap refresh lxd

and:

sudo snap refresh microcloud

For LXD installations that do not require remote management, administrators should evaluate whether the network API needs to remain enabled at all.

For environments that require remote access:

  • Restrict the API using host or network firewalls.
  • Permit connections only from dedicated management networks.
  • Avoid exposing the API directly to the public internet.
  • Use VPN or bastion-based administrative access where appropriate.
  • Segment container and virtualization management infrastructure from user networks.
  • Monitor all successful administrative API requests.
  • Review trusted certificates and remove entries that are no longer necessary.

Administrators should also review their trusted certificate stores.

Remove certificates belonging to decommissioned hosts, former administrators, unused automation systems, or identities that no longer require access.

Where suspicious activity is discovered, investigate the affected host and cluster before rotating credentials or modifying evidence.

Relevant sources of telemetry may include:

  • LXD and MicroCloud service logs
  • Linux system logs
  • Firewall and network flow records
  • Reverse proxy telemetry, if applicable
  • Host EDR data
  • Cloud network logs
  • Cluster configuration and membership history
  • Administrative change records

Look for unexpected instance creation, modification, deletion, snapshot activity, storage operations, networking changes, and configuration updates.

If exploitation is suspected and a privileged certificate identity was impersonated, defenders should treat potential host-level compromise seriously because Canonical confirms that root access may be possible depending on the victim identity’s permissions.

Incident responders should preserve relevant evidence and inspect the system for persistence, unauthorized accounts or certificates, modified services, new workloads, suspicious processes, and abnormal outbound network communication.

Organizations using Incus rather than Canonical LXD should separately update to Incus 7.6.0 or the relevant supported fixed release because the related project was affected by the same underlying certificate-chain trust issue.

Ubuntu also notes that its archive-packaged LXD versions for currently listed Ubuntu releases are either not shipped through the affected package path or not affected, while Canonical’s security guidance focuses on the Snap releases. Administrators should still verify the actual LXD distribution and version running in their environment rather than assuming exposure based solely on the Ubuntu release.

Disclaimer: Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-112816 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-112816 is a critical improper certificate validation vulnerability affecting Canonical LXD and MicroCloud. Vulnerable servers compare multiple certificates supplied in a client-controlled TLS chain against trusted certificates instead of limiting the authentication decision to the leaf certificate for which private-key possession was actually demonstrated. An attacker who can reach the HTTPS API and obtains the public certificate of a trusted identity can potentially authenticate as that identity without possessing its private key.

When was CVE-2026-112816 first discovered?

The issue was referred to Canonical by the Incus project and publicly disclosed by Canonical in late October 2026. Canonical’s security advisory was published on October 28, fixed releases followed across the relevant channels, and the CVE record was published on October 30. The available Canonical sources do not provide the exact date on which researchers first identified the underlying flaw.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-112816 on systems?

Successful exploitation can allow an unauthenticated attacker to impersonate a trusted LXD or MicroCloud client. The attacker receives the access associated with the impersonated identity, potentially including control over the cluster and managed virtual machines. If the trusted identity is sufficiently privileged, Canonical warns that exploitation can result in root access to the host. The flaw carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0.

Can CVE-2026-112816 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. LXD or MicroCloud systems that remain on vulnerable versions can still be exposed, particularly when their HTTPS API is reachable from an attacker-controlled system. The risk is higher when remote API access is broadly exposed and trusted client certificates can be obtained. There is currently no confirmed evidence in the referenced sources of exploitation in the wild, but public technical reproduction is now available, increasing the importance of prompt patching.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-112816?

Upgrade LXD to 6.10.1, 5.21.9, 5.0.11, or 4.0.15 as appropriate, and update MicroCloud to 3.4.1 or 2.1.5. Verify the installed version after updating. Until patching is complete, restrict access to the HTTPS API to trusted management hosts and networks. Canonical does not provide a configuration workaround that fully fixes the certificate-validation flaw, so upgrading remains the primary remediation.

items.title: 5 stars for sale: Inside the underground fake review trade
items.summary: Recently, our team exposed sophisticated scam kits designed to steal sensitive data and trick consumers. But underground marketplaces are not just for malware and stolen passwords. They also offer services designed to manipulate your opinion of the products and services you buy every day. In our latest research, we examined cybercrime forums where sellers advertise illicit “reputation management” services. For the right price, these underground operators offer to flood a product with glowing, five-star ratings or remove negative reviews. This shadowy industry works both ways—artificially boosting reputations and deliberately hiding legitimate complaints. A major shift we are seeing in this space is the adoption of new technology. We also found that cybercriminals are using AI to automate these fake review campaigns. This could allow them to quickly generate realistic, human-sounding feedback in large volumes without much manual effort. 5 stars as a service In the first example, discovered on a major English-language underground forum, a seller operating under the handle “aqenova” advertises both five-star review generation and negative review removal services. The seller’s operations span widely used platforms, including Google, Trustpilot, Yelp, and various mobile app stores. By simply asking prospective buyers, “Just tell me which platform reviews you need?” the seller presents reputation manipulation as something buyers can just order on demand. Five-star reviews and removal services Decoding the seller’s FAQ Analyzing another seller’s (TrustForge) “Frequently Asked Questions” section revealed some surprising details about how these operations reportedly run behind the scenes. First, the seller emphasizes that real people manually post these reviews, offering a guarantee for both successful delivery and “non-drop”—meaning the platform won’t flag and remove the feedback later. Remember, a real person posting a review doesn’t mean they’re a real customer. The important question is whether they actually used the product or service and are describing an honest experience. Second, it appears this is a well-coordinated team effort rather than a solo operation, as the seller charges an extra fee if a buyer wants the main operator to write the review text personally. However, what caught our attention most was their confidence in beating platform checks. The seller guarantees their fake reviews will stay active, claiming they rely on a closely guarded “private method.” According to TrustForge’s own statements, this method has allowed them to post more than 10,000 fake reviews. Reputation management FAQ The clean-up crew: Making bad reviews disappear A single negative review is often all it takes to create a bad first impression of a product or service. When those negative comments start to pile up, they can completely ruin a business’s reputation and bottom line. Recognizing how desperate businesses can be to protect their image, our research team discovered underground services specifically offering to remove “fake” or “unfair” reviews from major platforms like Google and Trustpilot. Of course, the boundary between what is genuinely fake and what a business simply considers “unfair” can be blurry. Businesses can legitimately challenge fabricated reviews, but these services raise concerns about whether genuine customer complaints could also be targeted. If legitimate customer complaints disappear, consumers lose information that could help them decide where to spend their money. An offer to remove “fake” or “unfair” Google reviews An offer to remove ”fake” or “unfair” review Google reviews On average, having a single review removed through these underground services costs between $100 and $200 . However, the pricing jumps dramatically depending on the platform. For instance, one seller advertised Airbnb review removal for around $1,100 per review. When you check a business’s reviews, you’re looking for patterns in other customers’ experiences. If genuine complaints disappear, you could miss repeated problems with refunds, product quality, or customer service. $1,100 to remove a “fake” or “unfair” Airbnb review Artificial intelligence, artificial reviews During the last few months, our research team spotted an interesting thread on an underground forum where two users discussed using AI to mimic human E-E-A-T. E-E-A-T stands for Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness. It is a quality evaluation framework outlined in Google’s Search Quality Rater Guidelines , which human evaluators use to assess content quality. E-E-A-T itself is not a direct ranking factor. In the discussion we observed, one user asked the community if it was possible to use AI to effectively fake these qualities when writing product reviews and artificially boost website rankings. The answer was a resounding yes. Another user claimed they had never experienced problems getting Google to index their completely AI-generated reviews. AI vs. E-E-A-T Behind the scenes: The IP addresses for fake reviews To keep fake reviews from being flagged and deleted, scammers need to look like everyday consumers. To help do this, they can use something called “residential and mobile proxies,” which route their traffic through other internet connections to disguise where it comes from. Think of an IP address as your computer’s caller ID. When scammers use bulk IP addresses from giant data centers, platforms may spot and block that traffic as coming from commercially hosted infrastructure. Residential proxies, on the other hand, route traffic through real, physical home internet connections—just like the Wi-Fi you use in your living room. Mobile proxies work the same way, but use real cellular networks. Our team recently discovered a seller on an underground forum acting as a direct supplier of these residential and mobile connections. The seller explicitly advertises them as perfect for running fake review campaigns. Residential and mobile proxies advertised for fake review campaigns How to avoid being misled by fake reviews The main goal of this research isn’t to make you panic or stop trusting every online review you read. We want to raise awareness about what happens behind the scenes, so you can make more informed buying decisions. If a product or offer seems too good to be true, but is backed by a mountain of perfect five-star reviews, take a moment to pause. Scammers often use these artificially boosted ratings to make a bad deal look reassuring. Read recent reviews and some of the middle-rated ones, rather than relying on the overall score. Look for recurring details about the things that matter to you, such as durability, delivery, or getting your money back. Look for repeated wording or sudden bursts of glowing feedback. These signs don’t prove a review is fake, but they’re reasons to take a closer look. Check the seller’s contact details and return policy, too. Malwarebytes Browser Guard can also help block scam, phishing, and malicious websites you may encounter while shopping. Unsure about an offer, even with glowing reviews? Share the link or a screenshot with Malwarebytes Scam Guard for help checking for signs of a scam before you buy. Stop threats before they can do any harm. Malwarebytes Browser Guard blocks phishing pages and malicious sites automatically. Free, one click to install. Add it to your browser →

items.title: Applebee’s customer data exposed by password left in app
items.summary: Applebee’s has fixed a security flaw that exposed customers’ personal information after a researcher discovered a database password embedded in the restaurant chain’s Android app. The researcher, Robert Wiggins, found the password with help from AI . It gave him access to an internal Applebee’s customer database. A password written directly into an app’s code or configuration is known as a hardcoded credential. Anyone who extracts it may be able to use it to access the system. The exposed database contained: Names, email addresses, and email-verification status Dates of birth, phone numbers, and ZIP codes Veteran status Account-creation dates and login counts IP addresses from customers’ most recent logins, which can indicate their approximate location TechCrunch independently checked Wiggins’ findings. It created an Applebee’s account with dummy information, which Wiggins successfully retrieved from the database. According to TechCrunch, Wiggins could not find a suitable way to report the issue to Applebee’s or its parent company, Dine Brands, so he asked the publication to help contact them. TechCrunch held its story until the fix was confirmed. Applebee’s confirmed on October 29 that it had addressed the issue. It’s unclear how many customers’ records were in the database. Dine Brands says it has not found evidence of unauthorized access, but its investigation is ongoing. How to stay safe The database fields described by TechCrunch did not include payment card details or account passwords. That does not tell us whether anyone accessed the database before the fix, so customers should watch for targeted scams. Names, email addresses, phone numbers, and other personal details could help scammers make messages look relevant and convincing. Be wary of unexpected Applebee’s-themed emails, texts, or calls. Be especially skeptical of messages offering refunds or compensation, warning that your account will be closed, or asking you to “verify” payment details. Check security notices through a route you trust. Open the app directly or visit Applebee’s website yourself rather than following a link in an unexpected message. If necessary, contact the company using details you find independently. Unsure whether a message is a scam? Check it with Malwarebytes’ Scam Guard for an assessment and advice on what to do next. When sharing personal information, consider why the company needs it and whether you trust it to keep the information safe. Unsure where a link goes? We’ll check it. Check now

Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet
How we halved DNS build delay and cut memory use by 85%
items.summary: When I last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022 , the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as zone setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions. Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver . In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings. Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed? It should, and that is where we ended up. However, proving when it was safe took most of the work. A record event identifies what changed. A zone event can come from many Cloudflare products, may not say why the zone changed, and can alter data shared by several zones with the same name. Choosing too much work wastes capacity. Choosing too little can leave stale or incorrect DNS data at the edge. We built a targeted build planner that chooses the smallest build we can prove is safe, and a new scheduler that combines work for the same zone. Zone setting changes no longer rebuild zones with tens of millions of records. Together, they cut peak memory by 85%, and the extra headroom let us safely shorten waits the pipeline has always needed for resilience, halving the time from a DNS change to its data being written to Quicksilver. How DNS changes reach the edge A DNS zone is the collection of records and settings for a domain. Cloudflare uses a multi-stage pipeline to turn a change to that zone into data available across our global network . A customer changes a DNS record through the DNS Records API or dashboard, or another Cloudflare service changes a zone setting. The change is stored in a database. The database change or another system produces a Kafka event. The DNS Kafka Aggregator combines events from several Kafka topics and sends them to the Zone Builder. The Zone Builder reads the required zone data and converts it into keys understood by our authoritative DNS servers. The Zone Builder compares those keys with Quicksilver , our distributed key-value store. It writes only what changed, and Quicksilver propagates those changes across Cloudflare's network. This is a simplified view. The Zone Builder does not copy database rows directly to the edge. It combines records with zone settings, applies DNS serving rules, and organizes the result so our authoritative DNS servers can read it quickly. Why full builds stopped scaling The original Zone Builder had one useful property: it did not need to know why a zone changed. It rebuilt the desired state from the current database state. Read the current zone and its settings. Read every DNS record in the zone. Convert those records into Quicksilver keys. Compare the new keys with those already stored. Remove stale keys, write changed keys, and update zone metadata. The final write contains only changed keys. However, a full build still reads, encodes, and compares every record, and holds the whole zone in memory while it does so. That is cheap for a small zone. For our largest zones, with tens of millions of records, the zone does not fit in memory at all. I explain how we handle that below. Zone settings made targeting harder. Universal SSL is one example. Enabling or disabling it updates metadata and can change Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) records at the zone apex, the bare domain, such as example.com . CAA records tell certificate authorities whether they may issue a certificate for the domain. A full build only needed to know that the zone changed. A targeted build must answer three questions: Which DNS names can change? Can shared metadata or the list of published zones change? What previous state must be removed from Quicksilver? Answering those questions safely meant solving five problems, which the rest of this post covers in order: Events had to say what changed. Each change had to map to the smallest build that is still correct. Builds had to account for data shared by every zone with the same name. The database could change between the event and the build. Combining work could not lose a Kafka message. Making events say what changed We changed the event producer to include changed zone fields and settings, with previous and new values when available. We then traced each setting through the code that generates DNS output and classified what it could affect. Not every event was that specific. Some database functions only update a timestamp to say, in effect, "something about this zone changed." Sometimes that is harmless bookkeeping. Sometimes it means data changed elsewhere and must be read again. Those cases look identical in the event. Until we can identify the caller and its purpose, a timestamp-only update still causes a full build. The same rule applies to missing details, unknown events, or any change that may affect records anywhere in the zone. The planner never turns uncertainty into less work. Choosing the smallest safe build Quicksilver output has two parts that matter here. Record keys contain the DNS answers for one zone and name. A smaller shared metadata key tells our authoritative DNS servers how to use that zone, including where to find special records such as nameservers and wildcards. Some events change only record keys; others must update both. With that distinction, the planner can choose one of five build types: Resources only: Rebuild the records at specific DNS names, which we call resources, without changing zone metadata. Ordinary A, AAAA, TXT, and CNAME changes usually take this path. Resources and metadata: Rebuild specific names and shared metadata. Nameserver and wildcard changes use this path. Apex and metadata: Rebuild the zone apex and metadata. Settings such as Universal SSL can use this path. Purge: Remove a zone that should no longer be published. Full zone: Rebuild every record when smaller work cannot be proven safe. The rule is simple: every key a targeted build writes must be byte-for-byte identical to what a full build would write. If we cannot prove that, we do a full build. Removing old state works as it did for per-record builds in 2022. Record events include deleted records and the previous version of updated ones. The Zone Builder then scans Quicksilver for the existing keys under each name it rebuilds, removing any that the new build did not write. Full builds remain necessary when a change can affect records anywhere in the zone or when a zone may need to be published for the first time. There is one deliberate exception. A full build holds every record from the database and every existing Quicksilver key for the zone in memory at once, and our largest zones do not fit. Above a fixed record-count threshold, the Zone Builder never escalates to a full build. It rebuilds the apex, the metadata, and every name identified by the queued events instead. We accept this tradeoff because a full build of those zones cannot finish, and, while it retries, it holds back every other change on its Kafka partition. Many of the cases that would otherwise need a full build involve several zones sharing one name, and zone holds reduce that risk by stopping the same name from being added to another account. For the rare cases that remain, such as enabling a zone on another network, we can manually rebuild individual names in the zone. When one name means more than one zone Quicksilver stores each zone's record keys separately. It also stores one metadata key shared by every Cloudflare zone with that domain name. This shared key acts like a directory: it tells our authoritative DNS servers which internal zone IDs they may use when answering a query. Why can one name have several zone IDs? During customer onboarding, offboarding, and other lifecycle changes, multiple Cloudflare zone objects can briefly exist for the same public domain. We use a priority policy to choose a small, bounded set to publish. Consider four internal zones for example.com : Zone 101, Zone 202, Zone 303, and Zone 404. The metadata key currently lists Zones 101, 202, and 303. Zone 404 exists, but it is not selected. The numbers identify separate Cloudflare zone objects; customers still see one domain name. A TXT record change at www.example.com in Zone 202 affects only Zone 202's record keys, so the metadata key does not change. Nameserver and wildcard changes are different because the metadata key records information about them. Those builds must update both the zone's records and the metadata key. At execution time, the Zone Builder reads the current list again. If it writes the metadata key, it rebuilds the whole key from that fresh view rather than patching an older copy. It writes the triggering zone's records before the metadata that refers to them. Planning from the event, verifying before writing An event describes what happened in the past. A build may wait while more events arrive and the database changes, so planning happens twice. The event first creates a conservative work list. Immediately before execution, the Zone Builder reads a fresh publication snapshot: the current zone settings, whether this Zone Builder should publish the zone to its network, and which same-name zone IDs belong in the metadata key. Here, a network is a separate, isolated copy of Quicksilver for one environment. Each Zone Builder deployment writes to one network, and a zone can be enabled on some networks but not others. For example, a zone can be served from Cloudflare's global network and also from the China Network . Fresh state can change the result in four ways: A targeted build can become a full build if the zone now has a feature that requires complete-zone work. A build can become a purge if the zone should no longer be published to this network. A build can be skipped if the triggering zone no longer belongs in the metadata key. A metadata build can reconstruct the shared key from the current candidate set. The fresh read comes from read-only copies of the database, called replicas, so builds do not compete with customer writes. Kafka delivery and database replication move independently: an event can arrive before its database change is visible on a replica. The DNS Kafka Aggregator delays events long enough to cover normal lag, and a final database check rejects the read if that replica is still behind. Combining changes in one scheduler Record work and full-zone work previously used different schedulers. Each could combine its own work, but not work from the other scheduler. We replaced them with one unified scheduler. The planner decides what must be built, and the scheduler decides when it can run. When several events for one zone arrive before a build starts, the scheduler combines their work: An A record changes at www.example.com , requiring that name. A wildcard changes at *.example.com , requiring that name and shared metadata. The scheduler combines both names and the metadata update into one build. Merging only adds work. If any event requires the complete zone, the combined build becomes a full build. A purge overrides every rebuild because its desired result is that the zone is no longer published. The scheduler tracks two things separately: the DNS work that must be performed and the Kafka messages waiting to be acknowledged. A retry preserves both. Even when a full build or purge no longer needs the individual record names, the messages stay attached until the result is safely written. Keeping Kafka moving One slow build can delay unrelated customers even when workers are available. Kafka divides messages into ordered partitions. For each partition, it stores one committed offset: the point before which every message is known to be complete. Moving that offset past unfinished work could lose a customer change after a restart. When I last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022, the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as zone setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions.

Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver.

In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings.

Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed?

It should, and that is where we ended up. However, proving when it was safe took most of the work. A record event identifies what changed. A zone event can come from many Cloudflare products, may not say why the zone changed, and can alter data shared by several zones with the same name. Choosing too much work wastes capacity. Choosing too little can leave stale or incorrect DNS data at the edge.

We built a targeted build planner that chooses the smallest build we can prove is safe, and a new scheduler that combines work for the same zone. Zone setting changes no longer rebuild zones with tens of millions of records. Together, they cut peak memory by 85%, and the extra headroom let us safely shorten waits the pipeline has always needed for resilience, halving the time from a DNS change to its data being written to Quicksilver.

How DNS changes reach the edge

A DNS zone is the collection of records and settings for a domain. Cloudflare uses a multi-stage pipeline to turn a change to that zone into data available across our global network.

  1. A customer changes a DNS record through the DNS Records API or dashboard, or another Cloudflare service changes a zone setting.
  2. The change is stored in a database.
  3. The database change or another system produces a Kafka event.
  4. The DNS Kafka Aggregator combines events from several Kafka topics and sends them to the Zone Builder.
  5. The Zone Builder reads the required zone data and converts it into keys understood by our authoritative DNS servers.
  6. The Zone Builder compares those keys with Quicksilver, our distributed key-value store. It writes only what changed, and Quicksilver propagates those changes across Cloudflare's network.

This is a simplified view. The Zone Builder does not copy database rows directly to the edge. It combines records with zone settings, applies DNS serving rules, and organizes the result so our authoritative DNS servers can read it quickly.

Why full builds stopped scaling

The original Zone Builder had one useful property: it did not need to know why a zone changed. It rebuilt the desired state from the current database state.

  1. Read the current zone and its settings.
  2. Read every DNS record in the zone.
  3. Convert those records into Quicksilver keys.
  4. Compare the new keys with those already stored.
  5. Remove stale keys, write changed keys, and update zone metadata.

The final write contains only changed keys. However, a full build still reads, encodes, and compares every record, and holds the whole zone in memory while it does so. That is cheap for a small zone. For our largest zones, with tens of millions of records, the zone does not fit in memory at all. I explain how we handle that below.

Zone settings made targeting harder. Universal SSL is one example. Enabling or disabling it updates metadata and can change Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) records at the zone apex, the bare domain, such as example.com. CAA records tell certificate authorities whether they may issue a certificate for the domain.

A full build only needed to know that the zone changed. A targeted build must answer three questions:

  1. Which DNS names can change?
  2. Can shared metadata or the list of published zones change?
  3. What previous state must be removed from Quicksilver?

Answering those questions safely meant solving five problems, which the rest of this post covers in order:

  1. Events had to say what changed.
  2. Each change had to map to the smallest build that is still correct.
  3. Builds had to account for data shared by every zone with the same name.
  4. The database could change between the event and the build.
  5. Combining work could not lose a Kafka message.
Making events say what changed

We changed the event producer to include changed zone fields and settings, with previous and new values when available. We then traced each setting through the code that generates DNS output and classified what it could affect.

Not every event was that specific. Some database functions only update a timestamp to say, in effect, "something about this zone changed." Sometimes that is harmless bookkeeping. Sometimes it means data changed elsewhere and must be read again.

Those cases look identical in the event. Until we can identify the caller and its purpose, a timestamp-only update still causes a full build. The same rule applies to missing details, unknown events, or any change that may affect records anywhere in the zone. The planner never turns uncertainty into less work.

Choosing the smallest safe build

Quicksilver output has two parts that matter here. Record keys contain the DNS answers for one zone and name. A smaller shared metadata key tells our authoritative DNS servers how to use that zone, including where to find special records such as nameservers and wildcards. Some events change only record keys; others must update both.

With that distinction, the planner can choose one of five build types:

  1. Resources only: Rebuild the records at specific DNS names, which we call resources, without changing zone metadata. Ordinary A, AAAA, TXT, and CNAME changes usually take this path.
  2. Resources and metadata: Rebuild specific names and shared metadata. Nameserver and wildcard changes use this path.
  3. Apex and metadata: Rebuild the zone apex and metadata. Settings such as Universal SSL can use this path.
  4. Purge: Remove a zone that should no longer be published.
  5. Full zone: Rebuild every record when smaller work cannot be proven safe.

The rule is simple: every key a targeted build writes must be byte-for-byte identical to what a full build would write. If we cannot prove that, we do a full build.

Removing old state works as it did for per-record builds in 2022. Record events include deleted records and the previous version of updated ones. The Zone Builder then scans Quicksilver for the existing keys under each name it rebuilds, removing any that the new build did not write.

Full builds remain necessary when a change can affect records anywhere in the zone or when a zone may need to be published for the first time.

There is one deliberate exception. A full build holds every record from the database and every existing Quicksilver key for the zone in memory at once, and our largest zones do not fit. Above a fixed record-count threshold, the Zone Builder never escalates to a full build. It rebuilds the apex, the metadata, and every name identified by the queued events instead. We accept this tradeoff because a full build of those zones cannot finish, and, while it retries, it holds back every other change on its Kafka partition. Many of the cases that would otherwise need a full build involve several zones sharing one name, and zone holds reduce that risk by stopping the same name from being added to another account. For the rare cases that remain, such as enabling a zone on another network, we can manually rebuild individual names in the zone.

When one name means more than one zone

Quicksilver stores each zone's record keys separately. It also stores one metadata key shared by every Cloudflare zone with that domain name. This shared key acts like a directory: it tells our authoritative DNS servers which internal zone IDs they may use when answering a query.

Why can one name have several zone IDs? During customer onboarding, offboarding, and other lifecycle changes, multiple Cloudflare zone objects can briefly exist for the same public domain. We use a priority policy to choose a small, bounded set to publish.

Consider four internal zones for example.com: Zone 101, Zone 202, Zone 303, and Zone 404. The metadata key currently lists Zones 101, 202, and 303. Zone 404 exists, but it is not selected. The numbers identify separate Cloudflare zone objects; customers still see one domain name.

A TXT record change at www.example.com in Zone 202 affects only Zone 202's record keys, so the metadata key does not change. Nameserver and wildcard changes are different because the metadata key records information about them. Those builds must update both the zone's records and the metadata key.

At execution time, the Zone Builder reads the current list again. If it writes the metadata key, it rebuilds the whole key from that fresh view rather than patching an older copy. It writes the triggering zone's records before the metadata that refers to them.

Planning from the event, verifying before writing

An event describes what happened in the past. A build may wait while more events arrive and the database changes, so planning happens twice. The event first creates a conservative work list. Immediately before execution, the Zone Builder reads a fresh publication snapshot: the current zone settings, whether this Zone Builder should publish the zone to its network, and which same-name zone IDs belong in the metadata key. Here, a network is a separate, isolated copy of Quicksilver for one environment. Each Zone Builder deployment writes to one network, and a zone can be enabled on some networks but not others. For example, a zone can be served from Cloudflare's global network and also from the China Network.

Fresh state can change the result in four ways:

  1. A targeted build can become a full build if the zone now has a feature that requires complete-zone work.
  2. A build can become a purge if the zone should no longer be published to this network.
  3. A build can be skipped if the triggering zone no longer belongs in the metadata key.
  4. A metadata build can reconstruct the shared key from the current candidate set.

The fresh read comes from read-only copies of the database, called replicas, so builds do not compete with customer writes. Kafka delivery and database replication move independently: an event can arrive before its database change is visible on a replica. The DNS Kafka Aggregator delays events long enough to cover normal lag, and a final database check rejects the read if that replica is still behind.

Combining changes in one scheduler

Record work and full-zone work previously used different schedulers. Each could combine its own work, but not work from the other scheduler. We replaced them with one unified scheduler. The planner decides what must be built, and the scheduler decides when it can run.

When several events for one zone arrive before a build starts, the scheduler combines their work:

  1. An A record changes at www.example.com, requiring that name.
  2. A wildcard changes at *.example.com, requiring that name and shared metadata.
  3. The scheduler combines both names and the metadata update into one build.

Merging only adds work. If any event requires the complete zone, the combined build becomes a full build. A purge overrides every rebuild because its desired result is that the zone is no longer published.

The scheduler tracks two things separately: the DNS work that must be performed and the Kafka messages waiting to be acknowledged. A retry preserves both. Even when a full build or purge no longer needs the individual record names, the messages stay attached until the result is safely written.

The scheduler normally enforces this interval, but lets old queued work run before it blocks a Kafka partition for too long. Zone locks and retry delays still apply, so a failing build cannot run in a tight loop.

Each test runs a full build and a targeted build from the same database state, pins time-dependent values, and compares every Quicksilver key owned by the targeted plan byte for byte. Planner and scheduler tests cover classification, same-name zones, merging, purges, and escalation.

During rollout, we also ran a full build next to every targeted build and compared the output. It was expensive by design, reading the complete zone every time, so we used it only until the mirror comparison below gave us the same confidence.

Tests cannot reproduce every customer combination, so every release also runs through a mirror Zone Builder. It consumes the production Kafka stream and reads production database state, but writes to a separate Quicksilver environment that serves no customer traffic.

We built the DNS Mirror Dashboard to group those differences and keep examples for investigation. The critical groups in the screenshot below were each checked and confirmed safe before release. The diff rate is the share of compared zones where production and mirror disagreed on at least one key at the moment of comparison. Most of those are timing differences that disappear once both pipelines catch up, so we watch two things: that the rate stays low, and that no new kind of difference appears.

items.title: Hackers Could Exploit iPhone BootROM Flaws to Compromise Cryptocurrency Wallet Security
items.summary: Older iPhones used to store cryptocurrency seed phrases could expose owners to physical attacks that airplane mode cannot stop. OneKey founder Yishi has warned that wiping an aging iPhone and keeping it offline does not make it a secure cold wallet. The concern involves BootROM flaws that let attackers run code before iOS starts. However, this access does not automatically reveal protected wallet secrets. A seed phrase is the recovery secret that controls access to a cryptocurrency wallet . Yishi’s warning focuses on people keeping that secret on older Apple hardware, often believing that removing network access removes the main security risks. These attacks instead depend on someone gaining physical access to the device. The checkm8 exploit affects older iPhones through the iPhone X. A newer exploit, usbliter8, extends BootROM attacks to Apple’s A12 and A13 chips, including the iPhone XS, XR, iPhone 11 family, and second-generation iPhone SE. Researchers disclosed usbliter8 in June 2026. BootROM is the first code a device runs when switched on. It is built into the chip during manufacturing, so Apple cannot replace the vulnerable code through a normal iOS update. Cybersecurity News previously covered the usbliter8 BootROM vulnerability , explaining how it breaks the application processor’s trusted boot process. An attacker places a compatible iPhone into Device Firmware Update mode and connects special USB hardware. Carefully crafted USB traffic causes memory corruption, allowing attacker-controlled code to run before the operating system loads. Public demonstrations have used a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 board, showing that the required hardware need not be expensive. iPhone BootROM Flaws The technical weakness combines faulty USB controller behavior with missing memory restrictions during early startup. On affected chips, USB writes can reach memory outside their intended area. Researchers then redirect execution and load unsigned boot software, bypassing checks that normally restrict devices to Apple-approved code. The important limit is that usbliter8 does not directly compromise Apple’s Secure Enclave, the separate security component protecting sensitive keys and passcode operations. Researchers say encrypted user data remains behind additional barriers even after the main processor’s boot chain is compromised. Wallet theft would therefore require further weaknesses, access to decrypted information, or another attack against remaining protections. Yishi warned that weak passwords and outdated software can increase exposure. His warning describes a possible attack path, not evidence that every affected iPhone wallet can be emptied through BootROM access alone. Physical USB risks also extend beyond BootROM exploits. Earlier ChoiceJacking research showed how malicious charging equipment could manipulate input and approve data connections on vulnerable devices. That is a separate attack, but it reinforces why an offline phone still needs careful handling. Owners should check their device model, install available security updates, and avoid treating airplane mode as a complete defense. Updates cannot rewrite vulnerable BootROM, but they still address weaknesses elsewhere in the software. Strong device passcodes and wallet passwords remain important additional barriers. Anyone concerned that a stored seed was exposed should generate a new seed in a trusted environment and transfer funds. Creating another address from the original seed does not remove the underlying risk. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Hackers hijack Ukrainian and Russian alert apps to push fake nuclear and chemical warnings
items.summary: Hackers have hijacked emergency warning apps on both sides of the Russia-Ukraine war, using them to push false alerts of nuclear, chemical and street combat threats to civilians within hours of a temporary ceasefire coming to an end. Ukraine’s air force said on Sunday (1 November) that its public air raid alert app, which is used nationwide to warn people in real time of incoming Russian air attacks, had been compromised. For a short time, the app displayed warnings that Kyiv and other areas faced nuclear, chemical and street combat threats, with one message claiming that Russia’s Oreshnik hypersonic missile had been deployed. “The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the air force said on Telegram, adding: “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!” Air force spokesperson Yuriy Ignat later confirmed to AFP that the app had been hacked. Ukraine’s Centre for Strategic Communications (SPRAVDI) blamed Russia for the attack, while the Centre for Countering Disinformation said the threat-level information shown in the app “does not correspond to reality”. The country’s digital transformation ministry said the app was not operating, but that other alert methods, including air raid sirens, were still working. A separate alert app run by Kyiv’s city authorities was unaffected. “We are seeing emergency alert apps targeted specifically to induce civilian panic and confusion,” said Dray Agha, senior manager, tactical response at Huntress . “These mobile applications are highly visible targets for attackers.” Hours later, early on Monday (2 November), Russia’s Emergencies Ministry said its own mobile warning app, which alerts the public to incoming drone attacks and other threats, had suffered a “massive cyberattack” that allowed attackers to send “false information” to the public. The ministry said its teams were working to restore the service but did not say who it believed was responsible, and it is not yet clear whether the two incidents are linked. Both attacks coincided with the end of a localised truce in Ukraine’s Kherson region. The ceasefire, which ran from 27 October to 1 November, was the longest of the war so far, and Kyiv said Moscow had refused an offer to extend it. Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder of CyberSmart , said: “The reported cyberattacks on emergency alert apps in Ukraine and Russia are a concerning reminder that cyber threats can have consequences far beyond financial losses or stolen data. In Ukraine, hackers reportedly compromised an air raid warning app, sending false alerts about nuclear and chemical threats, while Russia’s emergency ministry also reported a cyberattack that allowed false information to be distributed. Although it’s not yet clear whether the incidents are connected, the implications are extremely serious.” “These systems are designed to protect lives, and compromising them risks causing widespread panic, spreading misinformation and undermining public trust in critical safety infrastructure. In a conflict where people rely on accurate warnings to seek shelter, the consequences of a genuine alert being ignored could be devastating.” ‘Mutually Assured Deception’ Don Smith, vice president, threat intelligence at the Sophos Counter Threat Unit , said the Ukrainian incident should be seen as part of a wider information war. “Disinformation is as much a part of war as bombs and bullets, targeted information attacks could aim to impact the mental resilience of the people of Ukraine. Their resilience is a key part of their ability to defend against the Russian military,” he said. “Usually the best information warfare is not obvious or explicit, where this very clearly is. It could indicate desperation from Russia.” Smith added that the near-simultaneous attack on Russia’s own app could reflect a tit-for-tat dynamic. “Mutually Assured Destruction is a doctrine used relating to nuclear war. If, as we assume, the Russian incident was a response to the Ukraine incident, Russia might consider that Mutually Assured Deception is at play.” Spencer Starkey, executive VP EMEA at SonicWall , said: “Cyber attacks have become a defining feature of modern warfare. Rather than relying solely on conventional military action, states and state-aligned groups increasingly use cyber operations to disrupt economies, undermine public confidence and apply pressure.” How were the apps compromised? Neither government has yet explained how the attackers gained access. Smith said the answer may lie in the systems that sit around the core warning infrastructure, rather than the infrastructure itself. “Whilst investigating a cyber attack against a TV channel some years ago, it was unclear what the motivation might be. We concluded that whilst it would be very difficult to disrupt the actual broadcast channels, the systems which supported the ‘banners’ under news items were pure IT systems and could actually be easily targeted,” he explained. “These early warning systems will operate in a similar way to allow for broadcasts to be submitted. It is possible that the account of an individual with access to submit broadcasts was compromised rather than the core system itself.” Starkey pointed to the familiar weaknesses that state-aligned attackers tend to exploit. “By exploiting common weaknesses such as unpatched systems, weak access controls or vulnerable third-party software, attackers can deploy ransomware, data-theft campaigns or destructive malware capable of halting operations at scale.” Graeme Stewart, head of public sector at Check Point , said the incidents should prompt scrutiny of warning systems elsewhere, including in the UK. “The UK’s system operates differently from the apps reportedly hacked in Ukraine and Russia, but the incidents raise serious questions about cybersecurity, particularly around who can access emergency warning systems, how alerts are authenticated and whether a compromised supplier could provide a way in.” Could it happen here? “The prospect of hackers being able to send fake nuclear or chemical attack warnings to millions of people is frightening, particularly when you consider how quickly fear can spread,” Stewart said. “In Britain, we’ve only experienced the national Emergency Alerts system a handful of times, and there’s still a novelty around it. Every time those alarms sound, social media lights up with people sharing screenshots, questioning what’s happening and speculating about why they’ve received one. Imagine that happening with a warning of an imminent nuclear attack, particularly in the middle of the night when people are frightened and struggling to verify what’s happening. Even if authorities corrected it within minutes, the damage could already have been done.” He warned that generative AI could amplify the impact of any false alert. “AI makes this more concerning because attackers could quickly flood social media with convincing fake footage, fabricated news reports and cloned voices of officials apparently confirming the threat. A single false alert could become the spark for a much wider misinformation crisis, with people making potentially dangerous decisions based on what they believe is happening.” Sirens still matter Ukraine’s reassurance that sirens were still operating while the app was offline underlines a key point for defenders: apps are only one layer of a national warning system. “Both nations rightly emphasise that apps are only supplementary to physical infrastructure like sirens and radio broadcasts,” said Agha. “A resilient national warning system must always rely on multiple independent communication channels so the public can verify threats.” Stewart agreed. “Authorities need to be able to correct false warnings immediately, using trusted channels that remain operational during a cyber-attack. The public also needs to understand how to verify an alert, particularly as criminals could imitate official warnings without ever gaining access to the genuine system.” Akhtar said the lessons apply well beyond Ukraine and Russia. “For countries and organisations alike who are responsible for critical systems, this highlights the importance of ensuring cybersecurity is treated as a fundamental part of public safety. Strong access controls, multi-factor authentication, regular security assessments and continuous monitoring are essential for preventing unauthorised access. Equally important is having reliable backup communication channels and robust incident response plans to ensure essential services can continue operating during an attack.” Stewart added: “Perhaps the greatest long-term concern is what repeated incidents would do to public confidence. If people begin questioning whether an emergency warning is genuine, precious minutes could be lost when a real threat emerges.” Akhtar concluded: “Ultimately, this incident demonstrates that when critical infrastructure is targeted, people’s safety and potentially their lives can be at risk and therefore should be treated with the utmost importance.”
