items.title: Hackers Using Microsoft Teams Messages and Calls to Trick Users and Gain Remote Access to System
items.summary: Hackers are using Microsoft Teams messages and voice calls to impersonate IT support staff, persuade employees to approve remote access, and move deeper into corporate networks. Two intrusions investigated by Microsoft show how a seemingly routine help desk conversation can lead to stolen data and access to highly privileged accounts. The attacks did not exploit a Microsoft Teams vulnerability. Instead, they combined social engineering, legitimate remote-support software, and weak Active Directory Certificate Services configurations. This Windows service, commonly called AD CS, issues digital certificates that can authenticate users and computers, making insecure settings particularly valuable to attackers. Microsoft researchers identified malicious JavaScript and Python scripts used for initial access and documented portable runtime variants supporting the intrusions. Their October 30 investigation described two separate certificate-abuse paths after the attackers secured remote control. Microsoft has not attributed the activity to a named threat actor. Hackers Using Microsoft Teams Messages and Calls Both incidents started with attackers posing as help desk personnel through Teams chats and calls. Support-themed display names and organization-themed tenant names made external accounts appear familiar. The approach mirrors earlier Teams and Quick Assist attacks that used trusted workplace tools to persuade employees to hand over control. The attackers guided employees into approving an interactive remote-support session, primarily through Quick Assist. That approval marked the critical turning point: the intruder could operate the workstation directly. Microsoft’s example also showed “External” and “Scam suspected” call indicators, highlighting warnings employees should examine before accepting unexpected support requests. Both incidents followed a shared entry and execution pattern (Source – Microsoft) Once connected, the attacker placed an archive in the Downloads folder, created an update-themed staging directory under the user’s profile, and extracted the files. Portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes then executed attacker-controlled code. One renamed executable retained metadata identifying it as Bun, showing why a reassuring filename alone cannot establish whether software is safe. The staged components checked Windows information, network settings, and running processes before contacting domain infrastructure. Similar Teams help desk calls have previously supported malware delivery and internal reconnaissance, but Microsoft stressed that investigators must validate each incident’s certificate activity rather than infer it from runtime use alone. Certificate Abuse, Data Theft, and Defensive Priorities In the first incident, the attacker exploited an ESC1-vulnerable certificate template. Its settings allowed a low-privileged requester to supply another identity and obtain an authentication certificate for that account. The initial phishing wave targeted three users, compromised one workstation, and produced certificates for three highly privileged accounts. About 90 minutes after disruption, another wave targeted 16 users and compromised a second workstation. The attacker obtained certificates for eight additional privileged accounts. Microsoft Defender blocked more than 1,000 subsequent SMB file-access attempts, but DCSync activity had already begun while containment was taking effect. One privileged account excluded from automated containment remained usable. The attacker used it to reach a file server and run a renamed Rclone utility, copying files to an external SFTP destination. Example Teams call displaying External and Scam suspected indicators (Source – Microsoft) The transfer command used 20 concurrent transfers and selected files up to three years old. The second incident followed ESC8 instead. PetitPotam forced a domain controller to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system. The attacker relayed that NTLM authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment, obtained a domain-controller certificate, and used certificate-based Kerberos authentication to acquire a ticket-granting ticket. Following Defender alerts, the customer isolated the workstation; no further progression was observed. Defenders should connect Teams interactions with remote-session records, process activity, certificate issuance, and Kerberos events. Earlier reporting on Teams collaboration feature abuse also explains how collaboration logs help reconstruct these timelines. Employees should verify unexpected support requests through a known internal channel before granting access. Microsoft recommends restricting external Teams access and unapproved remote tools, reviewing certificate-template permissions, and following its AD CS relay guidance . Enrollment endpoints should require HTTPS and Extended Protection for Authentication. Responders must revoke unauthorized certificates and separately review Kerberos tickets: resetting passwords alone does not remove certificate-backed access. Containment exclusions also need immediate review, because leaving one privileged identity available can preserve the attacker’s route even when other accounts are blocked. items.title: Northflank Security Breach Leads to Unauthorized AI API Key Usage, Customers Urged to Rotate Secrets
items.summary: Northflank urged customers to rotate all platform secrets after reports of unauthorized AI API key use, warning that environment variables across workloads, secret groups, and global settings may have been exposed. Northflank is investigating a security incident involving reported misuse of AI keys but has not confirmed the entry point, identified an attacker, or disclosed affected customers. Its credential rotation warning remains precautionary, not confirmation of widespread theft. Northflank’s published timeline begins with a Wiz threat alert at 11:43 UTC on October 30, 2026. Engineers reviewed the alert one minute later and deployed an initial network policy patch at 12:02 UTC. Further patches followed at 12:50 and 13:05 UTC, and the team requested support from the Wiz incident response team at 13:00 UTC. The timeline does not explain what those patches fixed. A network policy change alone does not establish how attackers entered the platform or reached customer secrets. Northflank Security Breach Northflank subsequently instructed users to treat environment variables as compromised and restrict public access to add-ons where enabled. Environment variables can hold API keys, database passwords, and other application credentials. Similar exposure concerns surfaced in the recent Railway security incident , where customers were also advised to replace stored secrets after possible unauthorized access. Northflank said the reported activity may fit a wider pattern of attacks targeting AI credentials. It pointed to similar IP addresses in Wiz’s “Black October” report , which described incidents across nine AI developer platforms during October. Wiz found a shared focus on stored environment variables but identified no single vulnerability connecting the attacks. The financial risk comes from LLMjacking, where attackers use stolen credentials to consume paid AI services at the victim’s expense. Previous reporting on LLMjacking attacks shows how compromised cloud keys can support unauthorized model access and resale. However, Northflank has not published a confirmed loss total or linked its incident to a named resale operation. Customers should revoke existing credentials through the issuing providers, generate replacements, and update affected Northflank secrets and workloads. Northflank also asked users to review AI provider usage and billing records for unexpected activity, then report suspicious usage to its support team and the relevant provider. Secret rotation is now available for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, MySQL, Redis, MinIO, and RabbitMQ add-ons. Northflank also enabled audit logs for all customers, including free users, giving more teams access to records that may help their investigation. The immediate priority is replacing all potentially exposed credentials, not only AI keys already showing abuse. Northflank’s latest guidance still covers secrets across workloads, shared secret groups, and global settings while its investigation remains open. items.title: Backporting security fixes at scale with Codex
items.summary: Stable Linux releases lack existing security fixes because backporting them is time-consuming and often thankless work. We’re using Codex to reduce the backporting process time from days to hours per fix, empowering human patch reviewers to rapidly submit fixes for critical software like Ubuntu Long Term Support, Fedora, and the Linux kernel. By October 29, our project helped deliver fixes for 149 distinct CVEs into stable Linux kernel releases, and several fixes to Fedora and Ubuntu packages. Deploying fixes to older software requires multiple steps, including adapting fixes to older code, checking dependencies, and ensuring the fix did not introduce new bugs. A single task (like tracking down a bug in a bad commit) can take a week or more of effort that no one sees or appreciates. Our Codex workflow has reduced the human effort required to prepare and review fixes. Excluding project-specific initial setup, preparing and reviewing a straightforward backport takes about 30 minutes of human attention; a more involved case can take around three hours. The workflow’s approach is twofold: agents perform activities like identifying missing fixes, adapting patches, assembling validation evidence, running tests, and preparing submission packets, while engineers review the patches and submit them to maintainers. Those estimates only cover patch preparation and review; regression testing and maintainer acceptance remain essential. But the reduced human commitment makes a substantial class of neglected security work practical to undertake. The patch backlog is large, but we now have a practical way to work through it. Do we have to decide between stability and security? Software has bugs, and we try to fix them when we can. The first place the fix happens is in the latest version of the software. Unfortunately, that’s often the only place where the fix happens. Backporting is the process of getting a fix from the latest source code to older versions. Fixes for big-name, critical bugs are indeed often backported quickly. But for many other bugs, the backporting process never happens. It is easy to understand why: software packaging is often done by volunteers who are already overworked, and backporting is frustrating, thankless work that gets little credit or publicity. For open source projects staffed by teams of volunteers, backports are (understandably) a low priority. As XFS developer Dave Chinner once described, this work is “ effectively a full time job ” that simply goes undone without sufficient resources. The lack of backports is a problem because almost no one runs the latest and greatest version of software that’s been freshly built with today’s code changes. People overwhelmingly prefer slightly older, more tested software packaged in “long term stable” releases. For example, about 95% of Ubuntu Linux installations are of the Long Term Support (LTS) variety. When looking at installed Linux kernel packages from Debian’s popcon , the overwhelming majority are based on older stable trees: Figure 1: A Codex-generated graph of recently installed kernel packages from Debian’s popcon. The overwhelming majority (about 96%) are older, stable releases, and not the latest kernel series. Users are faced with a decision: they can either stick with a stable, familiar version of software that has security flaws, or upgrade to a newer version that fixes those flaws but introduces other changes and new features they may not want. Many people purposely do not update to new releases; I think this is entirely justified and normal end-user behavior. Just recently, I updated my Mac to macOS 27 and couldn’t use a printer that had worked flawlessly for years (until Codex wrote a new, compatible printer driver). Similar situations effectively require older software. We should not have to make a choice between stability and security. Thousands of known CVEs lack stable-branch fixes A swarm of cyber-capable AI agents can cut through a network of stable, known-vulnerable software like a hot knife through butter. The scale of the problem is such that the software you are currently running likely contains unfixed security bugs that can be exploited by modern AI agents. As AI-assisted bug hunting makes it easier to identify vulnerabilities in older code, reducing this backlog becomes increasingly important. This is not merely theoretical. A fix for the latest high-profile bug, CVE-2026-98432 (a critical remotely exploitable flaw in the Linux TCP stack), still had not landed in distribution kernels weeks after being patched upstream. That bug is high-profile enough that it will soon be fixed everywhere. But fixes for more obscure bugs never get backported. I saw this during my sandbox escape research , and an old vulnerability in stable software was used as a part of the recently disclosed OpenAI hack . Let’s quantify the scale of the missing backport problem. To make counting simple, we can limit ourselves to known bugs (with assigned CVEs) that are patched in the latest release but missing from stable packages. For this example, we’ll look at the Linux kernel, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and Debian 13 Stable. I’m not singling out those projects—they are all run very well! I’m using them because they have documentation and accounting for unfixed CVEs. Other projects lack this transparency. Let’s look at the number of outstanding CVEs in the Linux kernel, by stable branch. The table below shows CVEs per supported stable branch that do not have a fix in that branch, but do have it in a newer branch. (Hence, older branches by definition have more unfixed CVEs.) The source is the kernel CVE team’s vulns.git as of September 18, 2026. This is not an exact bug count, as it both over- and under-counts due to several technicalities. It is also not a measure of exploitability. Rather, it’s a measuring stick showing that a substantial amount of known CVEs have not been fixed in stable kernel branches: Branch Unfixed CVEs % CVEs with an NVD Score High or Critical Severity 5.10.y 2,006 55.8% 213 (19.0%) 5.15.y 1,889 51.5% 195 (20.0%) 6.1.y 1,329 43.9% 99 (17.0%) 6.6.y 1,012 35.6% 65 (18.1%) 6.12.y 686 22.3% 21 (13.7%) 6.18.y 337 15.1% 3 (5.9%) The package landscape is not any better. These are non-kernel CVEs reported as open or affected in Debian 13 and Ubuntu 26.04 (raw data via their respective bulk CVE data feeds, compiled by Codex). These are distro-metadata findings, not individually source-confirmed vulnerabilities. Again, this is not meant to be an exact bug count, but more of a measuring stick indicating how many unfixed vulnerabilities remain in stable software packages: Distribution Source Packages with Unfixed CVEs Unique CVEs High or Critical Severity Debian 13 1,128 4,562 1,822 (39.9%) Ubuntu 26.04 1,028 770 335 (43.5%) Engineers and AI can accelerate backporting We realized this was an issue and have been fixing it proactively. First, we started with the equivalent of finding money on the sidewalk: there are bug fixes to known CVEs that apply cleanly to the stable kernel trees, but the fix was just never pulled into the kernel. We used Codex with GPT-5.6 to find these fixes, and asked the maintainers to apply the existing patches. They did, graciously. We then moved on to backporting patches that don’t apply as-is, starting with the most trivial to validate and review, and are slowly moving towards more complex changes. So far 149 CVE fixes in stable trees are currently applied; the list on our backport tracker just keeps growing . We’ve done the same for Linux distributions: we used Codex and GPT-5.6 to identify known vulnerabilities in shipping stable packages, and then backport and validate a fix. We have begun reaching out to Linux distributions with an initial batch of patches. If you run an open-source project or a Linux distribution and would like help backporting security fixes, please apply at trailofbits.com/patch-the-planet and we’ll be glad to assist. The big upside of stable software that does not add features is that we can, in theory, fix bugs before attackers exploit them. So, let’s continue to patch the planet!

items.title: The Linkerd Story: The people Behind The Service Mesh — A new documentary premieres at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026
items.summary: Join CNCF and Buoyant on November 9 in Salt Lake City for the premiere of a new documentary celebrating a decade of Linkerd, the evolution of service mesh technology, and the people who helped make it possible. Every open source project has a story. Behind the code are people with ideas, challenges to overcome, decisions to make, and a shared belief that technology can be better when built together. This November, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), in partnership with Buoyant, is excited to premiere The Linkerd Story: The People Behind The Service Mesh , a new documentary exploring the origins, evolution, and community behind one of cloud native’s pioneering open source projects. From the engineering challenges of Twitter’s early infrastructure to the creation of the first service mesh, the documentary takes viewers behind the scenes of Linkerd’s journey, told through the experiences of the creators, maintainers, contributors, and end users who have helped shape it. This documentary explores a story beyond technology. It’s about the relationships, persistence, and collective effort that turn an idea into an open source project used by organizations around the world. From an engineering challenge to a pioneering open source project Linkerd’s story begins at Twitter, where engineers were tackling the challenges of running increasingly complex distributed systems. Their experiences with Finagle, a library for managing communication between services, helped inspire a new approach to application networking. That approach became Linkerd, helping establish the service mesh category and changing how teams could manage reliability, security, and observability across distributed applications. The documentary explores the technical decisions that shaped the project, including its evolution into a Kubernetes-focused service mesh, the adoption of Rust for lightweight sidecar proxies, and the ongoing challenge of making complex infrastructure simpler to operate. Through firsthand accounts, viewers discover the experimentation, challenges, and collaboration behind these milestones. The people who make open source possible At the heart of the documentary is the Linkerd community. Contributors share stories of friendships, shared challenges, and the responsibility that comes with building technology organizations depend on. The film highlights the role of maintainers, ambassadors, and end users in helping the project grow, from contributing code and documentation to sharing knowledge and supporting others. It also explores Linkerd’s journey to becoming a CNCF graduated project and the importance of open governance, collaboration, and long-term sustainability. The documentary brings these themes to life through real-world experiences, including how Texas-based grocery retailer H-E-B used Linkerd while accelerating the rollout of its curbside services. These stories demonstrate that the impact of open source extends beyond technology, reaching the people and communities who depend on the systems it helps power. Ten years of Linkerd, and looking ahead As Linkerd marks a decade of development, the documentary reflects on what it takes to build an open source project that lasts. One contributor shares an ambition for Linkerd to continue for another hundred years, a reminder that long-term success depends not only on technical innovation but also on the people who sustain it. It’s a theme that reflects CNCF’s mission to support sustainable, community-driven cloud native projects. Join us for the documentary premiere We’re excited to share this story with the cloud native community at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026. Presented by CNCF in partnership with Buoyant, The Linkerd Story: The People Behind The Service Mesh offers a behind-the-scenes look at the people, decisions, and experiences that helped shape a decade of service mesh innovation. Premiere details Date: Monday, November 9, 2026 Time: 6:30 PM MST Location: Salt Palace Convention Center | Level 1 | Room 151 Event: KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 Whether you’ve contributed to Linkerd, used it in production, or are curious about the people behind cloud native innovation, we invite you to join us for this special premiere. Come celebrate the people behind the service mesh. We look forward to seeing you in Salt Lake City! Learn more about Linkerd and explore the CNCF project landscape .

items.title: POC Released for Windows WinSock Ancillary Privilege Escalation Vulnerability
items.summary: A public proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2023-21768 shows how attackers with local access can gain SYSTEM privileges through the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock. Researchers Valentina Palmiotti, known as chompie, and Ruben Boonen published the code. Their complete exploit targets vulnerable Windows 11 22H2 systems. The release concerns a vulnerability patched in January 2023, not a newly disclosed Windows flaw. IBM published the researchers’ technical analysis on March 21, 2023. The vulnerability carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and requires low-level local privileges, with no user interaction. It does not provide a direct route into a computer over the internet. The flaw sits in afd.sys, a Windows kernel driver that handles requests from the WinSock networking interface. According to IBM’s technical analysis, the researchers compared driver versions from December 2022 and January 2023 to understand Microsoft’s fix. Only one function, AfdNotifyRemoveIoCompletion, appeared to have changed, helping them narrow their investigation. The older code failed to check a memory pointer supplied from a user application. That missing check let a local attacker write to kernel memory, where Windows stores sensitive system data. Microsoft’s updated code added validation to ensure that pointers from user mode reference suitable user-space memory rather than protected kernel addresses. POC for Windows WinSock Ancillary Vulnerability The researchers said they diagnosed, reproduced, and turned the flaw into a working exploit in about one day, despite having no previous experience with this driver. Their findings show how comparing patched and unpatched software can reveal enough detail to build an attack quickly. The public GitHub repository describes the code as a demonstration. Its complete privilege escalation chain works on vulnerable Windows 11 22H2 installations, while the underlying memory-write capability works across vulnerable systems. These are separate claims, and the repository does not promise full exploit compatibility with every affected Windows version. To move from a limited memory write to broader control, the exploit changes Windows I/O ring objects. These objects support queued input and output work. The technique builds on research by Yarden Shafir and enables kernel memory reads and writes. The exploit then replaces a target process’s security token with one carrying SYSTEM privileges. IBM also reported that 360 IceSword Lab found a different exploit in the wild in January 2023. That sample used the ProcessSocketNotifications interface rather than the researchers’ direct driver approach. This report does not establish that attackers used the published GitHub code. Administrators should verify that affected devices received Microsoft’s fix or later applicable updates. IBM’s demonstration also worked without being blocked by HVCI, showing why that protection should not replace patching. Related coverage includes CVE-2024-38193 exploitation and the CVE-2025-32709 WinSock zero-day . Both involve the same driver, but are separate flaws with different causes and patches. items.title: Hackers Exploit Patched Synology NAS Vulnerabilities to Deploy C3RB3R Ransomware and Encrypt Files
items.summary: Synology NAS devices are facing C3RB3R ransomware attacks linked to 2024 security flaws , prompting the company to urge users to update outdated DiskStation Manager versions and packages. The warning followed reports from the 360 Security Team and Solar Emergency Response Team on October 29. Victims found their files encrypted with the .L0CK3D extension and a ransom note named read-me3.txt. Security teams provisionally identified the ransomware as C3RB3R. The available reporting does not establish how many devices have been compromised. The Synology security advisory , tracked as Synology-SA-24:20, covers three vulnerabilities disclosed following Pwn2Own 2024. Published on November 5, 2024, it received several updates as fixes became available across DSM branches. Although Appinn described the weaknesses as fixed by December 2024, Synology’s revision history shows that several patches arrived during November. Cyber Security News previously examined the critical CVE-2024-10441 flaw in Synology DSM , which carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and allows unauthenticated remote code execution without user interaction. Synology NAS Hit by C3RB3R Ransomware Attacks The advisory also lists CVE-2024-50629, a webapi flaw that lets remote attackers read limited files, and CVE-2024-10445. This update certificate validation flaw lets an adjacent attacker write limited files. These carry scores of 5.3 and 4.3, respectively. Multiple Synology NAS Ransomware Incidents Reported by Security Teams (source : Appinn ) Public reporting has not established which individual vulnerability was used in each ransomware incident or whether attackers combined them. Early coverage raised concerns because Solar reportedly investigated an affected device running DSM 7.4.1-90080 Update 1. At that stage, researchers were still examining the entry point and had not ruled out an unknown vulnerability. The later report attributed Synology’s findings to older, patched weaknesses. The published accounts do not explain the apparent mismatch or confirm a new zero-day attack. Synology NAS devices have faced ransomware threats before. Cyber Security News covered the Diskstation ransomware investigation , involving criminals who targeted Synology storage systems. That separate case provides background on the threat to NAS users. However, the available reports do not establish any connection to C3RB3R. Latest DSM patches fix two CVEs, but the attack entry point remains unknown (source : Appinn ) Synology’s advisory lists fixed releases including DSM 7.2.2-72806-1, 7.2.1-69057-6, 7.2-64570-4, 7.1.1-42962-7, and 6.2.4-25556-8. These are historical patch thresholds, not a recommendation to stop updating. Administrators should install the latest release supported by their NAS model and update official packages and third-party components. Appinn’s initial incident report recommends removing direct internet access to DSM management and SSH, using a VPN for remote connections, and checking for unusual logins, unknown administrators, and scheduled tasks. It also advises enabling two-factor authentication and keeping independent offline or off-site backups. For affected users, those separate backups may provide a route to recover encrypted files. Updating remains necessary, but it does not itself restore files already encrypted by ransomware. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

Multiple Synology NAS Ransomware Incidents Reported by Security Teams (source : Appinn )

Public reporting has not established which individual vulnerability was used in each ransomware incident or whether attackers combined them.

Early coverage raised concerns because Solar reportedly investigated an affected device running DSM 7.4.1-90080 Update 1. At that stage, researchers were still examining the entry point and had not ruled out an unknown vulnerability.

The later report attributed Synology’s findings to older, patched weaknesses. The published accounts do not explain the apparent mismatch or confirm a new zero-day attack.

Synology NAS devices have faced ransomware threats before. Cyber Security News covered the Diskstation ransomware investigation, involving criminals who targeted Synology storage systems. That separate case provides background on the threat to NAS users. However, the available reports do not establish any connection to C3RB3R.

Latest DSM patches fix two CVEs, but the attack entry point remains unknown (source : Appinn )

Synology’s advisory lists fixed releases including DSM 7.2.2-72806-1, 7.2.1-69057-6, 7.2-64570-4, 7.1.1-42962-7, and 6.2.4-25556-8. These are historical patch thresholds, not a recommendation to stop updating. Administrators should install the latest release supported by their NAS model and update official packages and third-party components.

Appinn’s initial incident report recommends removing direct internet access to DSM management and SSH, using a VPN for remote connections, and checking for unusual logins, unknown administrators, and scheduled tasks.

It also advises enabling two-factor authentication and keeping independent offline or off-site backups. For affected users, those separate backups may provide a route to recover encrypted files. Updating remains necessary, but it does not itself restore files already encrypted by ransomware.

items.title: Hackers Exploit ChatGPT’s Popularity With Fake Billing Notices That Target Credit Cards and OTPs
items.summary: Hackers are impersonating OpenAI in fake ChatGPT Plus billing emails that lead users to payment pages designed to steal credit card details and one-time passwords. The campaign combines convincing subscription warnings with a live operator who can decide when to request a verification code, potentially helping approve an unauthorized payment. The emails claim a subscription payment failed and urge recipients to update their billing information. This pressure mirrors other AI brand impersonation campaigns that exploit trust in popular services to collect financial information. In this operation, the checkout page keeps victims waiting while an attacker controls what appears next. Researchers from Fortra identified the phishing operation and documented its infrastructure in research published on October 26, 2026. Importantly, they observed phishing, not malware deployment: no executable download or compromise of victims’ computers was seen during the investigation. Hackers Exploit ChatGPT’s Popularity With Fake Billing Notices The attack begins with an email posing as an OpenAI payment notice. Links pass through tracking services or redirect wrappers before reaching a fake checkout hosted on short-lived WordPress instances. Researchers found the same landing page reused across multiple recipients within a sending wave, suggesting shared infrastructure behind separately tracked messages. The checkout imitates a payment form, recognizing card brands and formatting card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes as users type. Similar WordPress payment phishing schemes have used convincing checkout interfaces to steal card data and verification codes, although Fortra did not establish a connection to those operations. After submission, the page sends the card number, expiration date, security code, and cardholder name to the server. It then displays a loading animation indefinitely. The captured code explicitly instructs the page to keep the spinner running rather than process a response or advance automatically. Meanwhile, the browser repeatedly contacts an operator dashboard, maintaining the victim’s session and checking for instructions. A human operator can redirect the victim to a one-time-password capture page, display an error, or end the session. One test lasting four minutes and three seconds generated 969 requests, mostly dashboard polling traffic. This creates an opportunity to capture a bank verification code while the victim believes a subscription update is underway. Comparable real time OTP interception appears in other payment-fraud kits, but the observed ChatGPT operation uses repeated polling to receive instructions. Capturing a code could help authorize fraud; it does not mean every submission produces a successful transaction. Fortra found identical client-side code and a shared application identifier across independently deployed sites examined roughly a week apart. Sites disappeared and were replaced during the investigation. Whether attackers purchased hosting accounts themselves or compromised existing customer sites remains unresolved. The infrastructure also complicates investigation. Unexpected requests received generic errors, while a token-generating path appeared to influence access. Researchers reported that interception-based analysis disrupted the session flow, whereas passive browser inspection captured the payment submission and polling behavior without breaking it. For defenders, recurring page structures and dashboard traffic offer stronger detection opportunities than isolated addresses. Broader live financial phishing operations demonstrate why stolen verification codes need urgent attention. Users should verify billing through their account rather than an email link, while organizations should investigate matching messages and report fraudulent hosting. Broad infrastructure blocks require care because legitimate customers share the platform. items.title: Hackers Impersonate ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity AI Bots to Hunt for Passwords and API Keys
items.summary: Hackers are posing as trusted artificial intelligence bots to search websites for passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials. The campaign uses the names of ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and other AI services to disguise automated scanning, testing whether businesses will let requests through simply because they appear to come from a familiar provider. The operation highlights a weakness in how organizations recognize automated visitors: a claimed identity is not proof of origin. Similar AI crawler impersonation tactics have appeared in attacks against exposed development servers, where scanners used forged bot identities while looking for sensitive files. Here, the disguise supports credential hunting rather than ordinary web crawling. Cequence researchers identified the malicious scanning campaign and linked it to a single actor impersonating about 32 AI bots. In an October 28 report, CQ Prime research director Will Glazier said the actor reached 48% of Cequence-protected organizations receiving any AI bot traffic on one October day. The report describes a scanner, not a newly identified malware family. Hackers Impersonate ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity AI Bots Running from a major cloud provider, the scanner rotated through identities associated with OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Perplexity, and others. Instead of reading normal pages, it requested configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data. Researchers observed a target list containing roughly 90 file paths. The distinction matters because these files can provide access beyond the website itself. Previous exposed environment file attacks have shown how leaked cloud credentials can support privilege escalation and data theft. Cequence’s findings establish credential-seeking activity, however, not confirmed theft or subsequent compromise in this campaign. Each scanning address issued between 50 and 190 requests in roughly eight seconds before moving on. The actor worked through targets individually, around the clock, and first requested random, meaningless paths to identify websites that returned responses for every request. Activity affected financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy, and software organizations from at least late September through late October. The impersonation became clear when researchers compared behavior across requests. One machine claimed to represent several unrelated AI providers within seconds, while the scanner cycled evenly through all 32 identities. Fake Claude identities also reused Anthropic’s crawler contact address, even when claiming to represent a different Claude agent. Shared infrastructure and technical fingerprints connected the activity across targets. Why Identity Verification Matters More Than IP Blocklists Infrastructure turnover made address-based defenses difficult. The actor used more than 300 cloud addresses in one day and nearly 400 during one week. None of the addresses observed in late September appeared again a month later. External threat feeds flagged many addresses during their use, but the scanner had usually moved elsewhere by then. This campaign involves outsiders pretending to be agents, unlike AI agent credential exposure caused by legitimate tools handling secrets during routine work. Both problems make identity and access controls important, but they require different investigations: defenders must distinguish forged visitors from genuine agents whose permissions or data handling create risk. The scanner also distorted traffic measurements. At several organizations, it generated more than 80% of requests labeled as AI bot traffic. That does not mean genuine AI services launched the attacks; it shows how trusting a visitor’s self-description can turn malicious scanning into apparently legitimate activity in security dashboards. Cequence recommends verifying agents through signed requests, published address ranges, or direct integrations. Teams should also inspect behavior, particularly requests for credential files, and keep secrets, staging systems, and administration sites away from public access. Broader AI agent identity controls address ownership and permissions, but a familiar bot name alone should never justify access. Request burst 50–190 requests in about eight seconds Short, concentrated scanning activity. Identity pattern About 32 rotating AI bot identities Correlate inconsistent provider claims. Targeting pattern Roughly 90 file paths Repeated searches for sensitive files. items.title: Hackers Use CyberStrikeAI Agents to Automate Windows Domain Takeovers and Credential Theft
items.summary: Hackers are now using an AI-driven command framework called CyberStrikeAI to break into Windows networks and take over entire domains. Education organizations in Africa and Latin America were among the confirmed victims. The tool lets a language model decide which commands to run, so the operator no longer types each step by hand. CyberStrikeAI is an open-source, Go-based platform built for penetration testing. Criminals have already turned it toward real targets, and earlier reports showed how attackers targeted Fortinet FortiGate devices with the same framework. This new campaign shows the tool being used for something bigger: moving from a single weak server to full control of a network. Analysts at Securelist identified the campaign during routine threat monitoring. They described it as one of the first public cases of a language model being used inside a live intrusion. CyberStrikeAI control panel’s self-signed TLS certificate (Source – Securelist) The human operator sets a broad goal, and the AI model on the control server picks the tools, writes the commands, and reads the results. The malware on the victim machine is a plain implant with no AI inside it. Hackers Use CyberStrikeAI Agents The intrusion began with a person. The operator got into a compromised SQL Server, collected basic host details, dropped tools, and scanned the network. That took almost a day, and then the attackers went quiet for about two weeks. When they came back, the CyberStrikeAI agent took over. Within two minutes it set up persistence through a scheduled task named SystemUpdate and finished local checks. Over the next five hours it mapped the domain using PowerShell and LDAP queries. It also collected data needed for Kerberoasting and AS-REP Roasting, two methods for cracking account passwords. Other reports show how attackers coordinate 44 AI agents with this same platform, which suggests the approach is spreading. After a short pause of a few days, the final phase ran in under an hour. The agent moved sideways through SMB and WMI, dumped credentials from many machines, and exported database content. It pulled passwords from registry files and from the LSASS process using the comsvcs.dll MiniDump function. After it compromised the built-in domain administrator, it ran DCSync and Golden Ticket techniques with a renamed Mimikatz tool. The whole job, from agent install to domain admin, took only three to four days. The attackers tried to stay hidden. They encoded commands in Base64, split scripts into several files, and rebuilt them with certutil. DNSLog.cn (Source – Securelist) They also named one beacon svchosts.exe so it looked like a normal Windows process. Some scripts contained Chinese comments, and the attackers used the Chinese service dnslog.cn to find victim IP addresses. Server restarts mostly fell within UTC+8 business hours. Together these clues suggest a Chinese-speaking operator, but Securelist could not link the activity to any known group. Why Defenders Can Still Catch It The methods themselves are not new. The agent used well-known tools, and the AI mainly made the work faster and easier. Because the model runs on the attacker’s server, defenders will not see AI traffic or odd resource use inside their network. They will see the same actions a human intruder would take. That means ordinary detection rules still work. Teams should watch for remote scheduled tasks created with schtasks.exe, LSASS memory access, and WMI or WinRM commands from unusual hosts. A DCSync attack steals password hashes by posing as a domain controller. Event ID 4662 helps catch it when the request comes from a system that is not a real domain controller. Rotating the krbtgt account twice after any domain admin compromise cancels forged Golden Tickets. Defenders should also check for commands running from the sqlservr.exe process, since that was the likely way in. They should patch and lock down exposed SQL Servers and turn on LAPS. They should also limit replication rights and keep logs for process launches, PowerShell activity, and logons. Microsoft recently described AI agents targeting Microsoft 365 tenants, so cloud accounts linked to the domain need the same care. items.title: Hackers Hijack Swedish Supermarket Fridges and Raise Freezer Temperatures to 55°C
items.summary: Hackers have reportedly targeted refrigeration systems at Swedish supermarkets, leaving stores with spoiled food after freezers reached temperatures as high as 55°C. Several ICA locations and six Coop stores were affected overnight into November 2, forcing staff to clear damaged stock and restore cooling systems. The incidents follow similar attacks against French supermarkets in October, although no connection has been confirmed. According to Swedish broadcaster SVT, ICA Nära store manager Mats Olsson found water on the floor when he arrived at his shop in Böda, Öland. He reported a freezer temperature of 55°C, with refrigerators and freezers knocked out and their contents ruined. Swedish Stores Face Food Losses Affected ICA stores included locations in Sjöbo, Tomelilla, Brösarp and Sankt Olof in Skåne. Reports also covered Öland, Värmland and Stockholm. Six Coop stores in Gästrikland and Hälsingland were affected, but the full number of Swedish stores involved remained unclear. The ICA store in Sjöbo temporarily closed after reporting temperatures around 50°C. In Sankt Olof, store manager Dennis Vidal said workers were emptying freezers as cooling began to return, but the food was already ruined. At ICA Baronen in Stockholm, staff reported temperatures rising from 38°C to around 50°C. ICA press officer Gustaf Nilsson said the company was investigating and helping affected stores. Importantly, ICA said the affected shops had connections outside its central network. That distinction does not establish how attackers gained access, but it means the incident should not automatically be described as a breach of ICA’s central systems. The Swedish reports have not identified the controller brands, entry point, exploited software flaw or attackers. There is also no confirmed evidence that the same group targeted stores in Sweden and France. Any claim naming a specific vulnerability would therefore be premature. However, the earlier French incidents show why connected cooling equipment needs close attention. Cybersecurity News previously reported on supermarket refrigerators being remotely manipulated , with attackers reportedly changing settings to keep equipment in defrost mode. This function normally clears ice, but prolonged operation can raise temperatures and destroy stock. Hackers have reportedly targeted refrigeration systems at Swedish supermarkets, leaving stores with spoiled food after freezers reached temperatures as high as 55°C.

Several ICA locations and six Coop stores were affected overnight into November 2, forcing staff to clear damaged stock and restore cooling systems. The incidents follow similar attacks against French supermarkets in October, although no connection has been confirmed.

According to Swedish broadcaster SVT, ICA Nära store manager Mats Olsson found water on the floor when he arrived at his shop in Böda, Öland. He reported a freezer temperature of 55°C, with refrigerators and freezers knocked out and their contents ruined.

Swedish Stores Face Food Losses

Affected ICA stores included locations in Sjöbo, Tomelilla, Brösarp and Sankt Olof in Skåne. Reports also covered Öland, Värmland and Stockholm. Six Coop stores in Gästrikland and Hälsingland were affected, but the full number of Swedish stores involved remained unclear.

The ICA store in Sjöbo temporarily closed after reporting temperatures around 50°C. In Sankt Olof, store manager Dennis Vidal said workers were emptying freezers as cooling began to return, but the food was already ruined. At ICA Baronen in Stockholm, staff reported temperatures rising from 38°C to around 50°C.

ICA press officer Gustaf Nilsson said the company was investigating and helping affected stores. Importantly, ICA said the affected shops had connections outside its central network. That distinction does not establish how attackers gained access, but it means the incident should not automatically be described as a breach of ICA’s central systems.

The Swedish reports have not identified the controller brands, entry point, exploited software flaw or attackers. There is also no confirmed evidence that the same group targeted stores in Sweden and France. Any claim naming a specific vulnerability would therefore be premature.

However, the earlier French incidents show why connected cooling equipment needs close attention. Cybersecurity News previously reported on supermarket refrigerators being remotely manipulated, with attackers reportedly changing settings to keep equipment in defrost mode. This function normally clears ice, but prolonged operation can raise temperatures and destroy stock.

France’s national cyber response team, CERT-FR, confirmed compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, alongside Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb devices. Its official refrigeration security alert warned against exposing management interfaces directly to the internet. These findings concern the French incidents, not confirmed equipment at Swedish stores.

A related Cybersecurity News report on exposed Danfoss systems highlighted how widely refrigeration management pages could be reached online. Such exposure creates a direct route to equipment that controls physical conditions, rather than only business records or payment systems.

CERT-FR advises operators to remove public internet access, check controller settings, including defrost schedules, and restore remote access through a secure VPN or protected network. It also recommends firmware updates and changing default passwords. Operators should coordinate changes with refrigeration providers, including checking insurance terms before interrupting monitoring connections.

The agency also warns that resetting an unsupported controller is not enough. Without removing exposure and addressing the underlying weakness, the equipment can be compromised again, putting replacement stock at risk once cooling resumes and stores begin restocking their shelves.

items.title: Implementing Detection as Code as a multi-platform MSSP
items.summary: What was once considered to be a niche within a niche, Detection as Code has become a very popular method of managing detection rules across your SIEM environment. Seeing Detection as Code pipelines become commonplace has been incredibly heartening to watch over the last few years, as it brings with it very tangible benefits — removes the risk of configuration drift, allows for unit testing and strict style guides through CI/CD, and automated deployments. With AI in the picture, the benefits multiply massively with huge efficiency boosts in terms of writing and tuning rules, using those rules for threat hunting, and more. I’ve spent a long time tracking the evolution of Detection as Code in the Detection Engineering space in my last few years as a security engineer at an MSSP. I tried many different approaches to implementing DaC in a way that could truly scale, and scale in a way that could function cross-platform, as we support not one but four platforms simultaneously! I found very online discussing how they were dealing with the complexities that arise from dealing with this large of an environment. This article intends to address this use-case. First and foremost, a lot of the initial inspiration came from the incredible work done by NVISO Labs on their Detection Engineering: Practicing Detection-as-Code — NVISO Labs series of blogs. Many of the design decisions taken were inspired heavily by concepts outlined in this series, a lot of which will be readily apparent as I dig into the design principles. The Approach The number one consideration when it comes to implementing DaC is managing the downstream consumers of our detections. During the design phase, I played with a couple different methodologies for managing code: Specific git branches for different environments Monorepo vs. Multiple repos per client with submodules Multiple branches seemed like a good idea initially, but it’s really not what branches are designed for. Keeping branches synced up with rules is untenable, and the same kinds of issues presented themselves when it came to managing multiple repositories. It also led to valuable context being spread across different folders rather than being centralised in one place. The best and simplest approach I settled on was the same as NVISO’s — organising detection content into ‘Content Packs’ — JSON definitions that group detections up based on a similar purpose. We typically group detections based on their underlying log source, but other content packs cover particular attack stories or are customer-agnostic (e.g. the ‘Baseline’ content pack, a group of detections that all customers receive). This allowed for the simplest and best use for Git which was to keep the ‘main’ branch as production, and put work in progress detection rules behind ‘feature’ branches and gate any merge behind CI/CD tests. In-line with NVISO, a typical content pack looks something like: { "platform": "sentinel", "description": "Contains detections relating to Azure and Azure resource deployment and modification. Most detections require AzureActivity logs or other common tables.", "content": [ "detections/Sentinel/azure/Rare subscription-level operations in Azure", "detections/Sentinel/azure/Suspicious Resource Deployment", "detections/Sentinel/ueba/First time Azure Custom Script or Run command deployment", "detections/Sentinel/azure/Mass secret retrieval from Azure Key Vault", ... ] } Once I had settled on the concept of content packs for managing which rules are deployed to who, it completely opened the door for all kinds of use-cases, and is how we deploy specific sets of detections to specific environments. With content packs, the Detection Engineering team can seamlessly add detections onto a new or existing content pack and ship it out the door to all environments who need it. Content packs simplify the deployment process massively by controlling everything through a singular JSON file. Each customer is tracked individually through this file, and it specifies the platforms they have, and what content packs they should receive. ... "content-packs": [ "sentinel-baseline", "sentinel-azure", "sentinel-defenderxdr", "sentinel-active-directory", "sentinel-platform-alerts", "sentinel-monitored-domains" ], ...j Some customers may combine different SIEM and EDR platforms. Our configuration allows for mix and matching of content packs and platforms, with specific CI/CD pipelines that kick in for each. Detection as Code ensures each environment receives exactly the same detection rule, no matter what. Detections are stored as discrete files in native formats. For Sentinel, that’s JSON ARM templates, for Splunk it’s .conf files, etc. Each file is kept within a simple file structure: detections / sentinel/ active-directory/ aws/ azure/ Cloud Resource Deletion Time Anomaly.json ... splunk/ active-directory/ aws/ azure/ Cloud Resource Deletion Time Anomaly.json ... While working with the native files is not the most intuitive thing to a human, we’ve been able to build a toolchain that simplifies the process of managing and editing these rules which has allowed us to bypass many of the issues others run into — compiling pseudo-code into detection rules, generating rule metadata at deployment time, etc. We found that for our purposes, just storing the actual raw rule itself provided all the same benefits. With an AI agent in the picture, editing a JSON file is no issue at all. But what about Sigma and Cross-Platform rules? I decided early on to de-scope pseudo-code from the codebase altogether and rely on actual detection artifacts. Personally, I prefer to use Sigma rules as reference material rather than as a piece of code to be translated off of directly. While there are some automated tools that have gotten decently good at this, in 2026 it’s much quicker and accurate to throw an AI agent at that task instead. AI agents can also create the requisite metadata around the rule itself, further reducing the need for these tools. Managing cross-platform rules is indeed trickier without a shared piece of pseudo-code. But again, with AI agents being such a massive part of the detection development lifecycle, maintaining changes between multiple query languages and platforms and accounting for each nuance is shockingly easy. This has been one of the biggest enablers of this particular Detection as Code implementation. What about documentation? Each rule is stored alongside a markdown file in the same folder. The markdown file contains: The rule description A technical description explaining how the rule works Blindspots, gaps, and special SOC considerations Other bespoke info aligned to our SOC team This doco is stored as code and is linted and checked as part of the PR process. This ensures documentation is always updated in lockstep with the rule. The documentation is then rendered in our custom frontend (more on that later) and synced into Confluence at deployment time. For more information on writing good documentation, I would point you to this article I wrote a couple years ago on the subject. Deployment Workflow Pictured above is a high level diagram describing the deployment workflow. It’s not overly complicated — work is done on a new branch with simple tests run locally pre-commit to prevent any stupid mistakes slipping through. There, a PR is raised, where a much more complex validation pipeline is executed. The validation pipeline: Identifies the changes based on file type and platform (modified version of NVISO’s logic) Routes the change to the relevant platform validators Checks metadata and style against dozens of custom tests Remotely runs queries against lab environments Stages the rules in a lab environment to test the deployment will succeed in production And more 😉 Assuming the tests pass and the senior Detection Engineer is happy, the PR can be merged, where it is then checked into the main branch. The deployer will pick up the change if it’s part of a content pack, and any customer subscribed to that pack will receive that rule. In instances where the rule already exists and the platform supports it, the deployer will update the rule in-place rather than create a new one. For Splunk deployments, rules are tarred and uploaded to remote storage for retrieval and installation by other automated steps outside the scope of this article. The Detection Engineering Toolchain To support testing, we also have the capability to run searches against any environment from the DaC repository. This initially started as a way to manually test detection rules prior to deployment, but quickly grew to become a full-blown agent harness, fully capable of orchestrating long and detailed threat hunts fully autonomously. We then built integrations into threat intelligence products, custom skills, and other bespoke API tools that could empower an engineer or an AI agent to carry out full SOC and IR investigations completely. One of the other concepts I built was the idea of a data map . A data map is essentially a CSV inventory of all the tables going into an environment, alongside an event count. This data map is generated once daily per environment. For each table, an equivalent schema markdown file is generated, along with an entry added to an index.md file. This schema is not auto-generated, but rather hand curated with the MITRE data components it provides, the SIEM field it maps to, the fields in the table, and a section for analysts to make notes. --- type: logsource platform: sentinel mitre_datacomponent_name: - Cloud Service Modification - Instance Creation - Instance Deletion - Instance Modification - Cloud Service Enumeration - Cloud Service Disable mitre_datacomponent_id: - DC0069 - DC0076 - DC0081 - DC0073 - DC0083 - DC0090 mitre_logsource_name: azure:activity siem_logsource_name: AzureActivity --- # Context Entries from the Azure Activity log that provides insight into any subscription-level or management group level events that have occurred in Azure. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/reference/tables/azureactivity # Suggested Queries ## Check for ... ```kql AzureActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) ... ``` # Schema | Field Name | Data Type | Description | |------------|-----------|-------------| | _ResourceId | string | A unique identifier for the resource that the record is associated with | | ActivityStatus | string | | ... This concept was inspired by a post on the blog Cauchy which discussed a workflow for automatically maintaining documentation on each sourcetype in Splunk. We’ve expanded the scope to include Sentinel and the various other platforms we support, with the overlay of MITRE data components for downstream reporting. Detection Development Efficiencies Bringing all development into one repository has significantly decreased the time it takes to develop, test and deploy new rules. With an AI agent in the mix, an almost fully autonomous development process can be achieved: A CTI agent intakes a piece of CTI and synthesises it into potential detection opportunities. A detection agent for each platform with knowledge of each platform’s major log sources and style can enumerate the repository for similar detections and common query patterns. The detection agent can autonomously test the rules against live staging environments and adjust for any syntax errors or false positives it may turn up. The final output is generated onto a new branch ready for a detection engineer to review and put finishing touches on. This also has implications in other areas of the SOC, such as smooth integration into automated threat hunting ( ATHF ) and much more. Internally, I maintain a heavily modified fork of ATHF that runs on the toolchain discussed in this article for producing timely threat hunts. Potential Pitfalls In this kind of environment, ensuring mistakes don’t slip through the validation phase is absolutely critical, as the potential impact is now much larger. For this reason, QA needs to be rigorously implemented. Some of the methods we utilise: Branch protection Linting tests Automated staging against representative lab environments Required Approvers CI/CD security scanning Robust secret management for agents Agent sandboxing It’s also important that, if you choose to adopt a similar practice, you go through the effort of hand-selecting the rules you want to manage as code. There is an element of “wiping the slate clean” involved where we decided which rules we’d keep, and which rules offered little value (or just weren’t worth the time to update). It was then a very long and arduous process to manually transition each environment onto the new ruleset without compromising on detection capability. The Detection Engineering Frontend One of the many benefits AI has given us is the ability to create bespoke applications for specific purposes. Detection as Code is wonderful but not everyone likes engaging with a Git repository and raw markdown (especially when you want to open up to non-technical folks). Thus, the need for a frontend was born. Below is a fictionalised version of the ‘Detection Grid’, the part of the app which SOC analysts interface with for viewing rules. Here they can filter the list down, view alert stats (plugged into live ITSM data), and view the content packs a detection belongs to. A rule may be drilled down into to reveal its metadata and documentation, alongside a summary of how the alert is typically closed and the reasoning behind each closure: The metadata of a rule and alert volume stats. AI generated summary of closure reasons and the documentation section rendered from the markdown file in the DaC repository. Of course, a MITRE gap analysis tool is provided as well. By bundling the full MITRE STIX library into your app, you can do all kinds of enrichment on the info within your detection library. This is probably only 5% of the capabilities of the platform I’ve built around Detection as Code, but the point is that Detection as Code gives you an organic knowledge base of detection and security information you can build on top of. You can overlay threat hunting, gap analysis, data integrity, reporting, testing and validation and so much more. Detection as Code in 2026 is more than just version control, it’s a fusion centre for your whole SOC. I hope this article has given you some reading material and given you some food for thought on where you might take your Detection as Code implementation in the future. A big shoutout to NVISO and Cauchy who directly inspired the design of my particular configuration. Please consider reading them and the other authors on this publication, as without them none of this would have been possible. Implementing Detection as Code as a multi-platform MSSP was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

platform: sentinel

  - Instance Deletion
  - Instance Modification

  - DC0076
  - DC0081
  - DC0073
  - DC0083

## Check for ...

AzureActivity

...

| Field Name | Data Type | Description |
|------------|-----------|-------------|

Autodoxing ( permalink ) After 25 years of fighting for human rights amid the wreckage of bad tech policy, I'm here to tell you that the road to hell is paved with badly thought-through tech policy. The most galling thing about this wreckage is that it was both foreseeable and foreseen. Back when Sun Microsystems CEO Scott McNealy was telling the world "Privacy is dead, get over it," digital rights advocates were saying, "Not only are digital tools pretty dang good at helping you protect your privacy, but a society-wide abolition of privacy sets us up for infinite harms long into the future": https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/31/losing-the-crypto-wars/#surveillance-monopolism It wasn't just business leaders who hated privacy, it was also our political classes. Bill Clinton tried to put a backdoor into every microchip (no, really): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clipper_chip The NSA managed to enact a total prohibition on civilian access to working encryption, on the grounds that we're all safer if our spooks can spy on "bad guys" even if that means that every creep, petty crook, corporate or state-sponsored spy, and mafia can spy on us : https://pluralistic.net/2026/04/09/bernstein-2/#win-some-lose-some Even after that ban was overturned, governments encouraged the private sector to spy on us without limit, precaution or permission. Those private-sector troves of intimate, compromising data about every person alive constitute a warrantless, off-the-books surveillance system that cops, spies and government agencies can tap at will: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/13/petards-r-us/#nobus To protect these surveillance capabilities, private firms and governments colluded to pass "anticircumvention" laws that make it illegal to reverse engineer our devices and apps to add privacy blockers to them, with the effect that every device we own and every app we use spies on us constantly: https://pluralistic.net/2024/03/12/market-failure/#car-wars At the same time, states either failed to pass new privacy laws (as in the USA, where federal consumer privacy law was last updated in 1988), or passed privacy laws that went unenforced (as in the EU, where "pretending to be Irish" allows US tech giants to flout EU privacy law): https://pluralistic.net/2023/05/15/finnegans-snooze/#dirty-old-town Our surveillance free-for-all world is objectively very bad. Over and over, companies and agencies who have been permitted to nonconsensually harvest and retain our data demonstrate that they are not capable of keeping that data safe, and no matter how badly they fuck up, nothing changes. It's been nearly a decade since Equifax doxed 148 million Americans and not only is the company still in business, they've been permitted to buy up and absorb more commercial surveillance firms. US regulators let Equifax buy Teletrack in 2021. Canadian regulators let them buy the Food Industry Credit Bureau in 2023. The same year, Brazilian regulators let Equifax buy Boa Vista Serviços. This all despite the fact that Equifax blamed its breach on shitty security practices after a string of mergers that led to it haphazardly combining databases from newly acquired surveillance companies. Data isn't the new oil. Data is the new oily rag: profitable only if you can warehouse it in vast quantities under unsafe conditions and have society pick up the bill for every conflagration: https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-zucks-empire-of-oily-rags/ Equifax is a serial reoffender, but rather than getting the corporate death-penalty, they've been made to pay coins-down-the-back-of-the-sofa fines that amount to a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of the costs they imposed on society by amassing these vast, flaming storehouses of oily rags. Why wouldn't Equifax reoffend? Our policymakers keep demanding less privacy, not more, and their indifference to the consequences is (almost) comical. Take Malcolm Turnbull, the former Australian Prime Minister who uttered what remains, without a doubt, the single stupidest thing anyone anywhere has ever said about tech policy. Like many of his peers before, during, and since his reign, Turnbull had been trying to outlaw working encryption, insisting that every device have a Bill Clinton-esque back-door for the purpose of spying on "bad guys." When told that the laws of mathematics dictated that any measure that let Australia's cops spy on "bad guys" would also let bad guys spy on Australians, Turnbull replied, "The laws of mathematics are very commendable, but the only law that applies in Australia is the law of Australia": https://www.newscientist.com/article/2140747-laws-of-mathematics-dont-apply-here-says-australian-pm/ We could laugh Turnbull off…if he was an outlier. But while Turnbull had the world's stupidest rejoinder to the scientifically irrefutable fact that banning encryption will let bad guys hack everything , he was hardly alone in wanting to ban encryption. Banning encryption is current policy in Canada: https://blog.mozilla.org/netpolicy/2026/10/08/canadas-bill-c-22-threatens-encryption-users-privacy-and-the-security-of-digital-economies/ It's also current policy in the UK: https://pluralistic.net/2023/03/05/theyre-still-trying-to-ban-cryptography/ And in the EU: https://fightchatcontrol.eu/ The difference between Malcolm Turnbull and, say, Canadian PM Mark Carney is that Turnbull was stupid enough to try to defend his ban on encryption, while Carney simply shakes his head at his critics' naivete and continues to press forward with his catastrophic proposal to welcome every cybercriminal in the world to hack every morsel of Canadian data. When it comes to bad privacy policy, our political classes aren't content to rest on their laurels: hardly a week goes by without news of a new way to encourage (or even require ) the private sector to recklessly collect and retain our data, despite the dead certainty that this data will eventually end up breaching and getting plastered all over the internet. Take "age verification" laws. There's no such thing as "age verification" – there's just spying on everyone , all the time, creating (even more) records of all of our internet activities: https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/19/shes-dead-of-course/#consensus-hallucination Every promise of "privacy preserving" age verification is bullshit: https://pluralistic.net/2025/08/14/bellovin/#wont-someone-think-of-the-cryptographers If you think kids are experiencing internet harms today, just wait until we expose them to the harms of having even more of their data harvested, stored, breached, and weaponized against them: https://pluralistic.net/2026/06/23/destroy-the-village/#to-save-it If you want to protect kids from algorithmic manipulation and targeting by bad actors, what about banning spying on kids so no one can target them? https://made-not-found-by-danah-boyd.ghost.io/no-one-paid-me-to-disagree-with-jonathan-haidt-it-was-teenagers-who-taught-me-that-he-was-wrong/ Now, at this point, you might be thinking, "How can we know who the kids are so we know who not to spy on?" You can't. In order to not spy on kids, you'd just have to not spy on anyone : https://pluralistic.net/2023/04/09/how-to-make-a-child-safe-tiktok/ "Don't spy on anyone" is the kind of thing that has a reasonable chance of enhancing online privacy. But in the time-honored tradition of "we've tried nothing and we're all out of ideas," governments keep finding ways to make digital privacy worse , for example, by procuring Flock cameras for every lamp-post: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/09/high-crime-lmao-how-cops-are-treating-mass-surveillance-joke And then there's UK Labour: after the success of a pilot program for an incredibly effective and safe privacy-preserving way of analyzing the country's health records for research processes, they commissioned the Goldacre Report to evaluate the possibility of making this permanent: https://pluralistic.net/2024/03/08/the-fire-of-orodruin/#are-we-the-baddies After that report was completed and had a chance to be metabolized by policymakers, Labour acted upon it…by throwing it out and handing all of the country's health data to Palantir, a serial mishandler of data and violator of privacy: https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/30/legal-objections-palantir-nhs-platform-handling-data Here's the scariest thing about bad privacy policy: it has a long fuse. The harms of commercial and private-sector digital surveillance can occur years or even decades after the decision to permit it. There's a straight line from the post-9/11 decision to encourage public agencies to gather, merge and warehouse data on every person in America, and the ability of ICE ethnic cleansing squads to break down people's doors and drag them off to concentration camps; just as there's a straight line from the decision to do nothing about the breach of every Social Security Number and the later theft of all Social Security data by adolescent DOGE criminals: https://www.pcmag.com/news/is-your-ssn-in-the-national-public-data-breach-heres-how-to-find-out But despite how obvious these connections are, the fact that they're separated by a lot of time and space provides our policymakers with cover for making terrible decisions with foreseeably terrible outcomes. As a society, we lack object permanence, the ability to connect acts in the past with present-day phenomena. When the press reports on a "Black October" of catastrophic, AI-fueled data breaches and hack attacks, they don't mention a generation of policymakers' indifference and hostility to information security: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake Policymakers benefit from politics' eternal now , in which disasters simply befall us, without any history or precedent or cause. Remember the One Big Beautiful Bill? Its architects designed it to wreak its worst harms after the midterms, with Medicaid work rules and food aid restrictions starting in December, and cuts to affordable housing and rural hospitals phasing in through the year: https://www.tumblr.com/mostlysignssomeportents/832146932089700352 Black October is going to give way to Black November, Black December, Black 2027, and the Black 2030s – a string of cybersecurity catastrophes that will befall us until policymakers decide that keeping us safe is more important than making it easy for them to attack their chosen "bad guys." Here's a preview of Black November: there's a new strain of the Volta infostealer malware that uses AI tools to dox you even as it hacks you: https://www.wired.com/story/kernel-panic-volta-autodoxer-ai-infostealer-malware/ How that works: your computer gets hacked and your data gets stolen, then it gets merged with breach data from Ticketmaster, Disney, AT&T and other companies that have recklessly compiled vast troves of data on all of us, stored it insecurely, and leaked it onto the internet where it will live forever. Volta's makers prompt their LLM "to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim." This lets the criminals prioritize their victims based on the expected return from exploiting them. It augments this dossier by combing through your Gmail as well as your Doordash and Uber Eats profiles. This merged data makes it much easier for criminals to call you up or email you (or have a chatbot call you up or email you) and trick you into giving up even more data: https://pluralistic.net/2024/02/05/cyber-dunning-kruger/#swiss-cheese-security Volta seems especially interested in younger internet users, targeting "Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions." AI capabilities have made infostealers much worse, but the reason for that new potency lies in how AI capabilities are supercharged by breach data that is the foreseeable and foreseen consequence of generations of hostility to privacy on the part of policymakers and corporations who responded to the incentives policymakers created. We are living in the age of oily rags. For decades we fucked around with letting the private sector warehouse our data and weaken our security so that public sector agencies could plunder our data and our computers at will. Now, we keep finding out that everything is on fire. It's going to take a long time to fix this, but we can do it. We can build more secure systems. We can make it much more of a legal ball-ache for companies to gather our data in the first place, and we can legalize and promote the creation of privacy blockers for browsers, phones, computers, cars, thermostats and smart speakers. We can enact corporate death-penalties for breaches to reflect the true societal cost of warehousing our data. We can ban Flock cameras and tear down the post-9/11 "fusion centers" that neatly package up our data for use by DOGE fascists and ICE thugs. We can ban our spy agencies from hoarding defects in widely used software, and instead require them to divulge these bugs so vendors can fix them: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOBUS And before we do any of that, we can just stop making it worse by ending the campaigns to require companies to spy on us and deliberately introduce security defects into their products.
